The rounds — how money arrives
The rounds — how money arrives

Angel investor#

A person investing their own money, usually the first check a company ever takes.

Picture this: a founder you met through Grid110 needs $50K to build a prototype. No fund is going to write that check. You do, personally. That's angel investing — and it's what I'm doing now.

Why it matters

Angels are the only source of capital available before there is anything to diligence. That makes them structurally important — most companies that later raise institutional money were funded first by someone writing a personal cheque on judgment alone.

It also means the discipline is different. An angel has no LPs, no committee, and no mandate, so the decision is entirely their own. That is freedom and it is also the reason angel portfolios are so unevenly constructed.

What it looks like in practice

The realistic path is a portfolio, not a bet. Under the power law, a handful of cheques will produce almost all the return, which means concentration into two or three names is a good way to get nothing. Twenty to thirty positions is the number most experienced angels converge on.

The other lever is access. Angels who invest where they have genuine domain expertise or a real network see better deals earlier, and at pre-seed being early is most of the edge.

Where it goes wrong

  • Investing in three companies and calling it a portfolio. The power law requires more shots.
  • Writing cheques into rounds you didn't source, on terms someone else negotiated, without reading them.
  • Investing money that is needed within ten years. This asset class is illiquid for longer than people plan for.
  • Confusing being helpful with being informed — enthusiasm for a founder is not diligence.

Related terms

SyndicateA group investing together in one deal, usually organized by one person.Operator-angelAn angel who built or ran something before writing checks. The dominant profile at the top.Pre-seedThe earliest institutional round, usually before real revenue exists. The rounds — how money arrives

Pre-seed#

The earliest institutional round, usually before real revenue exists. Money to build the first version and hire two or three people.

Picture this: two founders, a demo that works on a good day, twelve users who love it. They raise $750K to spend a year finding out whether anyone will pay.

Why it matters

Pre-seed is the stage where the underwriting is almost entirely about the team and the timing, because there is no traction to analyse. It is also the stage where ownership is cheapest, which is the entire argument for being there.

The stage has become a real institutional category rather than a gap. Seed rounds grew large enough that a distinct earlier round was needed, and pre-seed filled it — which means the vocabulary of a seed round from a decade ago now describes a pre-seed one.

What it looks like in practice

A typical pre-seed funds twelve to eighteen months of building toward the evidence a seed round wants: a working product, early users, and a defensible story about who the customer is. Almost always on a SAFE rather than a priced round, because the legal cost of pricing a company this early is not worth paying.

The judgment is about the founder's rate of learning, not their current state. What matters is whether they have gone from nothing to something quickly, and whether their answers changed when the evidence did.

Where it goes wrong

  • Raising a pre-seed large enough that the seed round has to clear an unreasonable bar.
  • Expecting pre-seed metrics to predict anything. At this stage they mostly don't.
  • Treating the milestone plan as fixed, when the point of the stage is to find out what's true.
  • Underestimating how long the next raise takes, and running the plan to the last month.

Related terms

The rounds — how money arrives

Seed#

The round that funds the search for product-market fit. There's usually a product and some early customers, but the business model isn't proven.

Picture this: same company a year later — $8K a month in revenue, 40 paying customers. They raise $3M to figure out if that becomes $80K a month.

Why it matters

Seed is where a company stops asking whether anyone wants this and starts asking whether the wanting can be turned into a business. The money buys the search for product-market fit, and the round is sized to give that search enough time.

It is also the stage where the evidence bar becomes real. A pre-seed can be funded on a story; a seed usually needs something that happened — users, revenue, retention, or a named set of design partners.

What it looks like in practice

Seed rounds are large enough now that they often behave like the Series A of a decade ago: a real lead, real diligence, sometimes a priced round with a board seat. The structure varies more than at pre-seed, which makes it worth being explicit about what is being bought.

The milestone that matters is whatever unlocks a Series A, and that is usually evidence of repeatability — the same motion producing the same result more than once, without the founder doing all of it personally.

Where it goes wrong

  • Raising a seed against a Series A bar that has moved since the plan was written.
  • Spending the round scaling before fit exists, which is the classic way to die with money in the bank.
  • Treating early revenue as fit without checking whether it retains.
  • Sizing the round to eighteen months when the milestone realistically takes twenty-four.

The rounds — how money arrives

Series A#

The first big round. You're no longer proving the thing works; you're proving it scales.

Picture this: $150K a month in revenue growing 15% monthly. They raise $12M to hire a sales team and find out if growth survives contact with a real go-to-market motion.

Why it matters

Series A is where the question changes from whether it works to whether it scales, and the evidence required changes with it. Investors are underwriting a repeatable motion — acquisition that works without the founder, retention that holds, and unit economics that survive being multiplied.

It is also where governance arrives properly: a priced round, a real board, protective provisions, and a set of rights that will persist for the life of the company.

What it looks like in practice

The bar is usually expressed in revenue but is really about consistency. Growth that comes from one channel, repeatably, with retention behind it, beats a larger number assembled from unrelated deals.

The gap between seed and Series A is where most companies die, and the cause is usually a mismatch between what the seed round funded and what the A round expects. That gap has widened as A-round bars rose.

Where it goes wrong

  • Optimising for the revenue number and ignoring retention, which is what actually gets diligenced.
  • Raising on a single large customer that makes the growth look repeatable when it isn't.
  • Assuming the Series A bar is what it was when the seed was raised.
  • Treating the board that arrives with the round as a formality.

Related terms

The rounds — how money arrives

Series B, C, and beyond#

Progressively larger rounds for expansion — new markets, new products, sometimes preparing to go public. Series C can run into the hundreds of millions.

Picture this: the average US unicorn raises more than six VC rounds before it gets there. Nobody arrives in one jump.

Why it matters

Later rounds are where the preference stack gets heavy and where early investors find out whether their ownership survived. Each round adds dilution and adds its own preference ahead of common, which is why the payout math at exit can look nothing like the cap table.

For a pre-seed investor these rounds mostly matter as markups and as dilution. Without pro rata rights and reserves, a position that started at 8% can be well under 3% by the time anything is realised.

What it looks like in practice

The character of the rounds changes as they go: growth funds care about efficiency metrics rather than potential, and the diligence shifts from judgment to arithmetic. By Series C the company is being valued on numbers a spreadsheet can check.

The average US unicorn raises more than six rounds before it gets there, which is the practical argument for reserves — the companies that work will ask for money many more times.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming a markup is a return. It's an unrealised number until there's a distribution.
  • Not modelling the preference stack that has accumulated by the later rounds.
  • Failing to reserve for follow-ons, and being diluted out of the one that works.
  • Reading a large round as validation without looking at the terms attached to it.

Related terms

The rounds — how money arrives

Bridge round#

A small round to get a company from where it is to its next real round or milestone. Usually on a SAFE or note rather than a priced round.

Picture this: a company has five months of cash and needs nine to hit the metrics that justify a Series A. Existing investors put in $1M to bridge the gap.

Why it matters

A bridge is a bet by existing investors that the company is close. That makes it one of the clearest signals available — insiders with the most information choosing to put more money in, or choosing not to.

The distinction that matters is whether it's a bridge or a pier. A bridge reaches something: a defined milestone that unlocks the next round. A pier extends into open water and runs out of money slightly later.

What it looks like in practice

Bridges are usually done on a SAFE or note rather than a priced round, because pricing the company mid-crisis is both hard and unhelpful. Terms often include a discount to the next round or warrant coverage to compensate for the risk.

The right time to raise one is well before it's needed. A bridge negotiated with six months of runway gets reasonable terms; the same conversation at two months does not.

Where it goes wrong

  • Raising a bridge with no defined milestone, which just moves the problem two quarters out.
  • Waiting until the position is desperate, when the terms reflect it.
  • Reading insider participation as a formality. If existing investors won't bridge, that's the signal.
  • Stacking multiple bridges, each with its own discount, until the next round's cap table is unworkable.

The rounds — how money arrives

Down round#

Raising at a lower valuation than the previous round. Painful, and the moment anti-dilution clauses come alive.

Picture this: a company raised at $40M in 2021. In 2023 the best offer is $18M. Everyone who invested at $40M just watched their stake shrink in value — and if they had ratchet protection, everyone else's stake shrinks in size to compensate.

Why it matters

A down round is where the protective terms stop being theoretical. Anti-dilution provisions fire, ownership shifts, and the mechanics that were negotiated years earlier determine who absorbs the loss.

The second-order effect is usually worse than the arithmetic. Down rounds damage morale, make options underwater, and signal to the market — which is why companies fight so hard to avoid them, sometimes by accepting structure that is worse than the lower price would have been.

What it looks like in practice

The mechanism to understand is the anti-dilution adjustment: full ratchet repricing earlier investors to the new price, or the far more common weighted average, which adjusts partially based on how much new money comes in.

Structure is the alternative to a lower headline price, and it is frequently the worse deal. A flat round with a 2x participating preference can cost common shareholders more than an honest down round would have.

Where it goes wrong

  • Accepting punitive structure to preserve a headline valuation.
  • Not modelling what the anti-dilution adjustment actually does to the cap table.
  • Letting options stay deep underwater rather than repricing, and losing the team.
  • Treating it as a failure of narrative rather than a repricing that reflects reality.

The rounds — how money arrives

Accelerator#

A program that gives small checks, mentorship, and a demo day in exchange for equity.

Picture this: Y Combinator writes $500K and takes about 1 in 100 applicants — roughly 150–200 companies out of 10,000+ applications. Plug and Play, Grid110, and Material Change are accelerators I came through.

Why it matters

Accelerators function as a filter and a signal. The selective ones have seen enough companies that acceptance carries information, which is why the strongest programmes have such disproportionate outcomes — the filter is doing much of the work.

For an investor they are a dealflow channel with known economics and known timing. The cost is that everyone else sees the same companies at the same demo day, on the same terms, which compresses the advantage of being there.

What it looks like in practice

The terms are usually a small cheque for a fixed percentage, plus mentorship and a demo day. The value varies enormously by programme: at the top the network and signal are worth far more than the money; further down the equity is expensive for what arrives.

The useful question about any programme is what its alumni do next — whether they raise, from whom, and at what rate. That number says more than the curriculum does.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating acceptance into any accelerator as equivalent signal. The distribution is extremely wide.
  • Sourcing only at demo day, where the price is set and competition is highest.
  • Ignoring how much equity a programme takes relative to what it provides.
  • Assuming the mentorship is the value. Usually it's the filter and the network.

The rounds — how money arrives

Lead investor#

The investor who sets the terms, does the deepest diligence, and usually takes the board seat. Everyone else follows their price.

Picture this: a $3M seed round where one fund puts in $2M and negotiates the term sheet. Six angels put in the rest at the same terms without negotiating anything.

Why it matters

The lead does the work everyone else free-rides on: the diligence, the price, the terms, and usually the board seat. That's why rounds stall without one — nobody wants to set the price, and everybody is willing to follow it.

For a small fund or an angel, the decision to lead or follow is strategic. Leading buys ownership, information, and a relationship. Following buys access at someone else's price with someone else's diligence.

What it looks like in practice

A lead typically takes a substantial share of the round, negotiates the term sheet, and takes the board seat. The commitment signals to the rest of the market that someone with real money at stake did the work.

The quality of the lead matters beyond the cheque. A lead with a strong reputation makes the rest of the round easier to fill, and a lead who negotiates aggressive terms leaves a structure the company lives with for a decade.

Where it goes wrong

  • Following into a round without reading the terms the lead negotiated.
  • Assuming a well-known lead did thorough diligence. Sometimes they didn't.
  • Trying to lead without the capital to fill a meaningful share of the round.
  • Choosing a lead on price alone, when the board relationship lasts far longer.

Related terms

The rounds — how money arrives

Syndicate#

A group investing together in one deal, usually organized by one person.

Picture this: an angel finds a deal, can only write $25K, but brings twelve friends who add $300K. The company gets one line on its cap table instead of thirteen.

Why it matters

Syndicates let a small cheque behave like a large one. The organiser gets to write a meaningful amount into a deal they sourced, the company gets one line on the cap table instead of a dozen, and the participants get access they couldn't reach individually.

The economics matter: the organiser usually takes carry on the syndicate, which makes this a way to build a track record and an investor base before raising an actual fund.

What it looks like in practice

Mechanically this is usually an SPV — a single-purpose vehicle that holds the investment, with the participants as members. That structure is what keeps the company's cap table clean and gives the organiser a defined role.

The reputational dynamic is the thing to understand. A syndicate lead is putting their judgment in front of their network repeatedly, which is a much faster feedback loop than a fund's ten- year cycle.

Where it goes wrong

  • Syndicating a deal you haven't diligenced, on the strength of who else is in it.
  • Ignoring the SPV's fees and carry when calculating the return to participants.
  • Building a syndicate of people who never actually fund their commitments.
  • Assuming syndicate access substitutes for the relationship a lead has with the company.

The paperwork — how the money is structured
The paperwork — how the money is structured

Term sheet#

A short, non-binding document laying out the deal: how much, at what price, and what rights the investor gets. The blueprint the lawyers build from.

Picture this: two pages that say $2M at a $10M pre-money valuation, 1x liquidation preference, one board seat, pro rata rights. Nobody's committed yet, but everyone now knows the shape of the deal.

Why it matters

The term sheet is short, non-binding, and decides almost everything. Once it's signed, the definitive documents are largely an exercise in writing down what it already says — which means the leverage is all before signature, not after.

The parts founders focus on are price and amount. The parts that determine control and payout are the preference, the protective provisions, the board, and the anti-dilution, and those are the ones worth spending negotiating capital on.

What it looks like in practice

The binding elements are usually confidentiality, exclusivity, and expenses — the no-shop in particular, which stops the company from talking to anyone else while the deal is documented.

Working from NVCA-standard terms shortens the process enormously, because the negotiation narrows to the things that actually differ rather than the whole document.

Where it goes wrong

  • Negotiating price hard and accepting everything else as standard.
  • Signing with a long no-shop and no deadline for closing.
  • Assuming non-binding means nothing is committed. Exclusivity is binding and it costs you leverage.
  • Not modelling the exit waterfall the terms produce before signing them.

The paperwork — how the money is structured

SAFE#

Simple Agreement for Future Equity. You give money now and get shares later, when the company raises a priced round. No valuation is set today, which is why it's fast and cheap.

Picture this: you wire $50K on a SAFE. Eighteen months later the company raises a Series A and your SAFE converts into actual shares at that point — not before.

Why it matters

The SAFE exists because pricing a company with no revenue is guesswork, and paying lawyers to do it properly costs more than the round justifies. It defers the valuation to the first priced round and lets the money arrive in days rather than months.

The trade is that dilution becomes invisible until it lands. A founder who has sold five SAFEs at different caps often does not know what they own, and the reckoning arrives all at once at conversion.

What it looks like in practice

Y Combinator introduced the SAFE in 2013 and moved to the post-money version in 2018. The change matters: post-money SAFEs fix the investor's percentage, so all the dilution from subsequent SAFEs falls on the founder rather than being shared.

The right discipline is to model conversion continuously — every SAFE sold, at every cap, against a realistic next-round price. That is a spreadsheet exercise that prevents a very common surprise.

Where it goes wrong

  • Stacking SAFEs at different caps without modelling the combined conversion.
  • Not knowing whether the SAFE is pre- or post-money, which changes who bears the dilution.
  • Treating the cap as a valuation. It's a ceiling on conversion price, not a price.
  • Raising so much on SAFEs that the priced round starts with most of the company already spoken for.

The paperwork — how the money is structured

Valuation cap#

The maximum company value at which your SAFE converts. It protects you from the company getting so valuable that your early risk buys almost nothing.

Picture this: you invest $500K on a SAFE with a $10M post-money cap. The Series A prices the company at $40M. Without the cap you'd get 1.25% of the company. With it, you get 5% — because your conversion is calculated as if the company were worth $10M.

Why it matters

The cap is what rewards the investor for going early. Without it, money that arrived eighteen months before the priced round converts at the same price as money that arrived the week before — which is not a deal anyone would take.

It's also the term most often mistaken for a valuation. A $8M cap is not a claim that the company is worth $8M; it's a ceiling on the price at which this particular money converts.

What it looks like in practice

At conversion the investor gets the better of the cap price or the round price. If the round prices below the cap, the cap is irrelevant and everyone converts at the round price.

Where a cap and a discount both exist, the standard is that the investor takes whichever produces more shares — not both. Reading which applies is worth doing before signing rather than at conversion.

Where it goes wrong

  • Quoting the cap as the company's valuation.
  • Setting a cap so high it provides no real protection to the early investor.
  • Setting it so low that the priced round starts with heavy dilution already committed.
  • Assuming cap and discount stack. They usually don't.

Post-money vs pre-money SAFE#

On a post-money SAFE, your percentage is locked and later SAFEs dilute the founders, not you. On a pre-money SAFE, later SAFEs dilute you too.

Picture this: post-money is the modern standard and the one founders most often underestimate — a common mistake is modeling dilution with pre-money math, signing a post-money SAFE, and discovering 5–10% more dilution than expected.

Why it matters

This is the single most consequential piece of small print in early-stage fundraising, and the one founders most often get wrong. A post-money SAFE fixes the investor's percentage of the company; a pre-money one doesn't.

The practical effect: with post-money SAFEs, every additional SAFE you sell dilutes you and not the existing SAFE holders. Sell enough of them and the founder's stake at conversion is materially smaller than the arithmetic they did at the time.

What it looks like in practice

Y Combinator moved to post-money in 2018 specifically to make the investor's ownership certain and calculable. That certainty is real and it comes directly out of the founder's share.

The discipline is to maintain a running conversion model — all instruments, all caps, against a realistic priced round — and update it every time another SAFE is signed. The number to watch is founder ownership post-conversion, not the cap on any individual note.

Where it goes wrong

  • Not knowing which version you're signing. They look almost identical.
  • Assuming later SAFEs dilute earlier ones. Under post-money they don't.
  • Modelling each SAFE in isolation rather than the whole stack at once.
  • Discovering the combined effect at the priced round, when nothing can be changed.

The paperwork — how the money is structured

Discount#

A percentage off the next round's price, as thanks for going early.

Picture this: a 20% discount means when the Series A prices at $10M, you convert as if it were $8M. If your SAFE has both a cap and a discount, you get whichever is better for you.

Why it matters

A discount is the simplest version of the same idea as a cap: money that arrived earlier converts cheaper. Where a cap protects against a very high round price, a discount just gives a fixed percentage advantage regardless of price.

On its own a discount is weak protection. If the company does extremely well and prices the next round very high, a 20% discount on a huge number is still a huge number — which is exactly the scenario a cap exists to handle.

What it looks like in practice

Typical discounts run 10–25%, with 20% the common default. In a bridge, discounts are often the main compensation for taking the risk of going in before the round is settled.

Where both a cap and a discount are present, the investor takes whichever gives more shares. Rarely both, and the drafting should say so explicitly.

Where it goes wrong

  • Relying on a discount alone in a company that might price very high.
  • Assuming discount and cap stack unless the document says they do.
  • Setting different discounts across a stack of notes, which complicates conversion for no benefit.
  • Treating the discount as the whole negotiation when the cap matters more.

The paperwork — how the money is structured

Convertible note#

Like a SAFE, but technically a loan — it has an interest rate and a maturity date. Mostly replaced by SAFEs at pre-seed because it's more complicated.

Why it matters

The convertible note predates the SAFE and does the same job with more machinery: it's debt, so it carries interest and a maturity date. Those two features are the whole difference, and they matter when things go badly.

A maturity date is a real obligation. If the company hasn't raised a priced round by then, the note is technically due — which in practice means a renegotiation, an extension, or a conversion on whatever terms can be agreed under pressure.

What it looks like in practice

Notes remain common in bridges and in markets where the SAFE never fully took over. The economic terms mirror SAFEs — cap, discount — with interest accruing and converting alongside principal.

The maturity date is the term to watch in diligence. A company with notes maturing inside the next year has a deadline that will shape its fundraising whether or not the founder frames it that way.

Where it goes wrong

  • Ignoring maturity dates until they arrive, when the leverage sits entirely with the holder.
  • Forgetting accrued interest converts too, which increases dilution beyond the principal.
  • Using a note where a SAFE would do, and paying for the extra complexity.
  • Assuming holders will always extend. Usually they do, and the terms change.

Priced round#

A round where the company's value is actually set and you buy shares at a real per-share price. Slower and more expensive than a SAFE because everything gets negotiated.

Why it matters

A priced round is where the company actually gets valued, preferred stock gets issued, and all the deferred questions from every SAFE get settled at once. It's also where governance arrives — a board, protective provisions, and a set of rights that persist.

The reason it takes longer and costs more is that it's the real thing. Everything the SAFE deferred has to be decided, documented, and agreed by everyone.

What it looks like in practice

The mechanics: a pre-money valuation is agreed, new preferred shares are issued, all outstanding SAFEs and notes convert, and the option pool is usually topped up — typically out of the pre- money, which means founders bear it.

The option pool shuffle is the part that surprises people. Agreeing a pre-money valuation and then agreeing a 15% post-round pool means the effective price is lower than the headline, because the pool comes out of the existing holders.

Where it goes wrong

  • Negotiating pre-money without settling the option pool, which changes the effective price.
  • Not modelling how the SAFE stack converts before agreeing the round price.
  • Underestimating the legal cost and time relative to a SAFE round.
  • Treating the governance terms as boilerplate because the price was the hard part.

Incorporation and the 83(b) election#

Setting the company up as a corporation, issuing founder stock, and filing the 83(b) election within 30 days so tax is assessed at today's near-zero value.

Picture this: two founders issue themselves 8,000,000 shares at $0.0001 — worth $800 total. They file 83(b) within 30 days and pay tax on $800. Miss the deadline and they are taxed on the value at each vesting date instead, which for a company that works can be a career-defining bill.

Why it matters

The 30-day 83(b) window is one of the few genuinely unforgivable deadlines in startup formation. There is no extension, no cure, and no workaround — and the cost of missing it scales with how well the company does.

For an investor this is a data-room hygiene check that occasionally uncovers something serious. Missing 83(b) filings, founder stock never actually issued, or IP sitting with an individual rather than the company are the kind of problems that are cheap to fix at pre-seed and expensive at Series A.

What it looks like in practice

The sequence is: incorporate, issue founder stock at a nominal price, put it on a vesting schedule, file 83(b) with the IRS within 30 days of issuance, and assign all relevant IP to the company. Standard formation packages handle all of it, and the cost of doing it properly is a rounding error against the cost of not.

The election applies to stock subject to vesting. Options are a different instrument with different timing, which is a common source of confusion when early employees ask.

Where it goes wrong

  • Missing the 30-day window. It cannot be fixed afterwards.
  • Filing 83(b) but keeping no proof of mailing, which leaves you unable to demonstrate it.
  • Issuing founder stock late, after the company already has value, so the nominal price no longer works.
  • Leaving IP assigned to individuals — especially work done before incorporation.

Delaware C-Corp vs. LLC#

The two common US structures. Venture-backed companies are almost always Delaware C-Corps; LLCs are for businesses that will not raise institutional equity.

Picture this: an LLC with a great product tries to raise a seed round. The fund's LPs cannot hold pass-through income without tax consequences, so the deal requires converting first — weeks of legal work and a tax event, at exactly the moment speed mattered.

Why it matters

Structure decides whether an institutional round is straightforward or a project. Funds expect Delaware C-Corp because the case law is deep and predictable, preferred stock works the way everyone assumes, and the tax treatment doesn't create problems for their LPs.

It also gates QSBS, which only applies to C-Corp stock. For a founder, choosing an LLC to save early tax can forfeit an exclusion worth millions later.

What it looks like in practice

LLCs make sense for consulting firms, real-estate vehicles, and anything designed to distribute profits rather than compound value toward an exit. C-Corps make sense for anything intending to raise venture money and issue options.

Converting an LLC to a C-Corp is possible and routinely done, but it costs time and legal fees at the worst moment, and it can reset the QSBS holding clock. Starting in the right structure is cheaper than fixing it.

Where it goes wrong

  • Choosing an LLC for early tax simplicity when institutional funding is the plan.
  • Assuming conversion is trivial. It is a real project with real cost.
  • Incorporating in your home state to save a few hundred dollars, then converting to Delaware anyway.
  • Forgetting that the QSBS clock starts at C-Corp stock issuance.

NVCA model documents#

The industry-standard set of venture financing templates, published free by the National Venture Capital Association.

Picture this: a seed round on NVCA docs with a short list of negotiated terms closes in three weeks. The same round on a lawyer's bespoke paper generates two extra rounds of redlines and $40,000 in fees arguing about clauses everyone would have accepted as standard.

Why it matters

Standardisation is the reason a priced round can close in weeks rather than months. When both sides start from the same base, negotiation narrows to the handful of terms that actually differ — price, board, preference — instead of re-litigating boilerplate.

Deviation from the model docs is itself a signal. It isn't automatically bad, but every departure should have a reason someone can state out loud.

What it looks like in practice

The set covers the term sheet, stock purchase agreement, certificate of incorporation, investor rights agreement, voting agreement, and right of first refusal and co-sale agreement. They're updated periodically and are free to download.

At pre-seed most rounds happen on SAFEs and never touch these. They become relevant at the first priced round, which is why founders often encounter them for the first time under time pressure.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming model docs means no negotiation. The economics still have to be agreed.
  • Accepting non-standard terms without asking why they were changed.
  • Paying for bespoke drafting on a standard early round.
  • Using an outdated version, which quietly reintroduces terms the market has moved past.

IP assignment agreement#

The document transferring ownership of work product from a founder, employee, or contractor to the company.

Picture this: a contractor built the original prototype in 2023 and was paid, but never signed an assignment. At Series A diligence it emerges that he still owns the core code. He now has enormous leverage and knows it.

Why it matters

In the US, paying someone does not by itself transfer copyright in what they made. Absent a written assignment, a contractor generally owns their work. For a company whose entire value is its technology, that's not a paperwork problem — it's a question of whether the company owns the thing it's selling.

It's one of the most common diligence findings at seed and Series A, and one of the most expensive to fix late, because the leverage sits entirely with the person who didn't sign.

What it looks like in practice

Everyone who touches the product signs before they start — founders, employees, contractors, advisors, the designer who did the logo. For work predating incorporation, founders sign an assignment covering it retroactively as part of formation.

The edge cases matter: work done on a previous employer's laptop or time can be claimed by that employer, and university affiliations often carry their own IP terms. Both are worth asking about directly in diligence.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming payment transfers ownership. It doesn't.
  • Missing contractors and freelancers, who are the most common gap.
  • Ignoring work done before incorporation or at a prior employer.
  • Discovering the gap during diligence, when the fix costs whatever the holder decides.

Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS)#

A US tax provision that can exclude a large share of capital gains on qualifying C-Corp stock held long enough — Section 1202.

Picture this: a founder holds qualifying stock for the required period and sells. A meaningful portion of the gain comes out federally tax-free. The same outcome through an LLC, or sold too early, is taxed in full.

Why it matters

QSBS is one of the largest tax benefits available to startup founders, employees, and early investors, and it's driven by decisions made at formation — entity type, when stock was issued, and how long it's held.

It also shapes behaviour at exit. A sale that would cross the holding threshold in two months is worth two months of patience, and founders who don't know the rule sometimes sign away a great deal of money without realising there was a choice.

What it looks like in practice

The conditions are specific: the issuer must be a domestic C-Corp, the stock acquired at original issuance rather than bought from someone else, the company under a gross asset ceiling at issuance, and the business in a qualifying trade — which excludes several service industries.

The thresholds and holding periods have been amended more than once, most recently in 2025, and they apply differently depending on when the stock was acquired. This is a check-with-a-tax- advisor area rather than a rule of thumb.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming it applies automatically. Every condition has to be met.
  • Selling shortly before the holding period is satisfied.
  • Operating as an LLC, which makes the stock ineligible.
  • Losing the documentation proving original issuance and the company's asset level at the time.

Ownership — who owns what, and how it shrinks

Pre-money valuation#

What the company is worth before the new money goes in.

Why it matters

Pre-money is the number that gets negotiated, and post-money is the number that determines ownership. Confusing them is the most common arithmetic error in a fundraise, and it always favours whoever understood it better.

The option pool makes it worse. A pool created out of the pre-money reduces the effective valuation without changing the headline, which is why the same nominal price can mean materially different ownership.

What it looks like in practice

The arithmetic is simply pre-money plus the amount raised equals post-money, and the investor's ownership is the amount raised divided by post-money. A $2M round on an $8M pre-money is 20% of the company, not 25%.

The negotiation that actually matters is pre-money and pool together. Agreeing one without the other leaves the most consequential number undecided.

Where it goes wrong

  • Agreeing a pre-money valuation without agreeing the option pool at the same time.
  • Quoting a valuation without saying which one it is.
  • Comparing your round's pre-money to another company's post-money.
  • Optimising for the headline number at the cost of the terms attached to it.

Post-money valuation#

Pre-money plus the new money.

Picture this: $8M pre-money, $2M invested → $10M post-money. The investor owns $2M ÷ $10M = 20%. Always check which number someone means; the difference is real money.

Why it matters

Post-money is what ownership is calculated from, which makes it the number that matters to an investor. It's also the number that sets the bar for the next round — a post-money that is too high relative to progress makes the following raise structurally harder.

For a fund it's the input to every ownership calculation and every markup. Getting it wrong propagates through the whole portfolio model.

What it looks like in practice

Post-money equals pre-money plus the round. Ownership equals the cheque divided by post-money — before accounting for any option pool created as part of the round, which dilutes everyone who was there before.

Post-money SAFEs use the same word for a related but distinct idea: the SAFE's post-money valuation fixes the holder's percentage at conversion, which is why the instrument behaves so differently from its pre-money predecessor.

Where it goes wrong

  • Calculating ownership off pre-money, which overstates it.
  • Ignoring the option pool when computing what you actually own after the round.
  • Setting a post-money that the next round's expected progress can't justify.
  • Reporting a markup based on a post-money that included a large pool top-up.

Cap table#

The spreadsheet of who owns what. Founders, employees, investors, and everyone's percentage.

Why it matters

The cap table records ownership, and people read it as a payout schedule. It isn't — the preference stack and the waterfall decide what anyone actually receives, and in a modest exit those can diverge from the percentages entirely.

A clean cap table is also a practical asset. Messy ones — dozens of small holders, undocumented promises, unassigned IP, missing 83(b) filings — slow rounds down and occasionally kill them.

What it looks like in practice

The useful version is fully diluted: all issued shares, all options granted and unallocated, all warrants, and all convertible instruments modelled at conversion. Anything less understates dilution.

It should be maintained continuously rather than reconstructed at each round. Companies that rebuild the cap table under time pressure during diligence are the ones that discover the problems at the worst moment.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reading percentages as a payout. The waterfall is what pays.
  • Keeping it on a spreadsheet that only one person updates.
  • Excluding unissued option pool and outstanding SAFEs from the fully diluted count.
  • Letting verbal equity promises accumulate outside the document.

Dilution#

Your percentage shrinking because new shares were created. It isn't theft — it's the cost of the company being worth more.

Picture this: you own 10% of a company worth $10M ($1M). They raise at $50M, and you're diluted to 8%. Your 8% is worth $4M. You own less of something much bigger.

Why it matters

Dilution is not a problem to be avoided — it's the cost of the capital that makes the company worth more. A smaller slice of a much bigger thing is the entire mechanism of venture. The failure is dilution without corresponding progress.

For an investor, dilution is what stands between an initial ownership percentage and the one that exists at exit. Without pro rata and reserves, that gap is large enough to change the fund's outcome.

What it looks like in practice

Sources compound: each priced round, each option pool top-up, each SAFE converting, each warrant exercised. A founding team at 100% commonly holds 10–20% by Series B, and that's a normal path rather than a bad one.

The lever an investor has is pro rata rights plus reserved capital. The lever a founder has is raising the right amount at the right time rather than the most available.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating dilution as something to minimise rather than something to spend well.
  • Forgetting the option pool, which is dilution that arrives without a cheque.
  • Modelling one round at a time rather than the full path to exit.
  • Holding pro rata rights and no reserves, which is the same as not having them.

Fully diluted shares#

The total share count if every option, warrant, and SAFE converted today. The honest denominator — always ask for percentages on a fully diluted basis.

Why it matters

Fully diluted is the only honest denominator. Ownership calculated on issued shares alone ignores the option pool, the warrants, and every convertible instrument — all of which will become shares.

It's also where quiet errors live. A percentage quoted on the wrong basis can be materially wrong, and it's the kind of error that survives until an acquisition makes it expensive.

What it looks like in practice

The count includes issued common and preferred, all options granted, the unallocated option pool, warrants, and convertible notes and SAFEs modelled at their conversion terms.

The unallocated pool is the item most often left out, and it's usually the largest. Excluding it makes every ownership percentage look better than it is.

Where it goes wrong

  • Quoting ownership on issued shares only.
  • Excluding the unallocated option pool from the count.
  • Ignoring SAFEs and notes because they haven't converted yet.
  • Using different bases in different documents, so the numbers never reconcile.

Option pool#

Shares set aside for future employees. Usually 10–20%.

Picture this: the "option pool shuffle" — an investor asks for a 15% pool to be created before the money goes in, which means it comes out of the founders' share, not the investor's. Standard practice, and worth knowing it's a negotiation, not a law of nature.

Why it matters

The option pool is how a company that can't pay market salaries competes for people, and it's dilution that arrives without any cash coming in. Where it comes from in a round is one of the more consequential negotiations founders don't realise they're having.

Created out of the pre-money, it's borne entirely by existing holders — which lowers the effective valuation below the headline. Created post-money, it's shared with the incoming investor.

What it looks like in practice

Pools are typically sized at 10–20% of the post-round company, informed by a hiring plan through to the next round. Investors usually push for enough to cover that plan so they aren't diluted by a top-up later.

Strike price comes from the 409A, which is why the timing of the appraisal relative to grants matters. Promising a strike price before the valuation refreshes is a common way to disappoint a new hire.

Where it goes wrong

  • Agreeing the pre-money before agreeing the pool size, which changes the effective price.
  • Sizing the pool from a hiring plan nobody believes.
  • Granting options against a stale 409A.
  • Leaving unallocated pool out of the fully diluted count.

Pro rata rights#

The right to invest again later to keep your percentage from shrinking.

Picture this: you own 5% after a seed round. At Series A you'd drop to 3.5%. Pro rata lets you write another check at the new price to stay at 5%. This is how a small early check keeps mattering in a company that works.

Why it matters

Pro rata is what allows an early investor to maintain ownership as the company raises more. Without it, a position that started meaningful is diluted through every subsequent round until it doesn't move the fund's outcome.

Under the power law this is close to the whole game for a small fund. The one company that works has to still be a meaningful position by the time it exits, and pro rata plus reserves is the only way that happens.

What it looks like in practice

The right is usually granted in the investor rights agreement, often limited to major investors above a threshold. It's a right to participate, not an obligation, and exercising it requires capital that has to have been reserved for the purpose.

In competitive later rounds pro rata gets squeezed — new investors want allocation, and existing holders are sometimes asked to waive. That's the moment the right proves whether it was real.

Where it goes wrong

  • Holding pro rata rights with no reserves to exercise them.
  • Accepting a threshold that excludes you from the right at the next round.
  • Waiving pro rata in the company's best interests without modelling what it costs the fund.
  • Assuming the right survives every round. Check whether it does.

Ownership target#

The percentage you're deliberately aiming to hold after investing. The discipline that connects your check size to the math.

Picture this: if you want 8% and the company is raising at a $12M post-money, your check needs to be about $960K. If you can only write $100K, you're not getting 8% — so either the target or the deal has to change.

Why it matters

The ownership target is what connects a fund's strategy to its arithmetic. Under the power law one company produces most of the return, so the question is whether the position in that company is large enough to return the fund.

It's the number that should drive cheque size, round selection, and reserve policy — and it's the one most often set by what was available rather than by what the model requires.

What it looks like in practice

The calculation runs backwards: what exit value is realistic, what ownership at exit would return the fund, and therefore what ownership at entry survives the expected dilution. That last step is where most targets are set too low.

A small fund can hit a meaningful target because the fund is small. A large fund needs either a large position or a much larger outcome, which is why fund size constrains strategy so tightly.

Where it goes wrong

  • Setting the target at entry without modelling dilution through to exit.
  • Taking whatever allocation is offered rather than what the model needs.
  • Ignoring that reserves are what defend the target.
  • Applying the same target across stages with very different dilution paths.

Vesting and the cliff#

Equity earned over time rather than granted outright. The cliff is the initial period where nothing vests at all, then a chunk vests at once.

Picture this: the standard is four years with a one-year cliff. Leave at month eleven and you own nothing. Stay to month twelve and 25% vests that day, with the rest arriving monthly for three more years.

Why it matters

Vesting is what stops a co-founder who leaves after five months from owning a third of the company forever — which is the single most destructive thing that can happen to a cap table, because it makes every future round harder to raise.

Investors require founder vesting for exactly this reason, and often reset it at the first priced round even for founders who have been there for years. That reset feels punitive and isn't; it's the price of everyone else's confidence that the team stays.

What it looks like in practice

Four years with a one-year cliff and monthly vesting thereafter is the near-universal default for both founders and employees. Deviations exist — longer schedules at later-stage companies, shorter for advisors — but the default is what gets assumed unless stated.

For founder stock the mechanism is usually a repurchase right: the founder owns all the shares immediately, and the company can buy back the unvested portion if they leave. That structure is what makes the 83(b) election both possible and important.

Where it goes wrong

  • Founders skipping vesting on themselves because they trust each other. The trust isn't the point.
  • Setting no cliff, so someone who leaves in month two keeps something.
  • Forgetting that a vesting reset at the first priced round is normal, and treating it as an insult.
  • Not documenting the schedule, so the leaver and the company remember it differently.

Vesting acceleration#

Vesting speeding up on a trigger. Single trigger fires on a change of control; double trigger requires both an acquisition and the person being let go.

Picture this: a founder with double-trigger acceleration is acquired and kept on — vesting continues as normal. Acquired and terminated within the window — the balance vests immediately. Single trigger would have vested everything the day the deal closed.

Why it matters

Acceleration decides who gets paid what in an acquisition, and it's negotiated years before anyone knows whether there will be one. Single trigger is founder-friendly and acquirer-hostile: it means the team's equity fully vests on close, removing the retention the acquirer is partly paying for.

That's why single trigger can reduce the price or kill a deal outright. Double trigger is the market standard because it protects the individual against being acquired and discarded, without removing the acquirer's retention.

What it looks like in practice

Double trigger typically requires the acquisition plus termination without cause, or resignation for good reason, within a defined window — commonly twelve months after close. "Good reason" usually covers a material demotion, a pay cut, or being made to relocate.

Partial acceleration is a common compromise, especially for executives: some fraction vests on the change of control, the rest on the second trigger.

Where it goes wrong

  • Pushing for single trigger and finding it reduces the acquisition price.
  • Leaving "good reason" undefined, which makes the protection unenforceable in practice.
  • Assuming acceleration is standard for employees. Usually it isn't beyond the senior team.
  • Negotiating it at the acquisition rather than at grant, when there is no leverage.

Ownership — who owns what, and how it shrinks

Co-founder equity split#

How founding equity is divided between the people starting the company.

Picture this: an equal split decided in week two, before anyone knows who will still be here in year three. Two years later one founder is running the company and the other left for a job, still holding a third of it because nobody set up vesting.

Why it matters

This is the decision most likely to destroy a company from the inside, and it gets made early, fast, and emotionally. Resentment about the split compounds silently for years and surfaces at the worst possible moment — usually during a fundraise or an acquisition.

For an investor it's a real diligence item. A split that doesn't reflect contribution, or a large stake held by someone no longer involved, is a structural problem that gets harder to fix with every round.

What it looks like in practice

The split matters far less than the vesting attached to it. An imperfect split with four-year vesting self-corrects, because whoever leaves early keeps proportionally little. A perfect split with no vesting is a live grenade.

Equal splits are common and often right, particularly where founders are genuinely co-equal. What makes them dangerous is using equality to avoid a difficult conversation about roles, commitment, and what happens if someone wants out.

Where it goes wrong

  • Splitting equity without vesting, which makes every other mistake permanent.
  • Weighting heavily toward whoever had the idea. Execution is where the value is created.
  • Avoiding the conversation because it's uncomfortable, and letting resentment accumulate instead.
  • Giving a large stake to someone part-time who never becomes full-time.

Advisor equity grants#

Small equity grants to advisors in exchange for ongoing help — typically a fraction of a percent, vesting over one to two years.

Picture this: 0.25% over two years for monthly calls and warm introductions. The advisor makes two introductions in month one, then stops responding. Without vesting, they'd have kept the whole grant.

Why it matters

Advisor equity is cheap in isolation and expensive in aggregate. Eight advisors at 0.25% is 2% of the company — more than the entire seed-stage option budget for early engineers, given to people whose contribution is usually unmeasured.

It also clutters a cap table. A long list of small holders makes future rounds administratively slower and signals a founder who traded equity for reassurance.

What it looks like in practice

Typical grants run from about 0.1% for light involvement to around 1% for someone genuinely operationally engaged, vesting monthly over one or two years with a short cliff. The FAST agreement published by the Founder Institute is the common template and includes tiers by involvement.

The test worth applying before granting: name the specific thing this person will do in the next six months. If the answer is "credibility," it's a logo purchase, and logos rarely close rounds.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting equity for a name on a website with no defined commitment.
  • No vesting, so an advisor who disengages after a month keeps the full grant.
  • Accumulating advisors until the total exceeds what the early team holds.
  • Granting to someone whose value is a single introduction that could have been a thank-you.

409A valuation#

An independent appraisal of a company's common stock, used to set option strike prices at fair market value.

Picture this: the preferred sold at $2.40 in the seed round. The 409A comes back at $0.61 for common, because common lacks the preference and the protective rights. Employee options get struck at $0.61.

Why it matters

Issuing options below fair market value creates a tax problem for the employee — immediate taxation plus penalties under Section 409A — which turns a benefit into a liability. The appraisal exists to establish a defensible price and create safe-harbour protection.

The gap between preferred price and common price is the part founders find surprising and is entirely rational: common stock sits behind the whole preference stack and carries none of the rights, so it's genuinely worth less.

What it looks like in practice

409As are typically refreshed annually, or after any material event — a priced round, a large acquisition offer, a significant change in performance. Using a stale one after a round has closed forfeits the safe harbour.

There's a natural tension: a low 409A is good for employees because it lowers the strike price, but it has to be defensible. Appraisers who deliver aggressively low numbers create audit risk that lands years later.

Where it goes wrong

  • Issuing options against a 409A that predates the last financing.
  • Assuming common stock is worth the preferred price, or vice versa.
  • Choosing an appraiser for the answer rather than the rigour.
  • Promising a strike price to a hire before the valuation is refreshed.

Liquidation preference#

Who gets paid first when the company sells, and how much before anyone else sees a dollar.

Picture this: an investor puts in $5M with a 1x preference. Company sells for $20M — they take $5M off the top, then $15M is split among everyone. With a 2x preference they take $10M first, and only $10M is left for the founders and team.

Why it matters

This is the term that decides who actually gets paid, and it routinely overrides what the cap table appears to promise. Ownership percentage tells you how the proceeds split after the preference stack is satisfied — not before. In a big exit that distinction evaporates, because every investor converts to common and takes their percentage. In a modest exit it is the whole story.

Founders negotiate hard on valuation and treat the preference as boilerplate. That is backwards. A higher valuation with a 2x participating preference is usually worse for the founder than a lower valuation with 1x non-participating, and the gap widens the worse the outcome gets.

What it looks like in practice

A company raises $20M across its life and sells for $30M. With a 1x non-participating preference, investors take their $20M back, and $10M is left for founders and employees to split. Investors could instead convert to common and take their percentage of $30M — they take whichever is larger, so at this price they take the preference.

Make it participating and the arithmetic changes: investors take the $20M and their percentage of the remaining $10M. Roughly $2M more leaves the common pool. Stack a 2x preference on the last round and the $30M sale can clear the preference stack entirely, and common gets nothing at all — on a company that just sold for $30M.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reading the cap table as a payout schedule. It is an ownership record. The waterfall is what pays.
  • Winning on valuation and losing on structure. Participation and multiples are where the real money moves.
  • Only modeling the good exit. Run the $30M case, not just the $300M case — the preference terms are irrelevant in one and decisive in the other.
  • Forgetting the stack compounds. Each round adds its own preference ahead of common, and they do not disappear.

Where the term comes from

Brad Feld and Jason Mendelson walked through venture term sheets clause by clause on Feld Thoughts across 2005 — price, liquidation preference, board composition, protective provisions, anti-dilution — at a point when almost nobody was explaining these terms to founders in public. The liquidation preference post remains the plainest account of how the economics actually pay out, and the series became the book Venture Deals.

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Participating preferred ("double dip")#

The investor takes their preference and then also shares in what's left.

Picture this: $5M invested, 1x participating, 25% ownership, $20M exit. They take $5M, then 25% of the remaining $15M ($3.75M) — $8.75M total instead of $5M. Founders feel this one.

Why it matters

Participation is the difference between a preference that expires when things go well and one that never expires. Non-participating preferred forces a choice: take the preference or convert and take your percentage. Participating takes both.

That choice is what makes non-participating fair in a good outcome. Remove it and the investor's return improves at every exit value, with the difference coming entirely out of common.

What it looks like in practice

In a $30M exit on $20M invested, 1x non-participating pays investors $20M. Participating pays $20M plus their percentage of the remaining $10M. The gap widens with the size of the preference and narrows as the exit grows.

Caps are the common compromise — participation until the investor has received some multiple of their money, then it stops. A 2x cap means participation ends once they've made twice their investment.

Where it goes wrong

  • Accepting participation to preserve a headline valuation. It usually costs more than the price difference.
  • Not modelling participating versus non-participating across a range of exit values.
  • Ignoring the cap, which changes the arithmetic substantially at higher exits.
  • Assuming participation is market. In most healthy seed and Series A rounds it isn't.

Anti-dilution#

Protection if the company later raises at a lower price. Two flavors, very different in severity.

Picture this: full ratchet re-prices all your old shares down to the new low price — the harshest version. Weighted average adjusts partially, based on how big the down round was. Weighted average is normal; full ratchet is a red flag worth pushing back on.

Why it matters

Anti-dilution protects an investor's price, not their percentage — a distinction that matters. If the company later sells stock more cheaply, the earlier investor's conversion price adjusts downward, so they get more shares for the same money.

The cost falls on common shareholders. The adjustment doesn't create value; it moves ownership from founders and employees to the protected investor at exactly the moment everyone is already demoralised.

What it looks like in practice

Full ratchet reprices the earlier investment entirely to the new, lower price — punitive, and rare outside distressed situations. Broad-based weighted average is the market standard, adjusting partially based on how much new stock is issued and at what price.

The difference between broad-based and narrow-based is which shares count in the denominator. Broad-based includes options and convertibles, produces a smaller adjustment, and is more founder-friendly.

Where it goes wrong

  • Accepting full ratchet, which can transfer enormous ownership in a modest down round.
  • Not knowing whether the weighted average is broad- or narrow-based.
  • Assuming it protects percentage. It protects price.
  • Forgetting that pay-to-play provisions can switch it off for investors who don't participate.

Board seat#

A formal seat on the board of directors, with a vote on major decisions. Usually goes to the lead investor.

Why it matters

The board is where the decisions that a shareholder vote can't reach get made — hiring and firing the CEO, approving budgets, authorising a sale. A board seat is a fundamentally different thing from an ownership percentage.

Directors also owe fiduciary duties to the company and all shareholders, not to the fund that appointed them. That's a real constraint and it's the reason investor directors sometimes vote against their own fund's short-term interest.

What it looks like in practice

Early boards are usually three to five people: one or two founders, the lead investor, and an independent. The independent seat matters more than founders expect, because it breaks deadlocks and is often the deciding vote in a crisis.

Board size grows with rounds and gets worse as it grows. A seven-person board turns working sessions into presentations, which is why tying seats to ownership thresholds rather than granting them permanently is worth negotiating.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting a permanent seat rather than one tied to continued ownership.
  • Expanding the board with every round until it can't have a real conversation.
  • Leaving the independent seat empty, so there's no tiebreaker.
  • Confusing a board seat with control. Protective provisions can matter more.

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Drag-along rights#

If enough shareholders agree to sell, they can force the rest to sell too. Stops one small holder from blocking an acquisition.

Why it matters

Drag-along solves the holdout problem. Without it, a small shareholder can block an acquisition the overwhelming majority wants, purely for leverage. With it, once the required majority approves, everyone is compelled to sell on the same terms.

For founders and small holders it means the decision to sell may not be theirs. The threshold that triggers it is therefore one of the more important numbers in the voting agreement.

What it looks like in practice

Typically triggered by approval from the board plus a majority of preferred and sometimes a majority of common. Where those thresholds sit determines who effectively controls an exit.

The protections worth negotiating are that dragged holders get the same price and terms as everyone else, and that they aren't forced into open-ended indemnity obligations beyond their share of the proceeds.

Where it goes wrong

  • Not knowing what threshold triggers it until an acquisition is on the table.
  • Agreeing to a drag that can be triggered by preferred alone.
  • Accepting unlimited indemnity exposure as a dragged shareholder.
  • Assuming founders control the sale decision because they hold a majority of common.

Tag-along rights#

If big shareholders sell, small ones can join on the same terms. The mirror image of drag-along, protecting the little guy.

Why it matters

Tag-along is the mirror of drag-along, and it protects minority holders rather than compelling them. If a major shareholder sells, everyone else gets to participate proportionally on the same terms.

The problem it solves is a founder or large investor quietly selling their position at a good price while everyone else stays in. Tag-along makes that impossible without bringing the others along.

What it looks like in practice

It usually applies to sales above a threshold and gives other holders a defined window to elect to participate. In practice it makes large private secondary sales slower and more visible, which is much of the point.

It pairs with the right of first refusal in the standard NVCA co-sale agreement — the company and then investors get first refusal, and whatever isn't taken up is subject to tag-along.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming it applies to every sale rather than only above the threshold.
  • Missing the election window, which is usually short.
  • Not realising founder secondary sales may be exempted in the drafting.
  • Treating tag-along and ROFR as the same right. They operate in sequence.

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Pay-to-play#

If you don't participate in the next round, you lose your preferred protections and get converted down to common. It punishes investors who go quiet when things get hard.

Picture this: appears in roughly 10% of deals. It's founder-friendly and a real signal — an investor who accepts it is telling you they intend to keep supporting the company, not just ride the first check.

Why it matters

Pay-to-play forces investors to support the company in a hard round or lose their protections. Investors who don't participate pro rata have their preferred converted to common, stripping the preference and the anti-dilution.

It exists because down rounds reveal who is actually committed. An investor who wants downside protection but won't put in more money is taking a position the other investors have to fund.

What it looks like in practice

Provisions vary in severity: full conversion to common is the harshest, while some convert only the non-participating portion or move investors to a shadow series with reduced rights.

It appears most often in down rounds and recapitalisations, and it's frequently negotiated at that moment rather than being present from the start. That timing matters — it's a term added under pressure.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming an existing investor will participate. Funds run out of reserves, or out of conviction.
  • Not understanding what the conversion strips — often anti-dilution as well as the preference.
  • Applying it without a realistic view of which investors can actually follow on.
  • Reading a pay-to-play round as routine. It's a signal about the company's position.

Cram down#

A round priced so low, with terms so aggressive, that it effectively wipes out existing holders. Usually happens when a company needs cash and has no leverage.

Picture this: a company that raised at $60M can't raise again. A new investor offers $8M post-money with a 3x preference and full ratchet. Existing investors and employees are left with almost nothing. Technically a financing, functionally a reset.

Why it matters

A cram down is a financing structured so punitively that existing holders are effectively wiped out — a very low price, a heavy preference, and often pay-to-play attached. It happens when a company has no alternative.

The reason it matters as vocabulary is that it's the endpoint of the terms negotiated years earlier. Anti-dilution, preference stacking, and pay-to-play all become instruments in the same transaction.

What it looks like in practice

Typically the new money comes in senior to everything else, prior preferences are reduced or converted, and non-participating investors lose their protections. What was a meaningful position becomes a rounding error.

For a fund the practical question is whether to defend the position with more capital or accept the write-down. That decision is what reserves exist for, and it's usually made with poor information under time pressure.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating a cram down as a normal down round. The mechanics are different and far more severe.
  • Having no reserves, which removes the option to defend a position.
  • Ignoring the possibility when agreeing anti-dilution and pay-to-play terms years earlier.
  • Assuming existing relationships prevent it. Insolvency changes what people do.

No-shop#

A promise not to use your term sheet to shop for a better one. Standard, but the duration matters.

Picture this: 30–60 days is normal and fair. A 120-day no-shop with no obligation on the investor's side is a founder agreeing to stop fundraising while someone decides at leisure.

Why it matters

The no-shop is the binding half of a non-binding term sheet. Once signed, the company can't talk to other investors, which removes the competitive tension that produced the terms in the first place.

That's a reasonable ask — an investor about to spend money on diligence doesn't want to be a stalking horse — but the length matters enormously, because every day of exclusivity is a day of lost leverage.

What it looks like in practice

Thirty to sixty days is typical for a financing. Shorter is better for the company, and a hard outside date rather than an open-ended period is worth insisting on.

The same mechanism appears in acquisitions as exclusivity in the LOI, where the stakes are higher because a failed process after months of exclusivity leaves the company visibly unsold.

Where it goes wrong

  • Agreeing to a long no-shop with no closing deadline attached.
  • Signing a term sheet before other conversations have reached a comparable stage.
  • Assuming non-binding covers the whole document. Exclusivity binds.
  • Not clarifying what happens if the investor walks — whether the period ends immediately.

Right of First Refusal (ROFR)#

If a shareholder wants to sell, the company or its investors get first option to buy at that price. It controls who ends up on the cap table.

Why it matters

ROFR gives the company and its investors the ability to control who ends up on the cap table. If a shareholder wants to sell, the company and then existing investors get the chance to buy first on the same terms.

The purpose is to keep shares out of the hands of competitors, unknown parties, or anyone whose presence would complicate future rounds. The cost is that it makes any private sale slower and more visible.

What it looks like in practice

The standard NVCA structure runs in sequence: the company has first refusal, then investors, and whatever remains is subject to co-sale rights. Each step has a defined notice period.

In practice ROFR often prevents a sale simply by making it slow. A buyer who has to wait through two refusal windows to find out whether the deal survives frequently doesn't wait.

Where it goes wrong

  • Not budgeting time for the refusal windows when planning a secondary sale.
  • Assuming founder shares are exempt. Often they aren't.
  • Letting the company hold ROFR without the cash to exercise it, which just delays everything.
  • Confusing ROFR with a right of first offer, which works differently.

Redemption rights#

The right to force the company to buy back shares after some period. Rare and aggressive at pre-seed — it converts equity into something closer to debt.

Why it matters

Redemption gives investors the right to demand their money back after a set period, usually five to seven years. It exists because funds have finite lives and need a theoretical exit from a company that is neither failing nor selling.

In practice it's rarely exercised, because a company that could afford to redeem usually has better things to do with the cash, and one that can't is insolvent. Its real function is leverage — a reason for the company to engage with an exit conversation.

What it looks like in practice

Typically structured as redemption at the original price plus accrued dividends, exercisable by a majority of preferred after a defined period, and often payable in instalments rather than at once.

The clause matters most for the zombie case: a company doing fine, growing slowly, with no acquirer and no IPO path. Redemption is the only term that forces that conversation.

Where it goes wrong

  • Ignoring it because it's rarely exercised. It's leverage whether or not it fires.
  • Agreeing to redemption at a multiple rather than at cost.
  • Not checking how accrued dividends compound into the redemption amount.
  • Assuming the company will have the cash. Usually the ones asked don't.

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Side letter#

A separate agreement giving one investor terms the others don't have — extra reporting, fee breaks, co-investment rights.

Picture this: side letters are why distributions are complicated. Before paying anyone, the fund has to check what it privately promised each LP.

Why it matters

Side letters are how individual investors get terms the rest of the round doesn't. They're normal and often reasonable — a large investor asking for enhanced reporting, a strategic one asking for a specific right.

The risk is accumulation. A stack of side letters granting different rights to different parties creates obligations nobody tracks, and one MFN clause can propagate every concession to everyone.

What it looks like in practice

Common contents are enhanced information rights, guaranteed pro rata, MFN protection, and specific approval rights. In fund formation the same mechanism appears between GPs and individual LPs, often on fees.

The discipline is a single register of what has been granted to whom. Companies discover during diligence that they made commitments they no longer remember.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting side letters without keeping a central record of them.
  • Including MFN, so every later concession propagates backwards.
  • Giving governance rights in a side letter that contradict the main documents.
  • Assuming side letters expire at the next round unless they say so.

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Information rights#

The right to get regular financials and updates. Sounds procedural, but it's the difference between knowing a company is in trouble and finding out at the wake.

Why it matters

Information rights are the mechanism by which investors without a board seat stay informed. They're also an obligation on the company that recurs forever, which is why they're usually limited to investors above a threshold.

The cost is real but small when handled properly. Companies that run a disciplined monthly update satisfy their information rights as a by-product; companies that don't end up answering the same questions individually.

What it looks like in practice

Standard rights cover annual audited or reviewed financials, quarterly unaudited financials, an annual budget, and reasonable inspection rights. Major-investor thresholds keep the obligation manageable.

Inspection rights are the ones worth reading. Broad access to books and records can be burdensome and, with a strategic investor, occasionally sensitive.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting full rights to every small holder, creating an unmanageable reporting burden.
  • Ignoring them until an investor formally requests financials you don't produce.
  • Giving broad inspection rights to an investor with a competing portfolio company.
  • Treating them as a substitute for actually communicating with investors.

Related terms

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Protective provisions#

A list of things the company cannot do without preferred shareholder approval, regardless of who controls the board.

Picture this: investors hold 18% and no board majority. They still get a veto on selling the company, raising a senior round, changing the charter, or issuing new preferred. Minority economics, real control over specific decisions.

Why it matters

This is where control actually lives, and founders consistently underweight it because it isn't expressed as a percentage. You can own 70% of your company and still be unable to sell it.

The provisions are individually reasonable — no investor wants a company sold out from under them — and collectively they're the difference between a founder who can act and one who has to negotiate every significant decision.

What it looks like in practice

The standard NVCA list covers liquidation or sale, changes to the charter or bylaws, creating senior securities, increasing the option pool, changing board size, and taking on significant debt. That set is broadly accepted as market.

The negotiation is about what gets added beyond it, and about who votes. A single class vote across all preferred is very different from each series voting separately — the latter gives every round its own veto, which compounds painfully by Series C.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reading only the board and ownership terms and skipping this section.
  • Agreeing to series-by-series votes, so each round adds another party who can block.
  • Letting the list expand into ordinary operating decisions like hiring or budget.
  • Assuming a friendly investor won't use them. The document outlives the relationship.
