The protective terms — what investors ask for

Conversion rights#

The right of preferred shareholders to convert into common stock — voluntarily at any time, or automatically on a qualifying event.

Picture this: at a $400M exit, holding a $10M preference on 25% ownership means taking $10M or converting and taking $100M. Everyone converts. The preference was insurance that expired unused.

Why it matters

Conversion is what makes preferred stock work in both directions: downside protection through the preference, full upside through conversion. Investors take whichever is worth more, which is why the preference only binds in modest outcomes.

Understanding the conversion point — the exit value where converting beats taking the preference — tells you which regime you're in, and that changes who is aligned with whom in an acquisition negotiation.

What it looks like in practice

Automatic conversion is triggered by a qualified IPO, defined by a minimum offering size and sometimes a minimum price, or by a vote of a specified majority of preferred. That vote threshold is the term worth reading closely.

It matters because a small group of holders can otherwise block a conversion the rest of the company needs, which is the mechanism behind most hold-up situations at IPO or acquisition.

Where it goes wrong

  • Ignoring the automatic conversion thresholds until an IPO is actually on the table.
  • Setting the qualified IPO bar so high that no realistic offering clears it.
  • Assuming all preferred converts together when each series may vote separately.
  • Forgetting that anti-dilution adjusts the conversion ratio, not just the price.

Related terms

Conversion pointThe exit value at which an investor stops preferring their liquidation preference and would rather convert to common. The protective terms — what investors ask for

Voting agreement#

The agreement binding shareholders to vote their shares a particular way — most importantly on who sits on the board.

Picture this: the agreement says the board is five: two elected by common, two by preferred, one independent agreed by both. Everyone contractually votes that way, so board composition is settled years in advance rather than fought over annually.

Why it matters

Board composition is the most consequential governance term in a financing, and this is the document that fixes it. It converts an annual political question into a settled structure.

It usually also carries the drag-along, which means it's the document that can compel a shareholder to sell in an acquisition they oppose. Two very different powers living in the same agreement is a common surprise.

What it looks like in practice

The typical early structure is a small board with defined seats — founders, lead investor, one independent. The independent seat matters more than founders expect, because it decides deadlocks.

Board seats are sticky. An investor seat granted at seed usually persists through later rounds, and a fund that becomes a small holder can still occupy a seat years later unless the agreement ties the seat to continued ownership.

Where it goes wrong

  • Growing the board faster than the company, so every decision needs a large meeting.
  • Granting a permanent seat rather than tying it to an ownership threshold.
  • Not noticing the drag-along inside the same document.
  • Leaving the independent seat unfilled, so deadlocks have no resolution.

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Investor Rights Agreement (IRA)#

The agreement bundling the ongoing rights investors get after closing — information, registration, pro rata, and inspection.

Picture this: the term sheet is two pages about price. The IRA is thirty pages about what happens every quarter for the next decade — what gets reported, who can demand an IPO registration, and who has the right to keep buying.

Why it matters

The term sheet gets the attention and the IRA governs the relationship. Rights that seem minor at signing — inspection rights, registration rights, pro rata — determine how much of the founder's time investors can consume and how much of the next round they can take.

It's also where the difference between a well-run round and a messy one shows up later. Granting broad rights to many small investors creates an administrative burden that compounds every quarter.

What it looks like in practice

Most rounds limit the heavier rights to major investors above a threshold, which keeps the obligations manageable. Registration rights rarely get exercised but matter at IPO; pro rata rights matter at every subsequent round.

For a small fund the pro rata right is the most valuable thing in the document, because it's what allows concentration into winners without needing a new allocation.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting full information and inspection rights to every small holder.
  • Ignoring registration rights until an IPO makes them suddenly relevant.
  • Letting pro rata rights sit with investors who won't follow on, blocking allocation for those who will.
  • Negotiating hard on the term sheet and signing the IRA without reading it.

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Most Favored Nation (MFN) clause#

A promise that if someone later gets better terms, this investor gets them too.

Picture this: an angel invests on a SAFE with MFN and no cap. Six months later the company sells SAFEs at a $8M cap. The MFN investor automatically gets the $8M cap without negotiating for it.

Why it matters

MFN solves the pricing problem for an investor going first when nobody knows what the company is worth. Rather than guess, they take whatever the market later decides — which is why it's common in the earliest, least-priced money.

The cost to the company is a loss of flexibility. Every subsequent concession propagates backwards, which makes it hard to give a strategically important investor a special deal without giving it to everyone.

What it looks like in practice

It's most common on uncapped SAFEs and in side letters. The mechanics matter: what counts as a better term, whether it applies only to instruments of the same type, and whether it survives into the priced round or expires at conversion.

Stacked MFNs across many small investors are the failure mode. One concession to one party can cascade through a dozen agreements at once.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting MFN broadly, so no later investor can be given a bespoke term.
  • Leaving the definition of "better terms" vague, which produces disputes at conversion.
  • Not tracking who holds MFN, then discovering the cascade during a round.
  • Assuming it expires at the priced round when the drafting says otherwise.

Related terms

It protects you from the company getting so valuable that your early risk buys almost nothing.Side letterA separate agreement giving one investor terms the others don't have — extra reporting, fee breaks, co-investment rights.DiscountA percentage off the next round's price, as thanks for going early.Convertible noteLike a SAFE, but technically a loan — it has an interest rate and a maturity date. The protective terms — what investors ask for

Warrant coverage#

The right to buy additional shares at a set price later, usually expressed as a percentage of the amount invested.

Picture this: a $2M investment with 20% warrant coverage carries the right to buy another $400,000 of stock at the round price. If the company does well, that's cheap stock bought years later at an old valuation.

Why it matters

Warrants are the sweetener that gets a deal done when price alone won't. They show up most often in bridge rounds, venture debt, and situations where the investor is taking more risk than the headline terms compensate for.

For the company they're deferred dilution, and because they sit outside the ordinary cap table conversation they're easy to under-count. Fully diluted ownership includes them; a founder's mental model often doesn't.

What it looks like in practice

Coverage is quoted as a percentage of the investment, with a strike price usually set at the current or next round price and a long exercise window. Venture debt lenders commonly take warrants alongside interest, which is much of how that asset class makes its return.

In a bridge, warrant coverage is often the alternative to repricing — existing investors put in more money on the old terms and take warrants to compensate for the added risk.

Where it goes wrong

  • Leaving warrants out of the fully diluted count, so ownership math is quietly wrong.
  • Granting long-dated warrants at a low strike that overhang every later round.
  • Using warrants to avoid a difficult price conversation, and paying more in dilution than a lower price would have cost.
  • Forgetting they exist until an acquirer's diligence finds them.

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Deemed liquidation event#

The definition of what counts as a liquidation for the purpose of paying out preferences — usually including an acquisition, not just a winding up.

Picture this: the company is acquired for $80M. Nobody is liquidating anything, but the charter deems the sale a liquidation, so the preference stack pays out first exactly as it would in a wind-down.

Why it matters

Without this definition the liquidation preference would only apply to an actual liquidation, which is the outcome nobody is planning for. Deeming an acquisition a liquidation is what makes the preference meaningful in the scenario that actually happens.

The scope of the definition is negotiated and matters. Whether a majority-stake sale, an asset sale, or an exclusive licence of substantially all IP counts can determine whether preferences trigger at all.

What it looks like in practice

Standard definitions cover a merger or consolidation where existing holders no longer control the survivor, and a sale of substantially all assets. Broader versions catch exclusive licences and majority stake sales.

It's also the trigger that interacts with vesting acceleration, so the same definition often decides both who gets paid and whose equity vests.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming a preference only applies in bankruptcy. It applies to most exits.
  • Leaving asset sales or exclusive licences outside the definition, creating a route around the preference.
  • Not checking that the definition matches the one used in the vesting acceleration language.
  • Treating it as boilerplate when it decides whether the whole preference stack fires.

The protective terms — what investors ask for

Board observer seat#

The right to attend board meetings and receive materials, without a vote.

Picture this: a seed fund that owns 6% gets an observer seat. They see everything, ask questions, and can't vote. For an investor without the ownership to justify a full seat, it's most of the value at none of the governance cost.

Why it matters

Observer seats let a company give investors visibility without expanding the board, which matters because board size is one of the few things that gets worse monotonically. Every additional voting member makes decisions slower.

They're not free, though. Observers still consume preparation time, still ask questions, and still change what gets said in the room — and unlike directors they owe the company no fiduciary duty.

What it looks like in practice

Rights are usually limited to attending and receiving materials, with the company able to exclude the observer from sessions covering conflicts, litigation, or privileged legal advice. That carve-out is worth having explicitly.

The number accumulates quietly. Granting one per round produces a Series B board meeting with four directors and five observers, which changes the meeting from a working session into a performance.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting observer rights freely, then finding the room is too crowded to have a real conversation.
  • Omitting confidentiality obligations for observers.
  • Not reserving the right to exclude them from privileged or conflicted sessions.
  • Giving an observer seat to a fund that competes with a portfolio company.

The payout stack — who actually gets paid first

This is the part almost nobody explains, and it's where founder outcomes are decided.

The payout stack — who actually gets paid first

Common stock#

Plain ownership. Every share gets an equal slice. Founders and employees hold this. It gets paid last.

Why it matters

Common stock is what founders and employees hold, and it sits at the bottom of the payout stack. Everything preferred is owed gets paid first, which is why common can be worth nothing in an exit that looks like a success.

It's also why the 409A price for common is so much lower than the preferred price. Common carries none of the protections and none of the rights, and the market values that difference honestly.

What it looks like in practice

Common holders vote, but their voting power is constrained by protective provisions that require preferred approval for the decisions that matter most.

The number that determines whether common is worth anything is the total preference stack against the exit value. Below the stack, common gets nothing regardless of percentage.

Where it goes wrong

  • Valuing common at the preferred price when estimating what a stake is worth.
  • Assuming a majority of common means control of a sale decision.
  • Ignoring how the preference stack grows with each round.
  • Treating option grants as equivalent to the preferred price investors paid.

The payout stack — who actually gets paid first

Convertible preferred stock#

What investors actually buy. It gives the holder a choice at exit: take the liquidation preference, or convert to common and take their percentage — whichever pays more.

Picture this: over 99% of VC preferred stock is convertible, and nearly 100% of modern unicorn financings use it. It's not an exotic instrument; it's the default.

Why it matters

Convertible preferred is the standard venture instrument because it does two things at once: downside protection through the liquidation preference, and full upside through the right to convert to common.

That asymmetry is the entire structure of a venture investment. The investor takes the better of two outcomes at every exit value, which is what makes a portfolio of mostly-failures workable.

What it looks like in practice

The preferred rights ride along with it: the preference, anti-dilution, protective provisions, information rights, and usually a board seat. Conversion strips all of them, which is why conversion only happens when the economics justify it.

Each round issues its own series with its own terms, which is how the stack accumulates and why later rounds can have priority over earlier ones.

Where it goes wrong

  • Modelling an exit as though preferred converts, without checking whether it would.
  • Forgetting that conversion strips the protective provisions too, not just the preference.
  • Treating all series of preferred as one block when they may vote separately.
  • Ignoring accrued dividends, which increase the amount owed before common.

Series preferred#

Each round issues its own named class — Series A, Series B, Series C. They are not interchangeable. Each can carry different rights, and that's what determines the payout order.

Why it matters

Each financing round issues a new series — Series A Preferred, Series B Preferred — each with its own price, preference, and rights. They're not interchangeable, and the differences between them decide who gets paid first.

The complexity compounds. By Series C there may be four series with different preferences, different anti-dilution, and different voting requirements, and any of them may be able to block a transaction.

What it looks like in practice

The two structural questions are seniority — whether later series get paid before earlier ones — and whether series vote together as one class or separately.

Voting separately gives each round a veto, which becomes progressively harder to manage. Voting as a single class is simpler and more common in well-structured cap tables.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming all preferred is equivalent when modelling a waterfall.
  • Not knowing whether series vote together or separately.
  • Letting each round negotiate its own bespoke terms, so the stack becomes unmanageable.
  • Modelling only the most recent series and ignoring the ones underneath it.

The payout stack — who actually gets paid first

Original Issue Price (OIP)#

The per-share price an investor actually paid. Investment amount ÷ shares received. This is the number liquidation preferences are calculated from.

Why it matters

The OIP is the price a series was originally sold at, and it's the anchor for almost everything else — the liquidation preference is a multiple of it, and the conversion price starts equal to it.

It's a fixed historical fact, which is what makes it useful as a reference point. The conversion price moves with anti-dilution adjustments; the OIP doesn't.

What it looks like in practice

A 1x preference means 1x the OIP per share. Anti-dilution adjusts the conversion price below the OIP, which increases the number of common shares each preferred share converts into — but the preference stays anchored to the original price.

That separation is the part people find confusing, and it's why the two numbers diverge after a down round.

Where it goes wrong

  • Conflating OIP with the current conversion price after an anti-dilution adjustment.
  • Calculating the preference off the adjusted conversion price rather than the OIP.
  • Forgetting that each series has its own OIP.
  • Assuming OIP equals the post-money divided by shares. It's the actual price paid per share.

Par value#

A nominal legal value in the corporate charter, usually $0.001. Economically meaningless — don't confuse it with OIP.

Why it matters

Par value is a legal artifact, usually set at $0.0001, and it has almost nothing to do with what stock is worth. Its only real function is establishing a nominal floor below which shares can't be issued.

It matters in one practical place: founder stock issued at par at incorporation is what makes the 83(b) election cheap. Eight million shares at $0.0001 is $800 of taxable value.

What it looks like in practice

Delaware franchise tax can be calculated using the authorised shares method or the assumed par value capital method, and the difference between them can be thousands of dollars a year. Most startups use the second.

Beyond that, par value shows up in the charter and is otherwise ignored. It is not a valuation of anything.

Where it goes wrong

  • Confusing par value with fair market value or the 409A price.
  • Setting par value high, which raises the minimum issuance price for founder stock.
  • Using the wrong Delaware franchise tax calculation method and overpaying substantially.
  • Issuing founder stock below par, which isn't permitted.

The payout stack — who actually gets paid first

Seniority#

Later rounds usually get paid before earlier ones. Being first in is not being first paid.

Picture this: when Kabbage sold, Series F took $161M first, then Series E ($166M), then D ($50M), then C ($31M). Only $22M was left for Series A and B — even though common shareholders still held roughly 28% of the company.

Why it matters

Seniority decides the order of payment when there isn't enough to go around, which is exactly the situation the preference exists for. Later rounds often negotiate seniority over earlier ones, meaning the newest money gets paid first.

For an early investor that's the quiet risk in later rounds. A position that was first in line at seed can be third by Series C without anyone renegotiating the original terms.

What it looks like in practice

Two structures dominate. Stacked seniority pays the most recent series first, then works backwards. Pari passu pays all series proportionally at the same time.

Stacked is more common in later rounds where the incoming investor has leverage. Which structure applies is set in the charter and can be changed by a later financing if the protective provisions allow it.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming pari passu without checking the charter.
  • Ignoring that a later round can rewrite the seniority you agreed to.
  • Modelling a waterfall without the payment order, which makes the model wrong.
  • Reading seniority as only mattering in bankruptcy. It matters in every exit below the stack.

Pari passu#

Latin for "equal footing." Classes share proceeds in proportion to their preferences instead of one going first.

Picture this: two 1x series — Series A put in $10M, Series B put in $15M, $25M of preferences total. The company sells for only $5M. Series A gets (10÷25) × $5M = $2M; Series B gets (15÷25) × $5M = $3M. Founders get nothing.

Why it matters

Pari passu means all series of preferred rank equally and get paid proportionally rather than in order. When proceeds fall short, everyone takes the same percentage haircut.

It's the more founder-friendly and earlier-investor-friendly structure, because it prevents the newest money from jumping the queue. It's also simpler to model, which matters more than it sounds.

What it looks like in practice

If preferences total $40M and proceeds are $20M, pari passu pays every series 50% of what it's owed. Stacked seniority would pay the most recent series in full and leave earlier ones with nothing.

The structure is usually set at the first priced round and defended in later ones. Whether it survives depends on how much leverage the incoming investor has.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming pari passu is the default. In competitive later rounds it often isn't.
  • Not checking whether a new round's terms change the ranking of existing series.
  • Modelling proportional payment when the charter specifies an order.
  • Reading pari passu as protection against the size of the stack. It only governs order.

The payout stack — who actually gets paid first

Stacked preferences#

Preferences piling up round after round, so the amount owed before common sees a dollar keeps growing.

Picture this: same company, but Series B negotiated 2x instead of 1x on its $15M. Total preferences jump from $25M to $40M. Any exit under $40M now returns literally nothing to the founders and team.

Why it matters

Stacked preferences are the cumulative amount owed to all preferred before common receives anything, and they grow with every round. A company that has raised $60M across four rounds has a $60M hurdle before founders and employees see a dollar.

This is the arithmetic that makes a $50M exit on a company that raised $60M pay nothing to common, regardless of what the cap table says anyone owns.

What it looks like in practice

The stack grows with each round and can grow faster if any round carries a multiple. Two rounds at 1x plus one at 2x on a $30M raise produces a stack well above the cash raised.

The number worth tracking continuously is the exit value at which common starts to receive proceeds. It moves up with every financing, and it's the honest measure of whether employee equity is worth anything.

Where it goes wrong

  • Tracking the amount raised rather than the preference stack, which can be larger.
  • Ignoring accrued dividends, which add to the stack over time.
  • Not recalculating the break-even exit value after each round.
  • Granting employee options without knowing whether the stack makes them worthless.

Conversion point#

The exit value at which an investor stops preferring their liquidation preference and would rather convert to common. Below it, take the preference. Above it, convert.

Picture this: Series A put in $10M for 25%. On its own, it converts at a $40M exit. Then Series B invests $15M — and now at $40M, Series B takes its $15M first, leaving $25M, of which Series A's 25% is only $6.25M. Worse than its $10M preference. Series A's conversion point just moved from $40M to $55M because someone else joined the stack.

Why it matters

The conversion point is the exit value at which an investor does better converting to common than taking the preference. Below it, they take the preference; above it, they convert.

It's the number that tells you who is aligned with whom in an acquisition negotiation. Below the conversion point, preferred holders are indifferent to price increases within a range, and common holders are not.

What it looks like in practice

The calculation compares the preference amount to the investor's ownership percentage of the exit value. With a $10M preference on 25% ownership, conversion beats preference above a $40M exit.

Different series convert at different points because they have different preferences and different ownership. In a complex cap table there isn't one conversion point, there are several — which is why exit modelling needs the full waterfall.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming a single conversion point for a cap table with multiple series.
  • Ignoring participation, which changes the calculation entirely.
  • Modelling conversion without accounting for anti-dilution adjustments to the ratio.
  • Not knowing where the conversion point sits when negotiating an acquisition price.

Conversion price per share#

Liquidation preference divided by fully diluted shares. The shortcut for working out who converts first without trial and error — lowest converts first.

Picture this: Series A at $4.00, Series B at $6.50, Series C at $9.75. A converts, then B, then C. With six or twelve series in a mature company, this ordering rule is the only sane way through.

Why it matters

The conversion price determines how many common shares each preferred share becomes. It starts at the original issue price and moves down when anti-dilution provisions fire.

A lower conversion price means more common shares per preferred share, which is how anti- dilution protection actually delivers — not by changing what was paid, but by changing what it converts into.

What it looks like in practice

The conversion ratio is the original issue price divided by the current conversion price. Unadjusted, that's 1:1. After a down round with weighted-average anti-dilution, it might be 1:1.3.

The dilution lands on common. Those extra shares come from somewhere, and it's the founders and employees who hold the shares being diluted.

Where it goes wrong

  • Confusing the conversion price with the liquidation preference basis, which stays at OIP.
  • Forgetting that the conversion ratio changes the fully diluted count.
  • Modelling conversion at 1:1 after a down round has triggered anti-dilution.
  • Ignoring which anti-dilution formula applies, since they produce very different adjustments.

Disagreement range#

The band of exit values where different investors want opposite things, and every extra round widens it.

Picture this: between $55M and $80M, Series A wants to convert and Series B doesn't — a $25M band of conflict. Add Series C and the band stretches to $65M wide ($85M–$150M). Higher multiples and participation rights widen it further. This is the machinery behind board fights about whether to sell.

Why it matters

The disagreement range is the band of exit values where different shareholders want different outcomes. Below the conversion point preferred prefers the preference; common wants a higher price. Within that band the two groups are genuinely opposed.

This is where acquisitions get difficult, and it explains behaviour that otherwise looks irrational — an investor blocking a deal founders want, or founders resisting a deal that pays investors back.

What it looks like in practice

The range is widest when the preference stack is large relative to the likely exit value, which is the situation created by raising a lot at high valuations and then exiting modestly.

Understanding where it sits before entering an acquisition process tells you which conversations will be hard and who needs to be brought along. It's also an argument for not stacking preferences carelessly in the first place.

Where it goes wrong

  • Entering an acquisition process without modelling where interests diverge.
  • Assuming everyone wants the highest price. Below the conversion point, not everyone does.
  • Treating investor resistance as bad faith when it's the structure working as designed.
  • Building a preference stack that makes the disagreement range cover the likely outcomes.

Mandatory / automatic conversion#

A clause forcing preferred shareholders to convert to common when conditions are met — usually a qualifying IPO. It wipes out their liquidation preference.

Picture this: Palantir's charter required net IPO proceeds of at least $150M and a valuation of at least $5B to trigger automatic conversion.

Why it matters

Automatic conversion forces all preferred into common on a qualifying event, usually an IPO above a defined size. Without it, a company couldn't go public with a preference stack intact, because public markets won't price around one.

The threshold and the voting requirement are what matter. Set them wrong and a minority of holders can block the conversion the whole company needs.

What it looks like in practice

The trigger is typically a qualified IPO — a minimum offering size and sometimes a minimum price — or a vote of a specified majority of preferred, often voting as a single class.

Where series vote separately, each one has a veto, which is precisely the structure that produces hold-up problems at the moment of exit.

Where it goes wrong

  • Setting a qualified IPO threshold so high no realistic offering clears it.
  • Allowing series-by-series votes on conversion, creating multiple vetoes.
  • Not checking the threshold until an IPO is being planned.
  • Assuming automatic conversion covers acquisitions. Usually it covers IPOs and votes.

The hold-up problem#

When one investor class blocks something everyone else wants — like an IPO — because converting would pay them less than their preference.

Picture this: Series B paid $15M for 18.75%. A $65M sale pays them their full $15M preference. A $70M IPO — a higher valuation — forces conversion and pays them 18.75% × $70M = $13.1M. They lose $1.9M by the company doing better, so they rationally block the IPO. That is why mandatory conversion clauses exist.

Why it matters

The hold-up problem is what happens when a small holder has a veto and uses it for leverage. Their block isn't about the merits — it's about being paid to remove the block.

It's the reason drag-along rights and single-class conversion votes exist. Both are mechanisms for preventing a minority from extracting value at the moment everyone else needs a transaction to close.

What it looks like in practice

The structural defences are set years earlier: drag-along thresholds that don't require unanimity, conversion votes across all preferred as a single class, and protective provisions that aren't granted series by series.

Once a transaction is live the leverage sits with whoever can block it, and the options are to pay them or to abandon the deal. That's why this is a drafting problem rather than a negotiating one.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting series-by-series vetoes, which multiply the number of parties who can hold up a deal.
  • Setting drag-along thresholds near unanimity.
  • Assuming small holders will act reasonably when they have leverage and a real economic interest.
  • Discovering the veto structure during an acquisition rather than at the financing.

IPO ratchet#

A guarantee that an investor receives a minimum per-share value at IPO, regardless of the actual price.

Picture this: Square's Series E investors were guaranteed $18.56 per share. Square went public at $9. The company had to issue them additional shares to make up the difference.

Why it matters

An IPO ratchet guarantees a late-stage investor a minimum return at IPO by adjusting their conversion ratio if the offering prices below a threshold. If the IPO disappoints, they get more shares to compensate.

It's a late-stage term that appears when a company raises at a valuation the public market may not support, and it transfers that risk to everyone else on the cap table.

What it looks like in practice

The mechanism is the same as anti-dilution but triggered by the IPO price rather than a private round. Below the threshold, additional shares are issued to the protected investor, diluting common and earlier preferred.

Its presence is informative in itself. A ratchet suggests the last round priced above what the investor was confident the market would bear.

Where it goes wrong

  • Accepting a ratchet to preserve a headline valuation in a late round.
  • Not modelling what the ratchet costs common at a range of IPO prices.
  • Reading a high late-stage valuation without checking what structure supports it.
  • Assuming ratchets only exist in down rounds. They're a forward-looking protection.

How a fund is built
How a fund is built

Limited Partner (LP)#

The investor in a fund. Family offices, funds of funds, pension funds, exited founders, wealthy individuals. They commit money and don't pick companies. "Limited" refers to their liability, not their influence.

Why it matters

LPs supply essentially all the capital and take essentially none of the decisions. That asymmetry is the whole structure: they are buying a manager's judgment for a decade, with almost no ability to change course once committed.

Understanding who the LPs are explains most GP behaviour. A fund backed by endowments behaves differently from one backed by family offices, because the reporting expectations, the tolerance for illiquidity, and the pressure for distributions are all different.

What it looks like in practice

LPs are typically pensions, endowments, foundations, funds of funds, family offices, and high- net-worth individuals. Their liability is limited to what they commit, and that limitation depends on them staying out of management — which is why the LPAC is advisory rather than decision-making.

For an emerging manager the practical reality is that the first fund is usually raised from people who know you personally. Institutional LPs generally want to see a prior fund before committing to one.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating LPs as a single constituency. Their time horizons and liquidity needs differ enormously.
  • Promising liquidity a ten-year fund structure cannot deliver.
  • Under-communicating between capital calls, so the only contact is a request for money.
  • Assuming an LP who committed to Fund I will commit to Fund II. Re-up rates are earned.

How a fund is built

General Partner (GP)#

The entity that makes the investment decisions and carries unlimited liability for them. Earns carry.

Why it matters

The GP is the entity that manages the fund and bears unlimited liability for it, which is why it exists as a separate vehicle rather than as the individuals themselves. It's also the entity that receives carried interest.

The separation between the GP entity, the management company, and the fund itself is not bureaucratic decoration — it isolates liability, separates fee income from carry, and allows the economics to be split differently across the two.

What it looks like in practice

In practice the GP entity holds the carry and the management company employs the people and receives the management fee. Individual partners have interests in both, usually in different proportions.

The GP commit — the partners' own money in the fund — is what LPs look at to confirm alignment. A GP with no meaningful capital at risk is being paid to take risk with other people's money.

Where it goes wrong

  • Collapsing GP, ManCo, and fund in your mental model. They do different jobs.
  • Assuming carry splits match management company ownership. They usually don't.
  • Ignoring the unlimited liability the GP entity carries.
  • Underestimating how much LPs weigh the size and source of the GP commit.

Management Company (ManCo)#

The operating business — brand, staff, vendors, office. Paid by the management fee. The thing you'd actually go to work at.

Why it matters

The management company is the operating business: it employs the team, pays the rent, and receives the management fee. It persists across funds, which is what makes a firm a firm rather than a series of one-off vehicles.

That persistence is the point. Fund I ends, Fund II begins, and the ManCo carries the people, the brand, and the infrastructure across the boundary.

What it looks like in practice

The ManCo's revenue is management fees from every active fund, which is why fee income stacks as a firm raises successive vehicles. Its costs are salaries, premises, and operations.

The economics matter for an emerging manager: a small first fund generates a management fee that often can't support a team, which is why most first-time managers are underpaid or subsidising the firm personally.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming management fee is profit. It funds the entire operating business.
  • Sizing a first fund without checking whether the fee supports the team you need.
  • Confusing ManCo ownership with carry allocation.
  • Forgetting that fees step down after the investment period, which shrinks the budget.

How a fund is built

The Fund#

A limited partnership that holds the money and the shares. No employees. Most firms run several at once.

Picture this: all three exist so fee income, profit share, and investor capital sit in three different pockets. A firm can't quietly fund payroll out of investor money.

Why it matters

The fund is the vehicle that actually holds the investments — a limited partnership with a defined life, a defined size, and a defined strategy. Everything else in the structure exists to manage it.

Its finite life is the constraint that shapes venture behaviour. A ten-year fund cannot hold a position indefinitely, which is why GPs push for exits on timelines that sometimes have nothing to do with what's best for the company.

What it looks like in practice

A typical structure is ten years with two one-year extensions, an investment period of three to five years, and a defined strategy the LPA constrains the GP to follow.

Each fund is separate. A firm running Fund I, Fund II, and Fund III has three distinct pools with three sets of LPs, three waterfalls, and three sets of obligations — which is where conflicts between funds come from.

Where it goes wrong

  • Modelling a fund's return without accounting for its finite life.
  • Cross-investing between funds without addressing the conflict properly.
  • Assuming extensions are automatic. They usually require LP consent.
  • Ignoring that the strategy in the LPA is a constraint, not a description.

How a fund is built

LPA (Limited Partnership Agreement)#

The contract between the GP and the LPs. Fund life, fees, carry, what the fund may and may not invest in.

Why it matters

The LPA is the constitution of the fund. It sets the fee, the carry, the waterfall, the investment restrictions, the key person provisions, and the terms on which LPs can act if things go wrong.

It is also close to unamendable in practice — changing it requires a supermajority of LPs — which means terms negotiated during fundraising govern for a decade regardless of how circumstances change.

What it looks like in practice

The terms that matter most are the economics (fee, carry, hurdle, waterfall type), the constraints (concentration limits, geography, stage, follow-on reserves), and the protections (key person, no-fault divorce, LPAC consent rights).

ILPA publishes principles that many institutional LPs use as a reference, which has narrowed the range of what's considered market on several of these terms.

Where it goes wrong

  • Negotiating the fee and carry and skimming the rest.
  • Agreeing investment restrictions that the actual strategy will breach.
  • Assuming the LPA can be amended easily when the market changes.
  • Not reading the waterfall carefully enough to model when carry is actually received.

LPAC (Advisory Committee)#

A small group of LPs who advise the GP and vote on conflicts of interest.

Why it matters

The LPAC is where LPs get a voice without taking management control — which they must not do, because managing the fund would jeopardise their limited liability. It advises and consents on specific matters rather than directing the GP.

Its most important function is conflicts. When a GP wants to do something the LPA doesn't clearly permit — cross-fund investments, valuation methodology changes, related-party transactions — the LPAC is who approves it.

What it looks like in practice

Membership is typically the largest LPs plus a few chosen for perspective. It meets a few times a year, reviews valuations, and handles consent requests.

For an emerging manager the LPAC is also an early-warning system. LPs who are uncomfortable usually say so there first, and a GP who treats it as a formality misses the signal.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating the LPAC as a rubber stamp for conflicts.
  • Populating it only with the friendliest LPs, which removes its usefulness.
  • Letting it drift into management decisions, which risks LP limited liability.
  • Bringing conflicts to it after the fact rather than before.

How a fund is built

Capital call#

The fund asking LPs to actually send money they've already committed. Capital is drawn down over years, not paid upfront.

Picture this: an LP commits $500K. Year one the fund calls $100K. The other $400K stays in the LP's account until needed — which is exactly why a capital call notice period (usually 15 days) is in the LPA.

Why it matters

LPs commit capital but don't hand it over up front. It's drawn down as needed, which is what makes IRR the metric it is — money that sits with the LP isn't costing them return.

The mechanism also creates a real risk: an LP who can't fund a call is in default, and default provisions are severe. In a liquidity crisis, defaults cluster exactly when the fund most needs the money.

What it looks like in practice

Calls typically give ten business days' notice and are made pro rata across LPs. The LPA specifies what happens on default — usually forfeiture of a large share of the defaulting LP's interest.

Some funds use subscription credit lines to bridge calls, which smooths cash flow for LPs and flatters IRR by delaying the start of the clock. ILPA has pushed for disclosure of returns both with and without the line for this reason.

Where it goes wrong

  • Calling capital far ahead of deployment, which drags on IRR.
  • Not understanding the default provisions until an LP misses a call.
  • Using a credit line to flatter IRR without disclosing its effect.
  • Assuming committed capital is available on demand. Notice periods are real.

How a fund is built

Committed capital#

What LPs have legally promised the fund over its life. Not money in the bank — a binding IOU the fund is allowed to draw on. "A $100M fund" always means $100M committed.

Picture this: you hold a final close at $100M. The bank account might have $8M in it that morning. The other $92M is a promise you'll collect over five years, one capital call at a time.

Why it matters

Committed capital is the fund's headline size and the base most fees are calculated on during the investment period. It's a legal commitment, not cash in hand.

The distinction from contributed capital matters for every performance metric. TVPI and DPI are calculated on what was actually drawn, not on what was promised, which is why a fund early in its life can show odd-looking numbers.

What it looks like in practice

During the investment period management fees are usually charged on committed capital; afterwards they typically step down to invested or net invested capital, which reduces the fee as the fund winds down.

Reserves are held against committed capital too. A fund that deploys all its committed capital into initial cheques has nothing left to defend its winners, which is a portfolio construction error rather than a cash management one.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reporting performance against committed rather than contributed capital.
  • Deploying the full commitment into initial investments with no reserves.
  • Forgetting that fees on committed capital accrue whether or not money is deployed.
  • Assuming the full commitment will ever be called. Many funds don't call all of it.

Related terms

How a fund is built

Contributed capital (paid-in)#

The share of committed capital LPs have actually sent. This is the number performance metrics divide by, and the number the waterfall has to pay back before anyone earns a profit share.

Picture this: three years in, your $100M fund has called $60M. Committed is still $100M; contributed is $60M. Return $30M tomorrow and DPI is 0.5x — half of the $60M paid in, not half of the $100M promised. Mixing these two up is the most common beginner error in fund math.

Why it matters

Contributed capital is the money LPs have actually paid in, and it's the denominator for the metrics that matter. DPI and TVPI are both calculated against it.

It includes management fees, which is the part that surprises people. Fees are drawn from LP capital, so a fund that has called 30% of commitments has typically invested less than that into companies.

What it looks like in practice

Paid-in capital equals capital called for investments plus capital called for fees and expenses. The gap between paid-in and invested is the fee drag, and over a fund's life it's substantial — a 2% annual fee over ten years is 20% of committed capital.

That's why a fund needs to return meaningfully more than 1x invested capital just to return 1x to LPs.

Where it goes wrong

  • Calculating TVPI against invested capital rather than paid-in.
  • Forgetting that fees are drawn from LP capital and reduce what's available to invest.
  • Comparing funds at different points in their lives without adjusting for how much is paid in.
  • Assuming paid-in equals cost basis of the portfolio. It doesn't — fees sit in between.

Related terms

Committed capitalWhat LPs have legally promised the fund over its life. Not money in the bank — a binding IOU the fund is allowed to draw on. "A $100M fund" always…Capital callThe fund asking LPs to actually send money they've already committed. Capital is drawn down over years, not paid upfront.DPIDistributed to Paid-In. Cash actually returned. The number nobody can argue with.TVPITotal Value to Paid-In. Everything distributed plus what's still held, divided by money in. How a fund is built

First close#

The point where enough has been committed to start investing. Typically 10–25% of the target.

Picture this: VC Lab's rule of thumb is you can form the fund at 10% of target or $1M committed, whichever comes first.

Why it matters

First close is when a fund has enough commitments to start investing. It matters because it converts a fundraise from a pitch into a live vehicle — and because the LPs who come in at first close take the most risk.

For an emerging manager it's the hardest milestone in the whole process. Everyone wants to see who else is in, and someone has to go first.

What it looks like in practice

Funds usually hold multiple closes over twelve to eighteen months. Later LPs typically pay an equalisation amount — interest on the capital earlier LPs had at risk — so everyone ends up in the same economic position.

Anchor investors at first close often negotiate better terms: fee discounts, co-investment rights, or an LPAC seat. That's the price of going first.

Where it goes wrong

  • Waiting for a full fund before starting to invest, and missing the deals that justified the strategy.
  • Closing at a size too small to execute the stated strategy.
  • Granting anchor terms so favourable they distort the fund's economics.
  • Not handling equalisation properly, which creates inconsistency between LP cohorts.

Related terms

Committed capitalWhat LPs have legally promised the fund over its life. Not money in the bank — a binding IOU the fund is allowed to draw on. PACT#

A non-binding commitment letter used in VC Lab methodology. Signing it "hard circles" an LP as serious and moves them out of polite conversation.

Why it matters

PACT is VC Lab's standard for emerging manager fundraising — a short, standardised set of terms designed to compress the time between an LP saying yes and money actually arriving.

The problem it addresses is real: first-time managers spend enormous amounts of time negotiating bespoke terms with LPs who are each asking for something slightly different, and the negotiation itself is often what kills the fund.

What it looks like in practice

The approach mirrors what standardisation did for early-stage company financing. When both sides start from a common document, the conversation narrows to the few things that genuinely differ.

For a manager raising a first fund the practical value is speed and credibility — arriving with standard terms signals that you know what market looks like.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming standardisation removes the need to understand the terms.
  • Using a standard where an institutional LP expects a fully negotiated LPA.
  • Treating speed as the only goal when some terms genuinely warrant negotiation.
  • Not checking that the standard terms fit the actual strategy.

How a fund is built

GP commit#

The GP's own money in the fund — usually about 1%. Skin in the game.

Picture this: on a $10M fund, the GP is expected to put in around $100K of their own. LPs ask about this early.

Why it matters

The GP commit is the partners' own money in their own fund, and it's the clearest alignment signal available to an LP. A manager with meaningful personal capital at risk makes different decisions from one who only has upside.

The conventional benchmark is 1–2% of fund size, though LPs care more about what it represents to the individual than what it represents to the fund. A large percentage from someone wealthy signals less than a smaller one that matters.

What it looks like in practice

For emerging managers the GP commit is a real constraint — 2% of a $20M fund is $400,000, paid over the fund's life, by someone who has just given up a salary.

Some structures allow the commit to be funded by waiving management fees, which reduces the cash burden. LPs vary on whether they consider that genuine alignment.

Where it goes wrong

  • Funding the entire commit through fee waivers and calling it skin in the game.
  • Sizing a fund without accounting for the personal cash the commit requires.
  • Assuming a percentage is what matters rather than what it represents to the individual.
  • Forgetting the commit is called over time alongside LP capital, not paid up front.

Related terms

How a fund is built

Key person clause#

If named individuals leave, the fund stops making new investments until LPs agree otherwise. LPs invested in those people.

Why it matters

LPs invest in specific people, and the key person clause is what protects that. If the named individuals stop devoting substantially all their time to the fund, the investment period suspends automatically.

It's the main structural protection LPs have during a fund's life. Beyond it they have very little ability to change anything, which is why the clause gets negotiated carefully.

What it looks like in practice

Triggering usually suspends new investments until LPs vote to resume, replace the key person, or terminate the investment period. Follow-on investments in existing portfolio companies are typically still permitted.

For a solo GP the clause is absolute — there's no one else named. That concentration is one of the reasons institutional LPs are cautious about single-partner funds.

Where it goes wrong

  • Naming too many key persons, which weakens the protection.
  • Not defining what "substantially all time" means, leaving it arguable.
  • Ignoring the clause when a partner takes on outside commitments.
  • Assuming a trigger is recoverable. It requires an LP vote, and votes can fail.

Related terms

How a fund is built

Dry powder#

Committed money not yet invested.

Why it matters

Dry powder is capital committed but not yet deployed — the fund's remaining capacity. It determines what a fund can still do, both in new investments and in defending existing positions.

It matters most in a downturn. A fund with dry powder can support its portfolio through a hard period and buy at lower prices; a fully deployed fund can only watch.

What it looks like in practice

The number to track is uncalled commitments minus expected future fees, split between what's earmarked for new investments and what's reserved for follow-ons.

Industry-wide dry powder is also a market signal. Large accumulated dry powder tends to support valuations because the capital has to be deployed within the investment period, regardless of whether prices are attractive.

Where it goes wrong

  • Counting all uncalled capital as available, ignoring future management fees.
  • Deploying dry powder late in the investment period just because the clock is running.
  • Not distinguishing between dry powder for new deals and reserves for follow-ons.
  • Assuming a portfolio company's other investors have reserves. Often they don't.

How a fund is built

Fund duration / investment period#

A fund typically lives 10 years, with new investments made only in the first 3–5. The rest of the life is spent supporting companies and waiting for exits.

Why it matters

The investment period is when new investments can be made — typically the first three to five years. The fund's total life is usually ten years plus extensions, and everything after the investment period is management and harvest.

These dates drive a lot of behaviour that looks strange from the outside: why a GP is suddenly eager to deploy, why pressure for exits appears around year eight, and why a great company can be sold earlier than it should be.

What it looks like in practice

After the investment period, management fees typically step down and only follow-on investments in existing companies are permitted. Extensions past year ten usually require LPAC or LP consent, often granted in one-year increments.

The mismatch between a ten-year fund and a company that takes twelve years to exit is structural, and it's why secondary sales and continuation vehicles exist.

Where it goes wrong

  • Deploying quickly at the end of the investment period to avoid leaving capital uninvested.
  • Modelling a fund's return without accounting for the pressure to exit within its life.
  • Assuming extensions are automatic.
  • Forgetting that fee step-downs change the management company's budget significantly.

Related terms

How a fund is built

SPV (Special Purpose Vehicle)#

A one-deal fund. Pools money from several people into a single investment.

Picture this: you find a great deal but don't have a fund. You form an SPV, raise $400K from eight people, and the SPV writes one check. One line on the cap table.

Why it matters

An SPV is a single-purpose vehicle holding one investment. It lets a group invest together through one entity, which keeps the company's cap table clean and gives the organiser a defined role and usually carry.

For a fund, SPVs are how you take more of a winner than reserves allow. When a portfolio company raises a large round, an SPV lets the GP bring LPs and others into a position the fund alone couldn't fund.

What it looks like in practice

Costs matter more than they look: formation, administration, tax filings, and audit all recur annually for a vehicle holding one asset. On a small SPV that overhead is a meaningful drag on return.

Economics vary widely. Some SPVs carry no management fee and 10–20% carry; others charge both. The structure is worth reading before participating.

Where it goes wrong

  • Underestimating the annual administrative cost relative to the size of the investment.
  • Stacking SPV carry on top of fund carry without disclosing it clearly to LPs.
  • Using an SPV to concentrate into a position without the diligence a new investment would get.
  • Forgetting the SPV has its own life and its own wind-down obligations.

Related terms

Venture builder (studio)#

A firm that starts companies itself instead of investing in other people's. It supplies the idea, the founding team, and the first money, and keeps a large stake because it was there on day zero.

Picture this: a traditional fund might own 8% of a company after a pre-seed check. A venture builder that hired the founders and named the company holds 30–50% — but it is now running the business, not backing it. Different job, different risk, different hours.

Why it matters

A venture studio creates companies rather than investing in them — generating the idea, assembling the team, and holding a much larger stake than an investor would. Typically 30–50% rather than 10–20%.

The model trades portfolio breadth for ownership depth. Studios produce fewer companies and own much more of each, which changes the arithmetic of the power law considerably.

What it looks like in practice

The operational reality is that studios are expensive to run — they carry the cost of building companies internally, not just evaluating them. That cost has to be funded from somewhere, usually a combination of fund economics and services revenue.

The recurring difficulty is founder recruitment. A talented founder can start their own company and keep most of the equity, so studios have to offer something that justifies the difference.

Where it goes wrong

  • Applying investor portfolio math to a studio, where the ownership and cost structure differ.
  • Underestimating how hard it is to recruit strong founders into a large-dilution structure.
  • Building companies the studio can staff rather than ones the market wants.
  • Treating studio equity as equivalent to founder equity when incentives differ.

Related terms

How a fund makes money

Read this one top to bottom the first time — it builds in order: the words you need, then what the GP earns, then the tiers money runs down on its way out, then the safety nets that decide whether the GP keeps any of it. One fund runs through every example so the numbers stay comparable.

How a fund makes money

Distribution#

Cash — or sometimes shares — actually leaving the fund and landing with LPs. Not a valuation, not a markup. Money out the door.

Picture this: a portfolio company is acquired and $60M wires into the fund. That is not a distribution yet. It becomes one when the fund passes it onward. Every rule in this section is a rule about how each distribution gets sliced on its way out.

Why it matters

A distribution is the only moment an LP actually receives money. Everything before it — markups, TVPI, paper gains — is an estimate. This is why DPI is the metric experienced LPs trust and TVPI is the one they discount.

It's also the event that triggers the waterfall, and therefore the point at which the carry arrangement stops being theoretical.

What it looks like in practice

Distributions happen when a portfolio company exits or when the fund sells a position. The proceeds run through the waterfall in the LPA, which determines how much goes to LPs and how much to the GP as carry.

Timing is a GP decision within limits. Distributing quickly is good for LP IRR; holding creates option value but extends the fund's life and delays the return.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reading a markup as equivalent to a distribution. One is cash; the other is an opinion.
  • Distributing before the waterfall is properly calculated, creating clawback exposure.
  • Holding a liquid position for optionality past the point where LPs need the return.
  • Not modelling the tax consequences for LPs of distribution timing.

Related terms

DPIDistributed to Paid-In. Cash actually returned. The number nobody can argue with.Realized vs. unrealizedRealized means it's over: the fund sold, got acquired out, or wrote the position to zero. Unrealized means you still hold it and are estimating…Distribution waterfallThe rules for splitting up each distribution, applied in a fixed order. Picture four buckets stacked vertically: money fills the top one…Distribution in kindPaying LPs in shares instead of cash, usually once a portfolio company is public and the lockup has expired. Carry is computed on the share price…Return of capitalTier one, and the tier that decides everything above it. LPs get back every dollar they paid in before profit is said to exist. The fight is over…

How a fund makes money

Realized vs. unrealized#

Realized means it's over: the fund sold, got acquired out, or wrote the position to zero. Unrealized means you still hold it and are estimating what it's worth.

Picture this: carry is only ever paid on realized gains. A portfolio marked at $400M pays the GP exactly $0. This is the entire reason a fund manager can look rich on paper for eight years and still not have been paid.

Why it matters

Realised gains are cash that exists. Unrealised gains are a valuation — usually the price of the last round, which is an estimate produced by a negotiation between other people.

The gap between them is where most venture optimism lives. A fund reporting a 4x TVPI with a 0.3x DPI is reporting one fact and one hope, and the distinction matters enormously when markets reprice.

What it looks like in practice

Unrealised value is normally carried at the most recent round price, marked down when there's evidence of impairment. That convention means marks are sticky — a company that raised at a high valuation two years ago may still be carried there.

The discipline is to look at DPI alongside TVPI, and at the age of the marks. A portfolio whose value rests on rounds priced in a very different market is carrying more risk than the number suggests.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reporting TVPI without DPI alongside it.
  • Carrying a position at a stale round price long after the market moved.
  • Treating a markup as evidence of judgment. The next round's price isn't your decision.
  • Comparing funds on unrealised value at different points in their lives.

How a fund makes money

Cost basis#

What the fund paid for a position. It has to come back before a single dollar counts as profit.

Picture this: the fund puts $10M into a company that exits for $60M. Cost basis $10M, gain $50M. Carry is calculated on the $50M, never on the $60M. On this one deal that distinction is worth $2M.

Why it matters

Cost basis is what was actually paid for a position, and it's the denominator for MOIC and the reference point for gains and losses. Simple in principle, and easy to get wrong when follow-ons are involved.

A position built across three rounds at different prices has one blended cost basis, and that blend determines whether the position is profitable — not the price of any single cheque.

What it looks like in practice

Every follow-on increases cost basis, which means defending a position that ultimately fails increases the loss. That's the real cost of reserves deployed badly.

Conversely, follow-ons into a winner at a higher price dilute the multiple even as they increase absolute return. A 20x on the seed cheque becomes a 6x blended if enough capital went in at Series C prices.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reporting the multiple on the initial cheque rather than on total invested.
  • Ignoring how follow-ons blend down a headline multiple.
  • Forgetting that fees paid are part of what LPs contributed, even if not part of cost basis.
  • Modelling reserves without accounting for their effect on the position's return profile.

How a fund makes money

Write-off#

Marking a position to zero because the company died. It counts as realized — it just realizes a loss instead of a gain.

Picture this: in venture this is the normal outcome, not the exception. Whether those zeros get subtracted before the GP takes carry on the winners is the single biggest variable in this whole section.

Why it matters

Write-offs are the expected case, not the exception. Under the power law most positions return nothing, and a portfolio without write-offs usually means the manager wasn't taking enough risk to catch an outlier.

The discipline is timing. Carrying a dead company at cost for years overstates the portfolio and delays the honest conversation with LPs.

What it looks like in practice

A position is written off when there's no realistic prospect of recovery — the company has ceased operations, or the preference stack makes the position worthless regardless of outcome.

The second case is the one that gets missed. A company still operating can be worth nothing to an early investor if later rounds stacked preferences above them.

Where it goes wrong

  • Carrying dead positions at cost to protect the reported TVPI.
  • Writing off only on formal shutdown, ignoring positions where the stack makes recovery impossible.
  • Reading write-offs as failures of judgment rather than as the expected distribution of outcomes.
  • Not learning anything from them, which is the only thing they're actually good for.

Related terms

How a fund makes money

The ten-check fund (our running example)#

One fund, reused for every calculation below so the numbers stay comparable. $100M raised, ten $10M investments. Fees are set aside for clarity — a real $100M fund invests about $80M and spends the rest on a decade of management fee.

CompanyWhat happensBack to the fund
AExits year 4$60M
B, C, DDie$0
E–ILimp along, small exits$2M each = $10M
JExits year 9$50M
Total$120M

Picture this: $120M back on $100M in. Profit: $20M. Carry genuinely earned at 20%: $4M. That $4M is the honest answer every structure below is trying to reach. Watch how far some of them wander from it.

Why it matters

A worked example is the only way this arithmetic becomes intuitive. Ten cheques, one outcome that matters, and a set of fees and carry taken along the way — run the numbers once and the structural constraints of venture become obvious.

The lesson it teaches most clearly is that the fund's return depends almost entirely on the size of the position in the one company that works, which makes ownership and reserves the decisions that matter.

What it looks like in practice

The pattern that emerges from any version of this example: roughly half the positions return nothing, a few return capital or a small multiple, and one has to return several times the whole fund for the fund to perform.

That's why a small ownership stake in a great company can be worse for the fund than a large stake in a good one, and why fund size and cheque size have to be designed together rather than separately.

Where it goes wrong

  • Building a portfolio model on average outcomes. Averages don't describe power-law distributions.
  • Assuming ten positions is enough diversification to reliably catch an outlier.
  • Ignoring fee drag, which means the portfolio must return well above 1x for LPs to break even.
  • Modelling entry ownership without modelling dilution through to exit.

How a fund makes money

Management fee#

An annual charge to run the firm — roughly 2% of committed capital. Pays salaries, travel, legal, diligence.

Picture this: the ten-check fund charges $2M a year. Over ten years that's $20M — a fifth of the fund, gone before a single investment is made. Which is why LPs care so much about fund size.

Why it matters

The management fee funds the firm — salaries, premises, everything. It's not profit, and for a small fund it's frequently not enough. A $20M fund at 2% generates $400,000 a year, which does not support a team.

It's also drawn from LP capital, so it reduces what's available to invest. Over a ten-year fund a 2% fee consumes roughly 20% of committed capital, which is why the portfolio has to return meaningfully more than 1x before LPs see their money back.

What it looks like in practice

The standard structure charges on committed capital during the investment period, then steps down to invested or net invested capital afterwards. That step-down is significant for the management company's budget and is often underplanned.

Fee offsets are worth checking: where a GP receives board fees or transaction fees from portfolio companies, LPs typically expect those to offset the management fee.

Where it goes wrong

  • Sizing a fund without checking whether the fee supports the necessary team.
  • Treating the fee as compensation rather than as the firm's operating budget.
  • Not planning for the post-investment-period step-down.
  • Failing to offset portfolio company fees against the management fee, which LPs will notice.

How a fund makes money

Carried interest ("carry")#

The GP's cut of the fund's profit, usually 20%. Not 20% of the money returned — 20% of what's left over after every dollar LPs paid in has already gone home.

Picture this: the ten-check fund returns $120M. Profit is $20M, so carry is $4M and LPs keep $116M. Notice how small $4M looks beside a "$120M returned" headline. Carry is still what makes a fund manager wealthy; fees just keep the lights on.

Why it matters

Carry is the GP's share of profits and the entire economic reason to run a fund rather than take a salary. It's also where the alignment is: carry only pays if LPs make money first.

The size of the number is often misunderstood. Twenty percent of the profits on a fund that does well is a lot of money — but it arrives years after the work, only if the fund performs, and it's shared across the partnership.

What it looks like in practice

Carry is calculated through the waterfall, which determines when and how much is paid. The details — hurdle, catch-up, European versus American — change the timing and sometimes the total substantially.

Tax treatment is the perennial policy fight. Section 1061 requires a three-year holding period for carry to receive long-term capital gains treatment, which for venture is usually satisfied comfortably.

Where it goes wrong

  • Modelling carry without the waterfall. The structure determines when it's actually received.
  • Assuming carry is received as profits accrue. Under a European waterfall it comes at the end.
  • Forgetting carry is subject to clawback if later losses reverse earlier gains.
  • Ignoring vesting, which determines what a departing partner keeps.

How a fund makes money

2 and 20#

The standard package: 2% annual fee, 20% of profits.

The tension: fees are paid whether or not the fund performs. A big fund can pay its GPs well while returning nothing. That's why a serious emerging manager points at carry, not fees.

Why it matters

Two percent management fee and twenty percent carry is the industry default, and defaults are powerful — most funds land near it because deviating requires justification on both sides.

It's less universal than it sounds. Large funds often charge less than 2% because the absolute fee is enormous; top-performing managers sometimes charge 25–30% carry because they can.

What it looks like in practice

The variations that matter: fee percentage and the base it's charged on, carry percentage, whether there's a hurdle, and which waterfall applies. Two funds both described as "2 and 20" can have materially different economics.

For emerging managers the fee is often the binding constraint. A first fund small enough to raise generates a fee too small to operate on, which is why many first-time GPs are effectively subsidising their own firm.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming two funds quoting the same headline terms have the same economics.
  • Ignoring the fee base, which changes the absolute number substantially.
  • Negotiating carry percentage while ignoring the hurdle and waterfall structure.
  • Treating the standard as immutable when the market varies by fund size and track record.

How a fund makes money

Carry pool#

The fund's total carry, divided among the people at the firm. The GP entity earns it; individuals hold points in it.

Picture this: the ten-check fund's $4M is the pool. Two founding partners take 40% each, and the last 20% is spread across a principal, an associate and a platform hire. The principal's 5% comes to $200K — before vesting, and nine years after they started working on it.

Why it matters

The carry pool is how carried interest is divided among the partnership. It's the compensation structure that actually matters at a venture firm, and it's usually invisible from outside.

Allocation drives behaviour. A junior partner with a small carry allocation on a fund that may not pay for eight years has weak long-term incentives, which is one reason venture firms have retention problems at that level.

What it looks like in practice

Allocations are typically set per fund rather than firm-wide, which means each new fund is an opportunity to reallocate. Points are usually granted with vesting attached.

A portion is often reserved for future hires, so a fund raised today can accommodate a partner joining in year three without renegotiating everyone else's share.

Where it goes wrong

  • Allocating the full pool at fund formation with nothing reserved for future hires.
  • Setting allocations without vesting, so a departing partner keeps everything.
  • Assuming firm equity and carry allocation track each other. They usually don't.
  • Treating carry as a substitute for salary when it may not pay for a decade.

Distribution waterfall#

The rules for splitting up each distribution, applied in a fixed order. Picture four buckets stacked vertically: money fills the top one completely before a single dollar spills into the one below. Carry lives in the bottom bucket.

TierWho gets itUntil
1. Return of capital100% LPLPs have every dollar they paid in back
2. Preferred return100% LPLPs have earned the hurdle, usually 8%/yr
3. GP catch-up100% GPGP holds 20% of the profit paid so far
4. The split80% LP / 20% GPForever after

Most venture funds only run tiers 1 and 4 — capital back, then straight 80/20. Tiers 2 and 3 are private-equity furniture that shows up in VC mainly when a large institutional LP asks for them.

Picture this: the ten-check fund returns $120M. Tier 1 sends the first $100M straight to LPs. The $20M sitting above it is profit: LPs $16M, GP $4M. That's the whole idea. Every remaining term in this section is an argument about when the GP gets that $4M and what it was calculated on.

Why it matters

The waterfall is the mechanism that turns proceeds into payments, and its structure determines when the GP gets paid and how much risk LPs carry. It's the single most important economic section of the LPA.

The four tiers — return of capital, preferred return, GP catch-up, then the carry split — look procedural but each one is negotiated, and the differences compound across a fund's life.

What it looks like in practice

Money fills each tier completely before spilling into the next. LPs get their capital back, then their preferred return, then the GP catches up to its carry percentage, then everything splits at the agreed rate.

Whether the waterfall runs on the whole fund or deal by deal is the biggest single variable, and it changes the timing of GP payments by years.

Where it goes wrong

  • Modelling carry as a simple percentage of gains without running the tiers.
  • Ignoring which capital counts as returned — invested only, or invested plus fees.
  • Not checking whether the preferred return compounds.
  • Assuming the waterfall type is standard. It varies more than the fee and carry do.

How a fund makes money

Return of capital#

Tier one, and the tier that decides everything above it. LPs get back every dollar they paid in before profit is said to exist. The fight is over what counts as "paid in."

Picture this: a real $100M fund invests about $80M and spends $20M on ten years of management fee. Narrow reading — LPs are whole once $80M comes back, and the GP starts earning carry there. Proper reading, and the market standard — LPs are whole at $100M, fees included. On a fund returning $120M that one definition is the difference between $8M of carry and $4M. It's the first clause a serious LP turns to.

Why it matters

Return of capital is the first tier of the waterfall: LPs get their money back before anyone shares in profits. It's the foundation of the alignment, and the definition of "their money" is worth reading closely.

The question is whether it means capital invested in companies, or all capital contributed including fees and expenses. The difference is roughly 20% of the fund over its life, which is not a detail.

What it looks like in practice

LP-favourable structures return all contributed capital — investments plus fees plus expenses — before any carry is paid. GP-favourable ones return only invested capital, which lets carry start earlier.

The distinction also interacts with the waterfall type. Under an American waterfall the return- of-capital test may be applied deal by deal rather than across the whole fund.

Where it goes wrong

  • Not checking whether fees are included in the capital that must be returned.
  • Assuming return of capital means LPs are whole. It usually precedes the preferred return.
  • Modelling DPI of 1.0 as break-even for LPs when fees mean it isn't.
  • Overlooking how the definition interacts with deal-by-deal distributions.

Hurdle rate / preferred return#

Tier two. A minimum annual return LPs must receive before the GP earns any carry — usually 8%, compounding, on the capital actually drawn.

Picture this: most venture LPAs skip it entirely. An 8% hurdle is either irrelevant (a 3x fund sails past it) or unreachable (a 0.9x fund was never getting there), so the clause does most of its real work in private equity. The ten-check fund at 1.2x never clears it. When a hurdle does show up in a VC fund, the fight that follows is always about the catch-up.

Why it matters

The hurdle is the minimum return LPs receive before the GP participates in profits. It exists because LPs could have put the money in something safer, and the GP should only be paid for beating that alternative.

In venture, hurdles are less universal than in private equity — many venture funds have none, on the reasoning that venture risk is not comparable to a fixed return threshold. Where they exist, 8% is the conventional number.

What it looks like in practice

The hurdle is usually expressed as an annual IRR on contributed capital, and whether it compounds matters over a ten-year fund. It's calculated across the fund, not per deal, unless the LPA says otherwise.

The interaction with the catch-up is what determines the economics. A hurdle with a full catch- up behaves very differently from one without.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming a venture fund has a hurdle. Many don't.
  • Ignoring whether the preferred return compounds, which matters a great deal over ten years.
  • Modelling the hurdle without the catch-up tier that follows it.
  • Confusing a hard hurdle with a soft one — they produce very different outcomes.
