GP catch-up#

Tier three, and the one nobody explains. Once LPs have their capital and their preferred return, the GP takes 100% of the next dollars — not 20%, all of them — until they're holding 20% of all the profit paid out so far. Only then does the 80/20 split start.

The ten-check fund never reaches this tier, so take a stronger one: $100M in, $200M out, with $20M of preferred return accrued.

Picture this: LPs take $100M (capital), then $20M (pref). Profit paid so far: $20M, every dollar of it to LPs. Now the GP catches up — they take the next $5M at 100%, which makes profit $25M with $5M to the GP: exactly 20%. The final $75M splits 80/20 → LPs $60M, GP $15M. GP total: $20M, precisely 20% of the fund's $100M profit. The hurdle delayed the GP's money. With a full catch-up, it never cost them a dollar of it.

Why it matters

The catch-up is the tier that restores the GP to its full carry percentage after LPs have received their preferred return. Without it, a hurdle would permanently reduce the GP's share of total profits rather than just delaying it.

With a 100% catch-up, once the hurdle is met the GP receives all distributions until it has received 20% of total profits — then everything splits 80/20 as intended.

What it looks like in practice

The catch-up rate is negotiated. A 100% catch-up gets the GP to its full share quickly; a 50% catch-up splits distributions during the catch-up tier and takes longer.

This combination — hurdle plus full catch-up — is what makes a soft hurdle soft. The GP ends up with the same total percentage as if there were no hurdle, just later.

Where it goes wrong

  • Modelling a hurdle without the catch-up, which overstates the LP's share of total profits.
  • Assuming the catch-up rate is always 100%.
  • Not checking whether the catch-up applies to profits or to distributions.
  • Treating hurdle and catch-up as separate negotiations. They only make sense together.

Hard hurdle vs. soft hurdle#

A soft hurdle pairs the preferred return with a full catch-up, so once the fund clears the bar the GP still earns 20% of all profit. A hard hurdle has no catch-up — the GP earns carry only on profit above the hurdle, and never gets that first slice back.

Picture this: the $200M-on-$100M fund again. Soft hurdle: the GP ends at $20M. Hard hurdle: LPs keep $120M off the top and the GP splits only the remaining $80M → $16M. Same fund, same "20%" headline, $4M apart. So when a term sheet says "8% preferred return," the next question is always "with catch-up?"

Why it matters

A soft hurdle delays the GP's carry; a hard hurdle permanently reduces it. Under a soft hurdle with full catch-up, the GP eventually receives carry on all profits. Under a hard hurdle, the GP only receives carry on profits above the threshold.

The difference is substantial and it's expressed in a single word in the LPA. Soft hurdles dominate in practice, which is why they're often described simply as "a hurdle."

What it looks like in practice

With a soft hurdle and an 8% preferred return, once LPs clear 8% the catch-up gives the GP 20% of everything from the first dollar of profit. With a hard hurdle, the first 8% is permanently excluded from the carry calculation.

On a fund returning 3x, the difference between the two structures runs to a significant share of the total carry.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming a hurdle is hard when almost all are soft.
  • Modelling the two identically, which produces materially wrong carry numbers.
  • Negotiating the hurdle rate without establishing which type applies.
  • Ignoring the interaction with the catch-up rate, which determines the effective outcome.

How a fund makes money

European waterfall (whole-of-fund)#

Carry is worked out on the fund as one single pot. Everything LPs paid in comes back first — every investment, plus fees, plus expenses — before the GP sees a cent. The default today, and effectively mandatory for a first-time manager.

Picture this: the ten-check fund, year by year. Year 4 — Company A returns $60M, all of it to LPs, who are still $40M short of whole. Carry: $0. Years 5–8 — three companies die, five return $2M each, LPs reach $70M. Carry: $0. Year 9 — Company J returns $50M. The first $30M finishes paying LPs back; the last $20M is the fund's profit and splits 80/20. GP carry: $4M, first dollar received in year 9. Exactly what was earned, nine years after the work started.

Why it matters

Under a European waterfall no carry is paid until LPs have received all their contributed capital plus the preferred return across the entire fund. It's the LP-favourable structure and the standard in Europe, increasingly common everywhere.

The practical effect is that clawback risk mostly disappears, because the GP isn't paid until the fund's overall outcome is known.

What it looks like in practice

For the GP it means carry arrives late — often year seven or later — which is a real cash-flow problem for a firm whose partners need to be paid in the meantime. That's part of why management fees matter so much.

For LPs it removes the risk of paying carry on early winners and then watching later losses reverse the gains without a reliable way to get the money back.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming European means no clawback provision is needed. One is still included.
  • Modelling GP cash flows as though carry arrives with each exit.
  • Treating the two waterfall types as economically equivalent over the fund's life. Timing has real value.
  • Not checking which structure applies before modelling fund economics.

American waterfall (deal-by-deal)#

Carry is worked out one investment at a time. A company exits, LPs get that deal's cost back, and the gain splits 80/20 immediately. The GP gets paid years earlier — and can end up holding carry the fund never earned.

Picture this: same fund, same ten companies, same outcomes. Year 4 — Company A returns $60M: hand LPs back the $10M cost, split the $50M gain → GP takes $10M. Years 5–8 — the write-offs and small exits pay no carry, but nothing takes the year-4 money back either. Year 9 — Company J returns $50M: return the $10M cost, split the $40M gain → GP takes another $8M. Final tally: $18M of carry paid out by a fund that made $20M of profit. They earned $4M. They are holding $18M.

Why it matters

Under an American waterfall carry is calculated on each investment as it exits, which means the GP receives carry on early winners before the fund's overall outcome is known.

That's GP-favourable on timing and creates the risk the clawback exists to address: carry paid on an early success may have to be returned if later losses mean LPs didn't actually clear their preferred return across the fund.

What it looks like in practice

Because of that risk, deal-by-deal structures come with protective machinery: interim clawback tests, escrow accounts holding back a portion of carry, and personal guarantees from individual partners.

The structure has become less common as LPs have pushed back, and ILPA's principles explicitly favour whole-of-fund distribution.

Where it goes wrong

  • Spending carry received under a deal-by-deal waterfall before the clawback risk has passed.
  • Agreeing to deal-by-deal without escrow or interim testing.
  • Assuming the clawback is enforceable in practice. Recovering paid carry from individuals is hard.
  • Modelling the fund's economics without accounting for the timing difference this creates.

The same fund, both ways#

The comparison worth memorizing. Identical fund, identical companies, identical outcomes — only the waterfall clause changes.

EuropeanAmerican (deal-by-deal)
Carry paid in year 4$0$10M
Carry paid in year 9$4M$8M
Total carry taken$4M$18M
Carry actually earned$4M$4M
Owed back at wind-down$0$14M
GP's first dollarYear 9Year 4

Picture this: the headline split is 20% in both columns. The dollars are 4.5x apart and the timing is five years apart. Every term that follows — loss carryforward, clawback, escrow, interim tests, tax — exists to answer one question: does that $14M actually come back?

Why it matters

Running one set of portfolio outcomes through both waterfall structures is the fastest way to see that the total carry can be identical while the timing — and therefore the risk — is completely different.

The comparison also shows where the clawback risk comes from, and why LPs care about the structure even when the headline carry percentage is the same.

What it looks like in practice

The pattern that emerges: with an early winner and later losses, the American waterfall pays carry that the European one would never have paid. Whether that money comes back depends entirely on whether the clawback works.

Where all the outcomes are positive, the two structures converge on the same total and differ only in when the GP receives it — which still has real value given the time involved.

Where it goes wrong

  • Concluding the structures are equivalent because total carry can match. Timing and risk differ.
  • Modelling only the good scenario, where the difference is smallest.
  • Ignoring the float — the value to the GP of receiving money years earlier.
  • Assuming clawback fully neutralises the difference. In practice recovery is imperfect.

Loss carryforward#

The clause that decides how brutal an American waterfall really is. Before the GP takes carry on a winner, the LPA may require that losses already realized on other deals be paid back to LPs first. Three flavors, GP-friendly to LP-friendly: pure deal-by-deal (only that deal's cost comes back), deal-by-deal with loss carryforward (realized write-offs come back too), and whole-of-fund — which is just European by another name.

Picture this: rerun year 9 of the ten-check fund with a loss carryforward. $70M of losses are on the books by then — three write-offs, plus five companies that returned $2M on $10M each. Company J's $50M can't cover them, so the GP's year-9 carry drops from $8M to $0 and total carry taken falls from $18M to $10M. Whether your losses land before or after your wins quietly decides how much carry you ever touch.

Why it matters

A loss carryforward provision requires realised losses to be netted against realised gains before carry is calculated. Without it, a deal-by-deal waterfall would pay carry on every winner while ignoring every loser.

It's one of the main protections that makes an American waterfall tolerable to LPs, and its absence is a red flag in an LPA.

What it looks like in practice

The mechanism carries forward realised losses and offsets them against subsequent gains, so carry is only paid on net profits rather than gross ones.

Variations matter: whether it covers only realised losses or also writes down unrealised positions, and whether it applies across the whole fund or only within a period.

Where it goes wrong

  • Agreeing to a deal-by-deal waterfall without a loss carryforward.
  • Applying it only to realised losses while ignoring obviously impaired positions.
  • Assuming it's standard. It has to be in the document.
  • Modelling carry on gross gains rather than net of carried-forward losses.

The float#

The advantage that survives even a perfect clawback: the GP had the money for years, and you never get that back.

Picture this: the deal-by-deal GP held $10M from year 4 to year 9. Five years of use on that money is worth roughly $4M at 7%. Even if every dollar of the $14M is returned on schedule and in full, the two structures were never actually equal.

Why it matters

The float is the value of holding money you may later have to return. Under a deal-by-deal waterfall a GP can receive carry in year four that isn't finally earned until year ten — and having that money for six years is worth something real.

It's the economic reason GPs prefer American waterfalls even when the total carry is identical, and the reason LPs push back.

What it looks like in practice

Escrow arrangements exist to reduce it: holding back a portion of carry until the fund's outcome is clearer means the GP doesn't have use of that money in the meantime.

It's rarely quantified explicitly in negotiations, but it's a meaningful part of what the waterfall type is actually worth to each side.

Where it goes wrong

  • Ignoring the float when comparing waterfall structures.
  • Spending floated carry, which makes a clawback obligation genuinely painful.
  • Assuming escrow removes it entirely. Escrow reduces it; it doesn't eliminate the timing benefit.
  • Treating it as a technicality rather than as real economic value.

How a fund makes money

Clawback#

The provision forcing a GP to hand back carry they were paid too early. It's the thing that makes an American waterfall defensible in theory: whatever happened deal by deal, the fund trues up to whole-fund math at the end and the GP repays the difference.

Picture this: the deal-by-deal GP took $18M from the ten-check fund and earned $4M, so the clawback says $14M goes back. Whether it actually does comes down to three clauses nobody reads: whether it's tested before wind-down, whether any of the carry sat in escrow, and whether it's owed gross or net of tax. The next three terms are those three clauses.

Why it matters

The clawback requires the GP to return carry that turns out not to have been earned once the fund's full outcome is known. It's the safety net under a deal-by-deal waterfall.

The problem is enforcement. By the time a clawback is triggered the money may have been distributed to individual partners, spent, and taxed — and recovering it from people who have left the firm is genuinely difficult.

What it looks like in practice

The protections that make it work in practice are escrow accounts holding back a share of carry, interim testing during the fund's life, and personal guarantees from individual partners.

Net-of-tax clawbacks limit the obligation to what the GP received after tax, which is reasonable from the GP's side and reduces the LP's recovery.

Where it goes wrong

  • Relying on a clawback provision with no escrow or guarantee behind it.
  • Assuming departed partners will return carry. Often the obligation is practically unenforceable.
  • Not testing the clawback position during the fund's life, so it only surfaces at the end.
  • Distributing carry to individuals without holding back for the potential obligation.

How a fund makes money

Wind-down#

The end of a fund's life. Remaining positions are sold or written off, the final waterfall is run, escrow is released, any clawback is collected, and the partnership dissolves.

Picture this: this is when a clawback finally gets tested in most LPAs — year 10 or later. A GP who took carry in year 4 has had six years to spend it, change firms, or become someone you'd have to sue. That gap is the entire reason interim tests and escrow exist.

Why it matters

Wind-down is the end of a fund's life: remaining positions are sold, distributed in kind, or written off, final distributions are made, and the clawback is settled.

It's where the residual problems surface. Positions that can't be sold, companies that are neither dead nor liquid, and LPs who want their money back regardless are all wind-down problems.

What it looks like in practice

GPs usually seek extensions rather than force bad exits, typically one year at a time with LP or LPAC consent. Beyond that the options are secondary sales of the remaining portfolio, distribution in kind, or a continuation vehicle.

The final accounting includes settling the clawback, releasing escrow, and closing the partnership — which can take a further year after the last position is resolved.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming extensions will be granted indefinitely.
  • Forcing exits at bad prices to meet a deadline rather than negotiating an extension.
  • Distributing illiquid securities to LPs who have no ability to hold or sell them.
  • Not planning for the clawback settlement, which is the last thing to close.

How a fund makes money

Interim clawback test#

A mid-life true-up. Instead of waiting for wind-down, the LPA reruns the whole-fund math on a schedule — often every two or three years, or at the end of the investment period — and makes the GP return any excess then.

Picture this: the deal-by-deal GP took $10M in year 4. A year-6 test reruns the numbers: the fund has returned $70M against $100M in, so earned carry is $0 and $10M goes back six years before the fund closes. Without an interim test, LPs spend a decade as unsecured creditors of a person.

Why it matters

An interim clawback test calculates, at defined points during the fund's life, whether the GP would owe money if the fund were wound up that day. It surfaces the problem early rather than at the end.

That's valuable because clawback recovery gets harder over time. A shortfall identified in year six can be addressed by withholding future carry; one identified in year eleven requires clawing back money that's been spent.

What it looks like in practice

Tests are typically run annually or at defined intervals, and a shortfall triggers either an escrow top-up or suspension of further carry distributions.

It's one of the ILPA-recommended protections for deal-by-deal structures, and its presence is a reasonable proxy for how LP-friendly the rest of the LPA is.

Where it goes wrong

  • Agreeing to deal-by-deal carry with no interim testing.
  • Running the test only at wind-down, when it's too late to be useful.
  • Ignoring a shortfall on the assumption later gains will cover it.
  • Not tying the test to a concrete remedy, which makes it informational rather than protective.

How a fund makes money

Escrow (carry holdback)#

The slice of every carry distribution the fund withholds against a future clawback — typically 20–30%, released at wind-down.

Picture this: the GP's $10M of year-4 carry arrives as $7M in the bank and $3M sitting in escrow. Which is why "the fund paid carry" and "the GP got the money" are two different sentences.

Why it matters

Escrow holds back a portion of carry distributions so there's money available if a clawback is later triggered. It converts an unenforceable promise into a funded one.

It also reduces the float, which is precisely why GPs resist it and LPs want it. The percentage held back is a direct negotiation over how much timing benefit the GP keeps.

What it looks like in practice

Typical holdbacks run 20–30% of carry distributions, released as the fund's outcome becomes clearer or at wind-down. The escrow is usually held by a third party rather than the GP.

It works alongside interim testing: the test determines whether there's a shortfall, and the escrow is where the money to cover it actually sits.

Where it goes wrong

  • Agreeing to a clawback with no escrow behind it.
  • Releasing escrow early because the fund looks like it will perform.
  • Holding escrow with the GP rather than a third party.
  • Setting the holdback percentage too low to cover a realistic shortfall.

How a fund makes money

Net-of-tax clawback#

The clause that turns a timing difference into a permanent dollar difference. Most clawbacks are capped at what the GP kept after paying tax on the carry — so when the money goes back, the tax already paid to the IRS does not come with it. LPs absorb that.

Picture this: the deal-by-deal GP took $18M and owes $14M back. At roughly 35% combined federal and California tax they kept $11.7M, and a net-of-tax clawback caps the repayment there. LPs are permanently short $2.3M — 11.5% of the fund's entire profit — under a structure that was supposed to be economically identical to European.

Why it matters

A net-of-tax clawback limits the GP's repayment obligation to what it actually kept after paying tax on the carry. The argument is straightforward: a GP who received $1M and paid $400,000 in tax shouldn't have to return $1M.

For LPs it's a real reduction in recovery, and it's one of the terms where reasonable positions genuinely conflict.

What it looks like in practice

The mechanics involve assumptions about the GP's tax rate, which are specified in the LPA rather than calculated individually. Whether the GP can amend prior returns to recover the tax affects how fair the provision is.

It's common enough to be considered market, but the specific assumed rate and whether it accounts for actual tax recovery are worth reading.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming the clawback is gross when the LPA specifies net-of-tax.
  • Modelling LP recovery at 100% of paid carry when the provision limits it.
  • Not checking the assumed tax rate, which can be set favourably to the GP.
  • Ignoring whether the GP can amend prior tax returns, which changes what's genuinely lost.

How a fund makes money

Carry vesting#

Carry belongs to the firm; your personal slice of the carry pool vests over time — commonly four to six years, often with a one-year cliff, and usually per-fund rather than per-person.

Picture this: you join the ten-check fund as a principal holding 5% of the pool, and you leave in year 3 of a four-year vest. You keep 75% of your 5% — which is 3.75% of $4M, or $150K — on a fund that won't distribute carry until year 9. You will be waiting six years after you left to find out what it was worth.

Why it matters

Carry vesting determines what a partner keeps if they leave before the fund pays out. Given that carry can take eight years to arrive, this is the term that actually governs partner retention.

It also matters to LPs, because a partnership where senior people can leave with full carry has weak continuity — and continuity is much of what LPs are buying.

What it looks like in practice

Typical schedules run four to five years, sometimes tied to the investment period rather than to calendar time. Good-leaver and bad-leaver provisions determine whether vested carry is kept or forfeited depending on the circumstances of departure.

The distinction between vested and unvested carry at departure is one of the more contested points in partnership agreements, and it's worth settling explicitly rather than by reference to general principles.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting carry with no vesting, which removes the retention it's meant to create.
  • Leaving good-leaver and bad-leaver definitions vague.
  • Vesting on calendar time when the work is concentrated in the investment period.
  • Not reallocating forfeited carry, so it sits unassigned.

How a fund makes money

Distribution in kind#

Paying LPs in shares instead of cash, usually once a portfolio company is public and the lockup has expired. Carry is computed on the share price the day the shares go out.

Picture this: the fund holds 2M shares of a newly public company at $30. Rather than sell into the market, it distributes the stock. The waterfall treats it as $60M returned — and every LP carries their own price risk from that morning forward.

Why it matters

A distribution in kind gives LPs securities rather than cash — usually shares in a company that has gone public. It transfers the decision about when to sell from the GP to the LP.

That can be helpful, since LPs have different tax positions and different views. It can also be unwelcome, since some LPs can't hold public equities and are forced to sell immediately, sometimes into a falling price.

What it looks like in practice

Most common after an IPO, once a lock-up expires. The LPA usually specifies how the securities are valued for the purpose of calculating carry, which matters because the price moves.

Coordinated distributions can move a stock if the position is large relative to trading volume, which is a real consideration for both the GP's reported return and the LPs' realised one.

Where it goes wrong

  • Distributing in kind to LPs who are unable to hold the securities.
  • Not specifying the valuation date, which determines the carry calculation.
  • Ignoring the market impact of a large coordinated distribution.
  • Treating the distribution date value as the return LPs actually achieved.

The three-year hold (Section 1061)#

Carry is taxed as capital gain, but since 2017 the underlying asset has to be held more than three years or the GP's carry on it is recharacterized as short-term and taxed at ordinary rates.

Picture this: a company you funded 26 months ago gets acquired. The LPs are thrilled; your carry on that exit is taxed near 37% instead of near 20%. Venture holding periods usually clear three years without trying, which is exactly why the rule bites private equity and hedge funds harder than it bites us.

Why it matters

Section 1061 requires carried interest to be held for more than three years to receive long-term capital gains treatment. Below that, it's taxed as short-term.

For venture the rule is rarely binding, because holding periods are typically far longer. It matters more for strategies with faster turnover, and it's the current form of a policy argument that has run for over a decade.

What it looks like in practice

The holding period applies to the underlying assets, not to the fund interest, which is the detail that trips people up. An early exit inside three years produces short-term treatment on that carry even in an otherwise long-lived fund.

The rule was introduced by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, extending the previous one-year requirement.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming the holding period runs from fund formation rather than from the asset.
  • Ignoring it for a fast acquisition inside three years.
  • Treating the current rule as settled policy. It has been repeatedly proposed for change.
  • Applying the rule without checking how it interacts with the specific fund structure.

Recycling#

Reinvesting early returns instead of distributing them, so more than 100% of the fund gets deployed. Usually capped, and often zero for new managers.

Why it matters

Recycling lets a fund reinvest early proceeds rather than distributing them, so more than 100% of committed capital ends up deployed. It's how a fund offsets the drag of management fees on invested capital.

Without recycling, a fund charging 2% for ten years invests only about 80% of what LPs committed. Recycling closes that gap.

What it looks like in practice

The LPA sets limits: usually a cap on the total that can be recycled, often 110–125% of commitments, and a time limit tied to the investment period.

It's generally LP-favourable because it puts more capital to work, but it also delays distributions, which affects IRR. The trade-off is between more invested capital and slower return of cash.

Where it goes wrong

  • Recycling beyond what the LPA permits.
  • Recycling late in the fund's life, when there isn't time for the investment to mature.
  • Modelling deployment at 100% of commitments when fees mean it's lower without recycling.
  • Ignoring the effect on IRR of delaying distributions.

MOIC#

Multiple on Invested Capital. The raw multiple. $1M in, $3M out = 3x. Ignores time completely.

Why it matters

MOIC is the simplest performance measure: what a position is worth divided by what was paid for it. No time adjustment, no fee adjustment — just the multiple.

Its simplicity is both the strength and the weakness. A 3x MOIC over four years and a 3x over twelve are the same number and completely different investments, which is why MOIC and IRR are always read together.

What it looks like in practice

MOIC is usually quoted per position or across a portfolio at the gross level — before fees and carry. TVPI is the LP-level equivalent, calculated after fees on contributed capital.

The gap between gross MOIC and net TVPI is the cost of the fund structure, and it's substantial. A gross 3x can be a net 2.2x once fees and carry are taken.

Where it goes wrong

  • Comparing gross MOIC to net TVPI, which flatters the fund.
  • Quoting MOIC without the holding period.
  • Calculating it on the initial cheque rather than total invested including follow-ons.
  • Reading an unrealised MOIC as though the value were established.

TVPI#

Total Value to Paid-In. Everything distributed plus what's still held, divided by money in. The headline number.

Picture this: $1M invested, $500K already returned, $1.5M still in the portfolio → TVPI = 2.0x.

Why it matters

TVPI is total value to paid-in: distributions plus remaining value, divided by what LPs have contributed. It's the headline number for a fund's performance and the one most vulnerable to optimistic marks.

TVPI equals DPI plus RVPI, which is the useful decomposition. A 3.0x TVPI made of 2.5x DPI is a very different fund from a 3.0x made of 0.2x DPI.

What it looks like in practice

Because it uses paid-in capital as the denominator, TVPI accounts for fees — LPs contributed that money too. That makes it a fairer measure than gross multiples.

Early in a fund's life TVPI is dominated by unrealised marks and is close to meaningless. The J-curve means it typically sits below 1.0x for the first several years as fees are drawn before value is created.

Where it goes wrong

  • Quoting TVPI without DPI, which hides how much is realised.
  • Comparing TVPI across funds of different vintages and ages.
  • Treating early-life TVPI as predictive. It mostly reflects marks and fee drag.
  • Calculating it against committed rather than paid-in capital.

DPI#

Distributed to Paid-In. Cash actually returned. The number nobody can argue with.

Picture this: in that same fund, DPI = 0.5x. TVPI says 2.0x, but only half your money has genuinely come home. When a fund brags about TVPI and goes quiet about DPI, that's the tell.

Why it matters

DPI is distributions to paid-in — cash actually returned divided by cash actually contributed. It's the number experienced LPs care about most, because it can't be marked up.

A DPI of 1.0 means LPs have their money back. Everything above that is real profit, and everything below it is still a promise.

What it looks like in practice

DPI takes years to become meaningful. A fund four years in with a DPI near zero is normal; the same fund at year nine is a problem.

The pairing with TVPI tells the story. A high TVPI with a low DPI means the value is all on paper — which may be fine, and may be a portfolio carrying stale marks from a different market.

Where it goes wrong

  • Ignoring DPI because TVPI looks good.
  • Comparing DPI across funds without adjusting for age.
  • Treating recallable distributions as permanent DPI.
  • Assuming a fund with strong marks will convert them into distributions.

RVPI#

Residual Value to Paid-In. What's still in the ground — paper value, self-reported.

Why it matters

RVPI is residual value to paid-in — what's still held, at current marks, divided by contributed capital. It's the unrealised half of TVPI, and the half that can change without anything happening.

It's the number most sensitive to valuation policy. A portfolio carried at stale round prices from a hotter market has an RVPI that overstates what the positions would fetch.

What it looks like in practice

RVPI declines over a fund's life as positions exit and value converts into DPI. A mature fund with a high RVPI and a low DPI has positions it hasn't been able to realise.

The quality question is how the marks were set. Last-round pricing is standard, but a round priced three years ago in different conditions is a weak basis for a current valuation.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reading RVPI as value that will be realised. Much of it won't be.
  • Not checking how old the marks underlying it are.
  • Comparing RVPI across managers with different valuation policies.
  • Expecting RVPI to stay flat. It should convert to DPI or be written down.

IRR#

Internal Rate of Return. The annualized return, accounting for timing.

Picture this: 3x over 3 years is a much better IRR than 3x over 12 years. IRR is also the most gameable number in venture — early markups inflate it — so read it beside DPI, never alone.

Why it matters

IRR is the annualised rate of return accounting for the timing of every cash flow. It's the measure that captures what MOIC can't — that money returned early is worth more than money returned late.

It's also the most manipulable venture metric. Because early cash flows dominate the calculation, a quick early exit or a subscription credit line can produce an IRR that flatters a mediocre fund.

What it looks like in practice

The distortions worth knowing: credit lines that delay capital calls raise IRR without changing the return; early distributions have outsized effect; and IRR is unstable early in a fund's life when the cash flows are few.

This is why ILPA pushes for reporting both with and without subscription lines, and why IRR should always be read alongside a multiple.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reading IRR without a multiple alongside it.
  • Comparing IRRs computed with and without subscription credit lines.
  • Taking early-life IRR seriously. It's dominated by fee outflows and noise.
  • Assuming a high IRR means large absolute returns. A fast small win produces both.

Markup#

Writing a company's value up because a later round priced it higher. Real signal, imaginary money.

Picture this: you invest at $10M. Two years later they raise at $60M. Your stake is marked up 6x. You have not received a dollar.

Why it matters

A markup is an increase in the carried value of a position, usually because a new round priced higher. It feels like performance and isn't — it's someone else's pricing decision recorded in your books.

Markups are also how early-stage funds show progress before any distributions exist, which creates an incentive to chase them. That incentive is worth being conscious of.

What it looks like in practice

The convention is to mark to the most recent priced round. That makes marks sticky and lumpy — nothing changes for two years, then everything changes at once.

A markup is genuine information about a company's trajectory, and it is not a realisation. The honest framing is that it raises the probability of a good outcome without delivering one.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reporting markups as returns.
  • Optimising for markups rather than for exits, which are different objectives.
  • Marking up on a round with heavy structure, where the headline price overstates value.
  • Failing to mark down when conditions clearly changed.

The Power Law#

One investment returns more than all the others combined. Not a quirk — the organizing principle of the whole asset class.

Picture this: 30 investments. 20 die. 8 return roughly the money. 1 returns 2x. And 1 returns 50x and pays for everything. The job isn't avoiding the 20 — it's guaranteeing you're in the 1.

Why it matters

Venture returns follow a power law: a very small number of investments produce most of the return, and the median investment returns little or nothing. This isn't a risk to be managed — it's the structure of the asset class.

Everything else in fund construction follows from it. Portfolio size, ownership targets, reserve policy, and the willingness to lose money on most positions are all consequences of this one fact.

What it looks like in practice

The practical implications are uncomfortable. You need enough positions to have a reasonable chance of catching an outlier, enough ownership in that outlier for it to matter, and the discipline to keep funding the winner rather than rescuing the losers.

It also means average outcomes are the wrong thing to model. A portfolio built to produce a reliable 2x will not produce a fund-returning outcome, because the strategies that avoid zeros also avoid the tail.

Where it goes wrong

  • Building a portfolio model on expected averages rather than on the tail.
  • Diversifying so broadly that no position can return the fund.
  • Concentrating so narrowly that missing the outlier is likely.
  • Deploying reserves to defend failing positions rather than to double down on the working one.

Doing the work
Doing the work

Deal flow#

The total number of opportunities you see per unit of time. Quality of deal flow is most of the job.

Picture this: an active early-stage firm sees roughly 1,000 opportunities a year.

Why it matters

Deal flow is the top of the funnel, and it constrains everything below it. You cannot invest in a company you never saw, which makes sourcing the one part of the job that has no substitute.

Quality matters more than volume past a point. A thousand inbound decks that don't match the thesis is worse than fifty that do, because screening has a real cost in attention.

What it looks like in practice

Sources divide into inbound (reputation, content, referrals) and outbound (research, cold outreach, communities). The best flow tends to come from being known for something specific rather than from being generally visible.

For a new manager the honest constraint is that dealflow is downstream of reputation, which takes years. Operating experience, a public point of view, and genuine helpfulness are the levers available before a track record exists.

Where it goes wrong

  • Optimising for volume when the constraint is relevance.
  • Relying entirely on warm intros, which reproduces the existing network's biases.
  • Not tracking where deals came from, so you can't tell which sources work.
  • Assuming good dealflow arrives automatically once a fund is announced.

Doing the work

The dealflow process#

Six steps, and they're a pipeline you manage rather than a thing that happens to you: sourcing → filtering → diligence → decision → closing → follow-up.

Picture this: most people entering venture think the job is step 3. It's mostly steps 1 and 2, and the funds that beat you are usually beating you at sourcing, not at analysis.

Why it matters

A defined process is what stops investing from being a series of ad hoc reactions. It makes decisions comparable, makes the reasons reviewable, and makes it possible to learn from what you passed on.

It also protects against the failure mode of enthusiasm: without a process, the company you happened to meet on a good day gets more attention than the better one you met when busy.

What it looks like in practice

The sequence is broadly sourcing, first-level screen, second-level review, diligence, memo, decision. Each stage should have an explicit reason to advance or stop, written down.

The written reason is the part that compounds. A pipeline with a recorded rationale for every pass becomes a dataset about your own judgment, which is the only way to find out whether it's any good.

Where it goes wrong

  • Running the process only for deals you're excited about.
  • Not recording pass reasons, which makes the anti-portfolio useless as a learning tool.
  • Letting stages blur, so diligence starts before a decision to diligence was made.
  • Making the process so heavy it can't move at the speed a competitive round requires.

Doing the work

First-level filter#

The fast, mechanical pass: sector, stage, geography, valuation range. Anything outside the thesis exits immediately, in seconds, without guilt.

Picture this: mine is — is it AI, does it touch trust or community, is it pre-seed, is it US? Four questions. If any is no, it's out, however much I like the founder.

Why it matters

The first filter is a cheap, fast check against the thesis: stage, sector, geography, and whether this is a venture-scale outcome at all. It exists to protect attention.

Most deals should die here, and quickly. A filter that passes half of what arrives isn't filtering — it's deferring the decision to a stage that costs much more time.

What it looks like in practice

Good first filters are mechanical and stated in advance, which makes them fast and makes the passes honest. They should be answerable from a deck and a five-minute look.

The cost of a tight filter is false negatives, and that cost is real. The mitigation is a written record, so patterns in what you rejected can be examined later.

Where it goes wrong

  • Making the first filter about quality rather than fit. Quality assessment is expensive.
  • Applying it inconsistently depending on who made the introduction.
  • Not writing down the reason, which makes false negatives invisible.
  • Setting it so loosely that everything reaches the second level.

Doing the work

Second-level filter#

The slower judgment pass on what survives: founder quality, traction, defensibility, differentiation. What your thesis tells you to weight, not just what it lets in.

Picture this: first-level is a gate anyone could operate from a written rule. Second-level is where your actual taste lives, and it's the thing a fund is really hiring when it hires you.

Why it matters

The second filter is where judgment starts. Having established the deal fits the thesis, the question becomes whether this specific team, in this specific market, at this specific moment, is worth the work of diligence.

It's the most expensive stage per deal before diligence proper, which is why the first filter has to do its job.

What it looks like in practice

Typically a founder meeting, a look at whatever evidence exists, and a view on the market and the timing. The output is a decision to diligence or a written pass.

The useful discipline is to name, before the meeting, what would have to be true for this to be interesting. Deciding the criteria after hearing the pitch is how enthusiasm becomes analysis.

Where it goes wrong

  • Deciding what matters after the meeting rather than before it.
  • Advancing deals because the founder was compelling rather than because the criteria were met.
  • Spending diligence-level effort at this stage on deals that will fail anyway.
  • Not writing the pass reason, which is the most useful artifact this stage produces.

Doing the work

Anti-portfolio#

The deals you passed on that went on to win. Kept deliberately by good investors.

Picture this: Bessemer publishes theirs. The point isn't self-flagellation — it's that your passes are data about your filter, and reviewing them is the only way to find out your filter is miscalibrated.

Why it matters

The anti-portfolio is the record of what you passed on and why. Kept honestly it's the only systematic way to audit your own judgment, because the successes you backed tell you far less than the successes you declined.

Under the power law, missing one outlier costs more than making several bad investments. That asymmetry makes the reasons for passing worth studying carefully.

What it looks like in practice

The value is entirely in the reasons, not the list. "Passed because we thought the market was too small" is a testable claim you can check three years later. "Passed, not a fit" teaches nothing.

Reviewing it periodically surfaces patterns — a systematic blind spot about a sector, a founder profile, or a business model that keeps being underestimated.

Where it goes wrong

  • Keeping the list without the reasons.
  • Only recording the misses that became famous, which biases the sample.
  • Treating it as embarrassment rather than as data.
  • Never reviewing it, which is the same as not keeping it.

Inbound vs. outbound#

Inbound arrives because someone sent it to you. Outbound is what you went and found.

Picture this: tracking the split is the honest measure of whether your network is real. An investor whose dealflow is 95% outbound doesn't have an edge yet — they have effort.

Why it matters

Inbound flow arrives because of who you are; outbound flow happens because of what you do. Both matter, and they select for different things.

Inbound is efficient and biased — it reflects your existing reputation and network, which means it systematically misses founders outside it. Outbound is expensive and is the only way to reach companies that would never have found you.

What it looks like in practice

For an established firm inbound dominates, and the work is filtering. For a new manager outbound is most of the job, and the leverage comes from being specific: a narrow thesis makes outbound research tractable and makes the outreach credible.

The best outbound doesn't look like outreach. It looks like being genuinely useful in a community where the founders you want already are.

Where it goes wrong

  • Waiting for inbound before a reputation exists to generate it.
  • Treating outbound as a volume exercise rather than a research one.
  • Not tracking which channel produced which investment.
  • Assuming inbound quality reflects the market rather than your own network.

Pipeline#

The set of companies you're actively tracking, with a stage attached to each. The difference between an investor and an enthusiast is that one of them can tell you what's in their pipeline this week.

Why it matters

The pipeline is the record of every company under consideration and where it sits. It's the operational artifact that makes a process a process rather than a feeling.

It also produces the numbers that let you improve: how many companies at each stage, how many advance, and where things die. Without it, you can't tell whether the problem is sourcing or conversion.

What it looks like in practice

Each entry needs a stage, a date, a source, and a reason for the current status. The reason field is what makes it valuable later.

Aging matters. Deals that sit in a stage indefinitely are usually passes that nobody wanted to write down, and they distort the picture of what's actually live.

Where it goes wrong

  • Keeping the pipeline in your head, which works until it doesn't.
  • Letting deals age in a stage rather than recording a pass.
  • Not recording the source, which makes it impossible to evaluate channels.
  • Tracking only active deals, which discards the anti-portfolio data.

Conviction#

The point at which you'd defend a company in a room of people who disagree. Distinct from interest, excitement, or liking the founder.

Picture this: the test I'd use — can I write the single sentence that must be true for this to work, and do I believe it? If I can only say "the team is great and the space is hot," that's interest, not conviction.

Why it matters

Conviction is the willingness to act on a judgment that others don't share — which is the only way to generate returns in a competitive market. If everyone agrees, the price already reflects it.

The difficulty is distinguishing conviction from stubbornness. Both feel identical from the inside, and only the written reasoning separates them afterwards.

What it looks like in practice

The discipline that helps is writing down what you believe and what would change your mind, before committing. That converts conviction into something testable rather than something felt.

Conviction should also be proportionate. High conviction justifies a larger position; it doesn't justify skipping diligence, and the two get conflated regularly.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating enthusiasm as conviction. They feel the same and aren't.
  • Not recording what would falsify the thesis, which makes updating impossible.
  • Using conviction as a reason to shorten diligence.
  • Maintaining conviction after the evidence changed, which is just commitment escalation.

Doing the work

Sourcing#

Actively finding companies rather than waiting.

Picture this: roughly 60% of venture deals come through networks. Which is precisely why my alumni relationships across Plug and Play, Grid110, and Material Change are the asset, not a line on a bio.

Why it matters

Sourcing is the active work of finding companies before anyone else does, and at pre-seed it's most of the edge. Once a company is running a process, the price is set by competition and the advantage is gone.

It's also the part of the job that compounds slowest and matters most. Relationships built three years before a company exists are what produce proprietary access.

What it looks like in practice

The approaches that work are specific rather than broad: depth in a sector, presence in a community, a public thesis that attracts the right founders, and relationships with the people founders talk to before they raise.

Geography still matters more than it should. Being physically present in an ecosystem produces flow that remote relationship-building doesn't replicate.

Where it goes wrong

  • Sourcing broadly rather than deeply, which produces volume without access.
  • Meeting founders only when they're raising.
  • Building a public thesis you don't actually invest against.
  • Neglecting the people around founders — operators, engineers, community organisers.

Doing the work

Due diligence#

Investigating before investing — team, market, product, numbers, references.

Picture this: at pre-seed there's often no revenue to diligence. So you're mostly diligencing the founder: do they see reality clearly, and do people who've worked with them want to again?

Why it matters

Diligence at pre-seed is not the same exercise as at later stages. There's no revenue to audit and no cohort data to analyse — the work is about the team, the market, and whether the claimed evidence is real.

The most valuable diligence is usually reference checking done properly: former colleagues, customers, and people who worked with the founders when things went badly.

What it looks like in practice

The checkable items are legal hygiene (IP assignment, 83(b) filings, clean cap table), the reality of claimed traction (are pilots paid, do customers actually use it), and references taken off-list rather than from the founder's own set.

Speed is a real constraint. Competitive rounds close in days, and diligence that takes six weeks means not investing. The answer is knowing in advance what you must check and what you can accept.

Where it goes wrong

  • Running enterprise-grade diligence on a pre-seed company and losing the deal.
  • Only taking references the founder provided.
  • Accepting traction claims without asking what "customer" and "pilot" mean specifically.
  • Skipping legal hygiene because it's boring. It's where the real problems hide.

Doing the work

The deal funnel#

The filtering ratio from lead to check. The average VC reviews about 101 startups per investment — 150 for IT-focused firms, 120 for early stage, 78 for healthcare.

Picture this — what happens to 100 startups:

  1. ~70 are gone within minutes, usually with no meeting at all
  2. ~30 get an informal coffee or video call
  3. ~10 survive to a partner meeting with a written memo
  4. fewer than 2 in 5 of those completing diligence get a term sheet
  5. and it takes 1.7 term sheets to produce 1 investment — roughly 40% of offers get declined or lost to a competing offer

Conviction isn't the bottleneck. Volume at the top is.

Why it matters

The funnel is the arithmetic of the process: how many companies seen produce how many investments. The ratios are brutal and worth knowing, because they determine how much sourcing is needed to deploy a fund.

It also localises problems. Poor conversion from screen to diligence is a filtering problem; poor conversion from term sheet to close is a competitiveness problem.

What it looks like in practice

Typical funnels are steep — hundreds of companies seen for a handful of investments. The exact ratios vary enormously by stage and strategy, which is why your own numbers matter more than benchmarks.

Working backwards is the useful exercise: to make eight investments a year at your observed conversion rates, how many companies do you need to see, and is that achievable with current sourcing?

Where it goes wrong

  • Not measuring the funnel, so sourcing needs are guessed at.
  • Comparing your ratios to another firm's without adjusting for stage and strategy.
  • Reading a steep funnel as a problem. It's normal.
  • Optimising conversion by lowering standards rather than by improving sourcing.

Doing the work

Term sheet conversion#

The fact that issuing a term sheet isn't winning the deal. At the term sheet, leverage flips to the founder.

Why it matters

Term sheet conversion is the share of term sheets issued that actually close. A low rate means you're losing deals after committing, which is expensive in time and worse in reputation.

It's a direct measure of competitiveness. Founders who take another offer after receiving yours are telling you something about price, terms, or how you're perceived.

What it looks like in practice

The causes divide into price, terms, and relationship. Price is the easiest to observe and often not the real reason — founders frequently choose a lower offer from an investor they'd rather work with.

Asking directly after a loss is worth doing. Most founders will tell you, and the answer is more useful than any inference.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming losses are always about price.
  • Not asking why, which discards the most useful feedback available.
  • Issuing term sheets speculatively, which damages credibility when they're withdrawn.
  • Tracking the rate without tracking the reasons.

Doing the work

Elimination by aspects#

How investors actually read pitches: hunting for a fatal flaw so they can stop reading. Not looking for reasons to say yes — looking for a reason to stop.

Picture this: of 100 companies that reach investors, about 70 disappear without ever getting a meeting. Which is why naming your weakness early works — it removes the flaw they were scanning for and signals self-awareness.

Why it matters

Elimination by aspects is the decision heuristic of screening on one criterion at a time and discarding anything that fails, rather than weighing everything together. It's fast and it's how most screening actually works.

The cost is that it discards companies that are exceptional on one dimension and weak on the criterion being applied first — which, in a power-law business, is exactly the profile of the outlier.

What it looks like in practice

The mitigation is ordering the criteria deliberately, applying the ones with the highest information value first, and keeping a record of what was eliminated at each stage.

It's also worth periodically re-examining eliminations under a different order, which is one of the more useful things the anti-portfolio can be used for.

Where it goes wrong

  • Applying criteria in whatever order they occur to you.
  • Eliminating on a criterion that's weakly related to outcomes.
  • Not recording eliminations, which makes the blind spots invisible.
  • Using it at every stage, when later stages should weigh factors together.

Doing the work

Cold outreach#

Contacting an investor with no introduction. Works better than founders assume.

Picture this: research on 80,000+ cold emails to 28,000 investors found nearly 10% replied with interest — and the best-written pitches got 13–17%. Plain language describing what you actually built beat polished marketing language.

Why it matters

Cold outreach is how you reach founders outside your network, which is where most companies are. Response rates are low, and the ones that respond are often the deals nobody else is looking at.

For an emerging manager without inbound flow it's not optional. It's also the only systematic correction to the network bias that warm introductions create.

What it looks like in practice

What works is specificity: evidence you've understood what they're building, a reason you specifically are relevant, and a short ask. What fails is anything that reads as a template.

Research is the whole job. A hundred well-targeted messages outperform a thousand generic ones by a wide margin, and the research is also how you find the companies worth writing to.

Where it goes wrong

  • Sending templated messages at volume.
  • Leading with your fund rather than with why you understand their problem.
  • Reaching out only when a company is already raising.
  • Judging the channel on response rate rather than on the quality of what it surfaces.

Doing the work

Evidence over projections#

Investors weight what already happened above what you forecast.

Picture this: "we have 40 customers paying $200/month" beats "our TAM is $8 billion" every single time. And yet: about 40% of YC-funded companies arrive as ideas with no revenue — so "too early" is rarely the real objection.

Why it matters

Projections are assumptions arranged in a spreadsheet. Evidence is something that already happened. At pre-seed there's little of the second and unlimited quantities of the first, which makes distinguishing them the core analytical skill.

A hockey-stick forecast contains no information — every deck has one. Three customers who renewed contains a great deal.

What it looks like in practice

The evidence that counts is behavioural: someone paid, someone kept using it, someone referred a colleague, someone signed before the product was finished. Each of those is a costly signal.

The useful question when shown a projection is what has to be true for it to happen, and then which of those things has already been demonstrated. Usually the answer is none of them, which is fine at pre-seed as long as everyone knows it.

Where it goes wrong

  • Diligencing the model rather than the assumptions underneath it.
  • Accepting stated intent — surveys, LOIs without money — as evidence.
  • Dismissing a company for having no projections when it has real usage.
  • Confusing a large pipeline with demonstrated demand.

Doing the work

Deal memo#

Your written case for an investment: what they do, why now, why these founders, the one thing that must be true, and an honest anti-memo arguing against.

Why it matters

The memo forces the argument to be written down, which is where vague enthusiasm either becomes a thesis or falls apart. Writing is the diligence — the gaps become visible when you try to make the case in prose.

It's also the artifact that makes learning possible. A memo written at the time, including the case against and what would falsify the thesis, is what lets you evaluate your own judgment years later.

What it looks like in practice

The section that matters most is the case against. A memo that only argues for the investment isn't analysis, it's advocacy — and the risks named honestly at the time are what make a later post-mortem useful.

Length is not the point. A tight two pages with a clear thesis, the evidence, the risks, and the falsifiers beats fifteen pages of description.

Where it goes wrong

  • Writing the memo to justify a decision already made.
  • Omitting or softening the case against.
  • Not stating what would falsify the thesis, which makes it unfalsifiable.
  • Never revisiting old memos, which is where the entire learning value sits.

Related terms

Doing the work

Investment committee (IC)#

The group that approves investments. For a solo angel, the IC is you — which makes writing the memo the only check on your own enthusiasm.

Why it matters

The IC is where the decision gets made and where individual enthusiasm meets collective scrutiny. Its function is to catch the errors a single person committed to a deal won't see.

It works when it genuinely can say no. An IC that ratifies whatever the sponsoring partner brings adds process without adding judgment.

What it looks like in practice

Structures vary from consensus to unanimity to a sponsoring-partner model where others advise. Each produces different behaviour: unanimity selects for uncontroversial deals, which in a power-law business is a real cost.

For a solo GP the IC is a discipline rather than a body — a written memo, a mandatory case against, and often an informal advisor who will push back honestly.

Where it goes wrong

  • Requiring unanimity, which systematically filters out contrarian bets.
  • Running an IC that has never actually declined a deal.
  • Bringing deals to IC without the memo circulated in advance.
  • As a solo GP, skipping the discipline because there's no one to present to.

Doing the work

Follow-on#

Investing again in a company you already own.

Why it matters

Follow-on investments are how a fund concentrates into what's working. Under the power law the initial cheque is rarely enough — the position in the company that returns the fund has to be large enough to matter at exit.

It's also where the hardest discipline lies, because the psychological pull is to support the struggling company rather than to pay a higher price for the successful one.

What it looks like in practice

The decision should be made as though it were a new investment at the current price, not as a defence of the existing position. Sunk cost is the dominant bias here and it's strong.

The arithmetic to watch is blended cost basis. Following on heavily at later prices reduces the multiple even as it increases absolute return, and whether that trade is right depends on the fund's size and stage.

Where it goes wrong

  • Following on to protect a position rather than because the current price is attractive.
  • Reserving equally across the portfolio rather than concentrating on the winners.
  • Ignoring the effect on blended cost basis and reported multiple.
  • Having pro rata rights and no capital reserved to exercise them.

Related terms

Doing the work

Reserves#

Money held back from the start for follow-ons.

Picture this: a fund that deploys 100% into first checks has nothing left when its best company raises again — and gets diluted out of its winner exactly when the winner is proving itself.

Why it matters

Reserves are the capital set aside for follow-ons. How much to reserve is one of the two or three decisions that most determine a fund's outcome, and it's made before you know which companies will need it.

Too little and you're diluted out of the winner. Too much and you've made fewer initial bets, reducing the chance of catching an outlier at all.

What it looks like in practice

Common ratios run from 1:1 to 1:2 between initial and reserve capital, varying with stage. Earlier-stage funds typically reserve more because there are more rounds ahead.

The allocation discipline matters as much as the amount. Reserves deployed to keep struggling companies alive are reserves not available for the one that works, and that trade is usually made implicitly rather than deliberately.

Where it goes wrong

  • Setting a reserve ratio without modelling the dilution path to exit.
  • Spreading reserves evenly rather than concentrating them.
  • Deploying reserves into companies that need money rather than ones that deserve it.
  • Reserving so heavily that the initial portfolio is too small to catch an outlier.

Related terms

Unicorn#

A company valued at $1B or more. The unit of measurement for whether an early investor got it right.

Why it matters

A unicorn is a private company valued at $1B or more. The term mattered when it was rare and means less now that there are many — including a substantial number whose valuations reflect structure rather than value.

For a fund the relevant fact is that a unicorn valuation is a private mark, not a realisation. Plenty of companies have crossed the threshold and later exited well below it.

What it looks like in practice

Research on unicorn formation is consistent on one point: they take multiple rounds and many years. The average US unicorn raises more than six rounds before reaching the threshold, which is the practical case for reserves.

The valuation itself frequently overstates the economics. A high headline price supported by a heavy liquidation preference or a ratchet is not equivalent to a company genuinely worth that number.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reading a unicorn valuation as an achieved outcome.
  • Ignoring the structure that supports a headline valuation.
  • Assuming the path is fast. It usually takes many rounds over many years.
  • Using unicorn count as a measure of fund performance rather than DPI.

Operator-angel#

An angel who built or ran something before writing checks. The dominant profile at the top.

Picture this: the power law among angels is brutal — only 181 individuals have backed 5+ unicorns, about 50 have reached 10, and just 6 have backed 20 or more. Peter Thiel leads at

  1. And the currently-active list looks different from the all-time list: **114 of the most

active recent angels don't appear in the lifetime top 100** at all. Being active now matters more than having been early once.

Why it matters

An operator-angel invests their own money and brings operating experience — someone who has actually built the thing they're now funding. The value is credibility with founders and genuinely useful judgment on execution.

It's also a real sourcing advantage. Founders talk to people who have done the job, which means operator-angels see companies before institutional investors do.

What it looks like in practice

The advantage is domain-specific and narrower than it feels. Experience scaling a marketplace transfers well to another marketplace and poorly to enterprise software.

The failure mode is treating operating experience as a substitute for investing discipline. Knowing how to run a company is not the same skill as knowing which companies to back, and the two are often confused.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming operating success transfers to investing judgment.
  • Advising outside your actual domain because founders defer to you.
  • Investing in what you'd have built rather than what the market wants.
  • Concentrating too heavily because domain confidence feels like conviction.

Concentration#

Venture returns and venture careers both follow a power law.

Picture this: roughly 5% of venture capitalists have generated about 90% of the industry's profits. And 70% of the top-100 individual angels are in California, 50 in San Francisco alone — which is a real headwind to name honestly for anyone investing from Seattle.

Why it matters

Concentration is the tension at the centre of portfolio construction. Under a power law you need a big enough position in the winner for it to matter — and you don't know in advance which one that is.

Too concentrated and missing the outlier is fatal. Too diversified and catching it doesn't help enough. Every fund resolves this differently and the resolution defines the strategy.

What it looks like in practice

The usual approach is broad at entry and concentrated through follow-ons: many initial positions, reserves deployed disproportionately into the ones showing signal.

LPAs frequently cap concentration — no more than some percentage of the fund in a single company — which constrains how far the strategy can go even when conviction is high.

Where it goes wrong

  • Concentrating at entry, before there's information to concentrate on.
  • Spreading reserves evenly, which is diversification disguised as follow-on strategy.
  • Breaching LPA concentration limits, which is a real covenant.
  • Modelling concentration on expected value rather than on the tail outcome.

Valuation overstatement#

Headline private valuations are inflated because preferred stock carries protections common stock doesn't. A "$1B company" is not worth $1B to everyone on the cap table.

Picture this: serious rankings discount stated unicorn valuations by roughly 50% to get to a common-share-equivalent value. When you read "valued at $2B," the honest number is closer to $1B.

Why it matters

Headline valuations systematically overstate what companies are worth, because the price reflects the most recent share class with the best terms — not the whole company. Research on this has found the gap to be substantial and widely distributed.

It matters for marks. A portfolio carried at post-money valuations is carrying a number that assumes every share is worth what the newest preferred share is worth, which is structurally untrue.

What it looks like in practice

The mechanism is the preference stack plus protective terms. A round with a 2x preference, a ratchet, and seniority is worth more per share than common — so multiplying that price by total shares overstates the enterprise.

The correction is to model the waterfall rather than the headline. That's more work and it's the only way to know what a position is actually worth.

Where it goes wrong

  • Marking positions at post-money without examining the structure behind the price.
  • Comparing valuations across companies with very different terms.
  • Reading a valuation increase as a value increase when structure was the concession.
  • Reporting portfolio value on headline marks without noting the assumption.

Human capital decay#

A track record ages. Recent wins say more about an investor than old ones.

Picture this: the Strebulaev–Jackson ranking applies a three-year half-life — a 2022 investment counts fully, 2019 counts 25%, 2016 counts 12.5%. Which is exactly why "114 of the most active recent angels aren't in the lifetime top 100" matters more than it sounds.

Why it matters

Teams degrade over time in ways that don't show up in the metrics until late. Founders disengage, key people leave, and the density of talent that made the early product good quietly thins.

For an investor it's a risk that's hard to observe from outside and easy to observe from a board seat, which is part of what board access is actually for.

What it looks like in practice

The observable signals are turnover among the strongest people, founders spending time on things that aren't the hard problem, and a hiring bar that has visibly moved.

Vesting and equity refresh are the structural mitigations. A team fully vested with no refresh has weak retention incentives at exactly the point where their experience is most valuable.

Where it goes wrong

  • Watching headcount rather than watching who left.
  • Ignoring full-vest cliffs for the early team, which is a predictable retention risk.
  • Assuming a strong founding team stays strong without renewal.
  • Reading growth as evidence that the team is intact.

Value add#

The measurable version of "we're helpful": taking a board seat, or leading the round rather than following.

Picture this: the ranking awards explicit bonus points for board seats and lead positions, because those are the two places involvement is actually observable.

Why it matters

Value add is what an investor contributes beyond capital. It's the most claimed and least verified thing in venture — every fund says it, and founders can tell within a quarter whether it's real.

The honest version is narrow. Most investors are genuinely useful at two or three specific things and unhelpful at everything else, and knowing which is more valuable than claiming breadth.

What it looks like in practice

The contributions that founders actually rate are hiring, customer introductions, help with the next round, and being available when something is going wrong. Strategic advice ranks lower than investors think.

The test is what portfolio founders say when asked by another founder, unprompted. That reference is the only real measure, and it's the one that produces future dealflow.

Where it goes wrong

  • Claiming broad value add rather than being specific about two or three things.
  • Offering advice when the founder needed an introduction.
  • Being available during diligence and unreachable afterwards.
  • Measuring value add by activity rather than by what founders say to each other.

Net profits (vs. gross)#

Returns after subtracting what you paid to get them. It penalizes deploying enormous capital to find a few winners.

Picture this: two investors both return $500M. One deployed $100M, the other $2B. Gross returns look similar; net profit says they're not remotely the same investor.

Why it matters

Gross returns are what the portfolio produced. Net returns are what LPs received after management fees and carry. The gap is large and it's the number that actually matters to anyone writing a cheque into a fund.

A gross 3x can become a net 2.2x or lower depending on fees and carry. Managers quote gross when it flatters and net when it doesn't, which is why the basis should always be stated.

What it looks like in practice

Over a ten-year fund a 2% annual fee consumes roughly 20% of committed capital, and carry takes 20% of profits above the return of capital. Both have to be modelled to get to a net number.

For an LP the comparison that matters is net-to-LP against public market equivalents, because that's the actual alternative use of the money.

Where it goes wrong

  • Comparing one fund's gross return to another's net.
  • Quoting a multiple without stating whether it's gross or net.
  • Ignoring fee drag when modelling what the portfolio has to return.
  • Assuming a strong gross portfolio automatically produces a strong net outcome.

Related terms

Doing the work

Warm introduction#

Being introduced to an investor by someone they already trust, rather than arriving cold.

Picture this: a founder emails a partner directly and gets no reply. A portfolio founder forwards the same deck with two sentences of endorsement and the meeting happens that week. Same company, same deck.

Why it matters

The introduction is a filter that costs the introducer something. Because their reputation is attached, a warm intro carries information a cold email cannot, which is why response rates differ by an order of magnitude.

The uncomfortable part is that it's also a network tax, and it falls hardest on founders without existing access. For an investor, over-reliance on warm intros is the mechanism by which a portfolio ends up looking exactly like the network that sourced it — which is a returns problem before it's anything else.

What it looks like in practice

The strongest introductions come from portfolio founders, because their incentive is clear and their judgment is tested. Next best are other investors who have looked and passed for reasons unrelated to quality — wrong stage, wrong sector, no allocation.

The forwardable email is the mechanic that makes it work: a short note the introducer can send without writing anything themselves. Founders who make the introducer do the work get fewer introductions.

Where it goes wrong

  • Asking for an intro before knowing whether the fund invests at your stage or in your sector.
  • Making the introducer write the pitch. Send something forwardable.
  • Treating intros as the only channel, and never building direct relationships.
  • As an investor, relying on them so heavily that dealflow only reflects the existing network.

Related terms

Partner meeting#

The meeting where a fund's partners decide together whether to invest, usually the last step before a term sheet.

Picture this: the founder has met one partner three times and thinks the deal is close. The partner meeting is where six people who have spent forty minutes on it each ask the questions that decide it.

Why it matters

The dynamic that founders miss is that their champion is the one being evaluated as much as the company. The sponsoring partner is spending internal credibility, and the questions in the room are partly about whether they've done the work.

It explains a lot of otherwise confusing behaviour — why a partner asks for a specific extra data point, why timelines slip a week, why enthusiastic meetings produce no term sheet. The champion needs ammunition for a room the founder isn't in.

What it looks like in practice

The useful preparation is to arm the champion: a clean one-pager, the three hardest objections answered, and the specific numbers that would come up. Ask them directly what the pushback will be — most will tell you.

Format varies by firm. Some vote, some require unanimity, some leave it to the sponsoring partner with the others as advisors. Knowing which applies changes how you prepare.

Where it goes wrong

  • Pitching the champion and never asking what the partnership will object to.
  • Assuming enthusiasm from one partner means the round is done.
  • Bringing new material to the partner meeting that the champion hasn't seen.
  • Reading a slow process as disinterest when it's usually an internal calendar.

Pitch deck#

The ten-to-fifteen slide document that gets a meeting and structures the conversation once you have one.

Picture this: the deck's job is not to explain the company completely. It's to make someone want a conversation. A deck that answers everything usually gets read instead of discussed, which is worse.

Why it matters

The deck is the artifact that circulates without you, so it has to survive being read by someone who wasn't in the room and has ninety seconds. That's a different design problem from presenting.

It's also a thinking test more than a design one. Vague decks usually indicate vague thinking, and investors read them that way — which is why a beautifully designed deck with no specific claim reads worse than an ugly one with sharp numbers.

What it looks like in practice

The conventional sequence works because it maps to how the decision gets made: problem, why now, solution, market, traction, business model, competition, team, and the ask. Deviating is fine; skipping the questions isn't.

The traction slide does most of the work at pre-seed, and when there's little to show, the team and the why-now carry it. Specific beats impressive: three real customers named beats a large chart of projections.

Where it goes wrong

  • Leading with the solution before establishing that the problem is expensive.
  • Top-down market sizing that produces a number nobody believes.
  • Hiding weak traction behind percentages with no absolute numbers.
  • Making it a reading document, so there's nothing left to talk about.

Investor update#

The regular written update to existing investors — usually monthly or quarterly — covering metrics, progress, problems, and asks.

Picture this: a founder sends a short update on the fifth of every month for two years. When they raise the next round, the investors already know the story, and two of them make introductions without being asked.

Why it matters

The update is the cheapest fundraising tool a founder has, and the most consistently skipped. Investors who have watched the numbers move for eighteen months make decisions faster than ones being told the story for the first time.

It's also a discipline. Writing down what was supposed to happen and what did, every month, is how a founder notices a trend that a dashboard hides. The updates that only appear when money is needed are the ones that tell an investor exactly what they need to know about the founder.

What it looks like in practice

The good ones are short and honest: the numbers that matter, what happened, what went wrong, and one or two specific asks. Specific asks are the part that generates help — "introductions welcome" produces nothing; "we need a head of clinical ops, ideally from a multi-site group" produces candidates.

Consistency beats polish. Monthly for two years builds a track record; sporadic beautiful updates build nothing.

Where it goes wrong

  • Only writing when things are going well, which makes silence a signal.
  • Burying bad news, which destroys trust exactly when you need help.
  • Vague asks that nobody can act on.
  • Making it so long that nobody reads it.

Related terms
