Doing the work

Fundraising process#

Running a raise as a time-boxed process with parallel conversations, rather than a sequence of individual approaches.

Picture this: twenty-five first meetings compressed into three weeks. Everyone is at the same stage, so a term sheet from one creates real urgency for the others. Spread the same meetings over five months and every conversation happens in isolation.

Why it matters

Fundraising dynamics are almost entirely about parallelism. A term sheet with a deadline is only leverage if other funds are far enough along to respond to it. Sequential raising gives you a series of conversations with no competitive tension in any of them.

It also protects the company. An open-ended raise consumes founder attention indefinitely and shows up in the metrics, which then makes the raise harder — the failure mode compounds.

What it looks like in practice

The mechanics: build the full target list first, sort into tiers, take a few second-tier meetings early to find the weak points in the pitch, then run the priority list in a tight window. Track everything, because a process with thirty funds in it is not something to run from memory.

Momentum is real and visible. Funds ask who else is looking, and the honest answer either helps or hurts. That's an argument for starting when the story is strongest, not when the runway demands it.

Where it goes wrong

  • Starting with the top choice, before the pitch has been tested.
  • Sequential meetings, which remove any competitive dynamic.
  • Beginning with under six months of runway, which is visible and prices into the terms.
  • Not tracking the process, so follow-ups slip and interest goes cold.

Related terms

Round sizing#

Deciding how much to raise — set by the milestones that make the next round possible, not by what's available.

Picture this: the right question is never "how much can we get?" It's "what has to be true for a Series A, how long does that take, and what does that cost?" Then add margin, because it always takes longer.

Why it matters

Raising too little is the more common and more dangerous error. A company that runs out before hitting its milestones raises from a position of weakness, and that shows up as a down round, a bridge on bad terms, or no round at all.

Raising too much is a real cost too — dilution now, and a valuation that sets a bar the next round has to clear. But the asymmetry is stark: excess dilution is survivable, running out isn't.

What it looks like in practice

Work backwards from the next round's expectations, convert those into a plan and a burn rate, and add buffer — eighteen to twenty-four months is the usual target, because the milestones slip and the raise itself takes months.

The dilution math is the counterweight. A typical seed sells 15–25%, and stacking oversized rounds early leaves founders with too little by Series B to stay motivated, which later investors notice and price.

Where it goes wrong

  • Sizing to what investors offer rather than to the milestone plan.
  • Planning exactly to the milestone with no buffer for slippage.
  • Raising a large round at a valuation the next round can't clear.
  • Ignoring that the raise itself consumes three to six months of runway.

Related terms

Doing the work

Investor objections#

The recurring reasons investors say no — market size, defensibility, team gaps, timing, traction — and how a founder handles them.

Picture this: the fourth investor in a row asks how you stop a large incumbent from shipping this. That's not four opinions, it's one unanswered question in the pitch.

Why it matters

Objections are the highest-quality free feedback a founder gets, and most of it is wasted because the instinct is to defend rather than record. The same objection appearing repeatedly is a defect in the story or in the business, and the two require different responses.

How a founder handles pushback is also being evaluated directly. Defensiveness in a pitch predicts defensiveness in a board meeting, and investors are underwriting a decade-long relationship.

What it looks like in practice

Track every objection and count them. The ones that recur are real; the one-offs are usually a specific fund's mandate. Then decide which are story problems, fixable by explaining better, and which are business problems that need evidence you don't yet have.

The strongest move is pre-empting the obvious one. Raising the incumbent question yourself, with an answer, converts your biggest weakness into a demonstration that you've thought about it harder than they have.

Where it goes wrong

  • Arguing with the objection instead of writing it down.
  • Treating every no as a fund-specific mandate issue.
  • Changing the pitch after every meeting, so nothing gets tested twice.
  • Never asking, at the end of a pass, what the actual reason was.

Related terms

Doing the work

Market timing ("why now")#

The argument for why this company is possible and necessary now, when it wasn't three years ago and won't be novel in three more.

Picture this: the same idea failed in 2015 because the model wasn't good enough and the data wasn't digitised. Both changed in the last eighteen months. That's a why-now — a specific thing that shifted, with a date attached.

Why it matters

Timing separates the companies that work from the identical companies that failed years earlier. Most good ideas have been tried; what changed is usually a cost curve, a regulation, a behaviour, or a platform.

For a pre-seed investor it's close to the whole thesis. You're not underwriting current traction because there isn't any — you're underwriting a bet that a specific window just opened and this team is positioned in it.

What it looks like in practice

A real why-now names a specific change with a date: inference cost fell by an order of magnitude, a regulation took effect, a platform opened an API, a behaviour became normal. "AI is changing everything" is not a why-now; it's a press release.

The strongest version also explains why the incumbent can't simply respond — usually because the change breaks an assumption their product or business model is built on.

Where it goes wrong

  • Citing a general trend rather than a specific, dated change.
  • Having no answer for why this failed before, when it usually did.
  • Confusing a technology becoming possible with customers becoming ready.
  • Assuming that if the timing is right, the window stays open. It's usually short.

Doing the work

Founder story#

The account of why this particular person is building this particular thing — the connection between their history and the problem.

Picture this: "I spent six years as a nurse practitioner watching claims get denied for reasons nobody could explain, and I built the spreadsheet that fixed it for my clinic" does more work than any market slide.

Why it matters

At pre-seed there is very little else to evaluate. The story is the evidence that the founder understands the problem at a level a smart outsider couldn't reach in six months of research, which is what makes them likely to make good decisions when the plan changes.

It also predicts persistence. Founders with a genuine connection to the problem stay through the years where nothing works, and pre-seed companies spend a lot of time in that state.

What it looks like in practice

The credible version is specific and slightly unflattering — the thing that went wrong, what it cost, what was tried first. Polished origin stories read as constructed, because they usually are.

It should also connect forward. The history explains the insight, the insight explains the product, and the product explains why this team gets there first. A story that doesn't reach the product is biography.

Where it goes wrong

  • Manufacturing a personal connection that doesn't exist. It shows.
  • Telling the story and never connecting it to why it produces an advantage.
  • Leading with credentials rather than with the specific experience.
  • Making it so central that the business case never gets made.

How companies are judged

Traction#

Evidence that people want the thing. Users, revenue, retention, usage.

Why it matters

Traction is whatever evidence exists that people want this, and what counts changes entirely by stage. At pre-seed it might be three design partners; at Series A it's retained revenue growing through a repeatable channel.

The word does a lot of concealing. "Traction" in a deck can mean signed contracts or a waitlist, and the difference is the whole investment decision.

What it looks like in practice

The useful hierarchy runs from cheapest signal to most expensive: interest, signups, usage, payment, retention, referral. Each step costs the customer more, which is exactly why each one carries more information.

Absolute numbers beat percentages at this stage. "Grew 300%" from four customers to twelve is a different claim from the same percentage at scale, and the percentage is usually chosen to obscure that.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reporting percentages without the absolute numbers underneath.
  • Counting unpaid pilots, waitlists, or LOIs as traction.
  • Presenting cumulative totals, which can only ever go up.
  • Showing acquisition without retention, which is the number that actually matters.

Related terms

How companies are judged

Burn rate#

How much cash a company spends per month.

Why it matters

Burn is the rate at which a company consumes cash, and it's the number that sets the clock on everything else. Every strategic decision at an early company is ultimately constrained by how many months remain.

The distinction between gross and net burn matters more than founders usually treat it. Net burn determines survival; gross burn determines how quickly things deteriorate if revenue moves.

What it looks like in practice

The convention is a three-month trailing average, because single months are distorted by annual payments, one-off legal costs, and timing of collections.

Burn multiple — net burn divided by net new ARR — is the efficiency version of the same idea and is increasingly what growth investors look at. It answers how much cash is consumed per dollar of new recurring revenue.

Where it goes wrong

  • Quoting a single unusually good month.
  • Reporting net burn without disclosing the gross figure.
  • Treating burn as a fixed number when it usually rises with headcount already committed.
  • Not knowing burn precisely, which is a real signal about operational discipline.

Related terms

RunwayHow many months until the money runs out.Gross burn vs. net burnGross burn is total cash going out. Net burn is that minus cash coming in — what actually shortens the runway.Runway extension leversThe specific moves available to buy more time — cutting cost, accelerating collections, raising a bridge, or growing revenue.Default alive / default deadWhether a company reaches profitability on current cash and current growth, without raising again.Round sizingDeciding how much to raise — set by the milestones that make the next round possible, not by what's available.

How companies are judged

Runway#

How many months until the money runs out.

Picture this: $600K in the bank, burning $50K a month = 12 months of runway. Fundraising takes about six, so this company should already be raising.

Why it matters

Runway is cash divided by net burn — the number of months before the company is out of money. It's the single most important operating number at an early company because it bounds every other decision.

The trap is that runway is usually calculated on today's burn, and burn rises. A plan that shows fourteen months at current spend often shows nine at planned spend, and the planned figure is the real one.

What it looks like in practice

Raising should start when there are nine to twelve months left, because the process takes three to six and the terms get worse as the buffer shrinks. Investors can see the position and it prices in.

The useful discipline is running two numbers: runway at current burn, and runway under the hiring plan. The gap between them is the decision that hasn't been made explicitly yet.

Where it goes wrong

  • Calculating on current burn when the plan increases spending.
  • Starting a raise with under six months, which visibly weakens the position.
  • Assuming a bridge will be available if the raise takes longer.
  • Reporting runway without saying which burn assumption it uses.

Related terms

How companies are judged

Lifestyle business#

A company that makes real money for its owners but has no path to becoming enormous. Nothing is wrong with it — it is just not what venture capital is built to fund.

Picture this: an agency doing $2M a year, throwing off $400K in profit to two founders, growing 10% a year. A wonderful outcome for them and a terrible one for a fund, because a 10% grower cannot return the fund no matter how well it is run. This is the most common reason a good company gets a pass, and saying it plainly is kinder than inventing a flaw.

Why it matters

A lifestyle business is one that can be profitable and durable without ever being large enough to return a venture fund. It's not a criticism of the business — it's a statement about fit.

Under the power law a fund needs outcomes large enough that one can return everything. A company that will comfortably reach $8M of revenue and stay there is a good business and a bad venture investment, and conflating those two judgments serves nobody.

What it looks like in practice

The honest version of the conversation happens early. A founder who wants a sustainable, profitable, independent company should not raise venture money, because the structure will force decisions they don't want.

The tell is usually in the ambition of the market definition combined with the founder's stated goals. Both are legitimate; they just have to match the funding structure.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating it as a pejorative. Most good businesses are lifestyle businesses.
  • Funding one with venture capital and then pressuring it to behave otherwise.
  • Assuming a founder who says they want independence will change their mind after a round.
  • Confusing current size with ceiling. The question is the ceiling.

Related terms

How companies are judged

Product-market fit#

The point where the market pulls the product out of the company instead of the company pushing it out.

Why it matters

Product-market fit is the dividing line that determines what a company should be doing. Before it, the job is learning — talking to users, changing the product, sometimes changing who it's for. After it, the job is scaling what already works.

Scaling before fit is the classic way to die with money in the bank: spending to acquire users who don't stay, at a rate that only accelerates the loss.

What it looks like in practice

The signals are behavioural rather than declarative. Users return without prompting, get upset when it breaks, tell colleagues unasked, and usage grows when nobody is pushing it. Compare that with a product where every user traces back to founder outreach and retention decays quietly after week one.

Fit is also segment-specific. Strong fit in one narrow segment and none in another is the normal shape, and the mistake is averaging across them.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating it as binary rather than as a gradient that varies by segment.
  • Reading enthusiasm as fit. People are generous, especially to founders they like.
  • Reading signups as fit. Retention is the signal; acquisition isn't.
  • Assuming it's permanent. Fit is relative to a market, and markets move.

Where the term comes from

Marc Andreessen's 2007 post "The Only Thing That Matters" defined the term in one line — being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market — while explicitly attributing the underlying rule to Andy Rachleff, then of Benchmark, as "Rachleff's Corollary of Startup Success."

TAM#

Total Addressable Market. The whole revenue opportunity if you won everything.

Picture this: treat a $10B TAM slide as a claim to check, not a fact. At pre-seed it's the least informative number in the deck.

Why it matters

Total addressable market is the ceiling on how big this could ever get, and its real function for a fund is checking whether the outcome could be large enough to matter under the power law.

It's also the most inflated number in any deck, which means an inflated one costs credibility rather than buying it. A defensible $400M market beats an indefensible $90B one.

What it looks like in practice

The credible construction is bottom-up: countable customers times realistic contract value. That produces a smaller number and a much better conversation, because every input can be examined and argued with.

TAM also isn't static. Markets expand when a product makes something possible that wasn't before, and the strongest version of the argument explains that expansion rather than claiming a share of an existing total.

Where it goes wrong

  • Quoting an analyst report's industry figure.
  • The 1% fallacy, which describes no plan at all.
  • Defining the market to include people who will never buy this.
  • Presenting TAM alone without the serviceable and obtainable slices.

How companies are judged

KPI#

The handful of metrics a company actually steers by.

Why it matters

KPIs are the small set of numbers a company manages by. The value is in the selection: measuring everything is equivalent to measuring nothing, because attention is the scarce resource.

For an investor the KPIs a founder chooses are informative in themselves. A team tracking signups and pageviews is thinking differently from one tracking activation and cohort retention.

What it looks like in practice

Good KPIs are few, leading rather than lagging, and hard to move without genuinely improving the business. Revenue is a lagging indicator; activation and retention predict it.

They should change as the company's stage changes. The metrics that matter while searching for fit are not the ones that matter while scaling, and carrying the old set forward is a common source of misdirected effort.

Where it goes wrong

  • Tracking so many metrics that none of them drives a decision.
  • Choosing vanity metrics that only go up.
  • Keeping the same KPIs across stages with very different questions.
  • Reporting KPIs without the context of what would count as good.

Related terms

How companies are judged

Retention / churn#

Whether people who started using it are still using it. The least gameable number a young company has.

Picture this: growth can be bought. Retention can't. A company adding 40% more users monthly while losing 30% of last month's is not growing, it's leaking — and at pre-seed, retention is usually the only real evidence product-market fit is coming.

Why it matters

Retention is the closest thing to a single measure of whether a product is any good. Acquisition can be bought; retention has to be earned, which is why it's the number that predicts everything downstream.

Churn compounds exactly as hard as growth. A business losing 5% of customers monthly has an average customer life of about twenty months and has to run hard just to stand still.

What it looks like in practice

Logo churn and revenue churn can diverge instructively. Losing many small accounts while retaining large ones is a very different business from the reverse, and a blended number hides which one you have.

The most useful view is by cohort, plotted against age. A curve that flattens means a durable base; one that keeps declining means the company has to keep replacing everyone forever.

Where it goes wrong

  • Tracking only logo churn while revenue concentrates in a few fragile accounts.
  • Averaging across segments, which hides that one is fine and another is bleeding.
  • Treating churn as a customer-success problem when it's usually a product-fit problem.
  • Not asking departing customers why. It's the cheapest research available and the most avoided.

Related terms

Above 100% means the existing base grows without adding anyone.Lifetime value (LTV)The total gross profit expected from a customer across the whole relationship. A projection, not a measurement.Product-market fitThe point where the market pulls the product out of the company instead of the company pushing it out.ActivationThe moment a new user first gets real value — and the share of signups who reach it.

How companies are judged

Net revenue retention (NRR)#

What last year's customers are worth this year, including expansion, minus churn. Above 100% means the existing base grows without adding anyone.

Picture this: 120% NRR means a company that signed zero new customers would still grow 20%. That's the number that makes enterprise investors lean in.

Why it matters

NRR measures what happens to revenue from existing customers over a year, including expansion, contraction, and churn. Above 100% means the existing base grows without a single new logo.

That's the quiet engine behind most exceptional SaaS businesses. A company at 130% NRR grows meaningfully every year even if sales stops entirely, which is a fundamentally different asset from one at 85%.

What it looks like in practice

It's calculated on a cohort of customers at the start of a period, comparing their revenue at the end — so it captures upsell and downgrade as well as loss.

The pricing structure largely determines it. Per-seat and usage-based models produce natural expansion; flat pricing cannot exceed 100% without a renegotiation.

Where it goes wrong

  • Including new customers in the calculation, which inflates it.
  • Reporting NRR without gross retention alongside, which hides heavy churn masked by upsell.
  • Comparing NRR across companies with different contract structures.
  • Assuming a high NRR from a small number of expanding accounts is durable.

Related terms

How companies are judged

Default alive / default dead#

Whether a company reaches profitability on current cash and current growth, without raising again.

Picture this: Paul Graham's framing, and the most useful question to ask a founder at pre-seed — not "how much runway do you have" but "does your current trajectory get you to safety, or does it require me and someone after me?"

Why it matters

The question is whether a company reaches profitability on current trajectory before it runs out of money. Default alive means yes on existing growth and burn; default dead means no, and the company is dependent on raising again.

It reframes fundraising from a milestone into a dependency. A default-dead company has handed its survival to a market it doesn't control, and markets close.

What it looks like in practice

The calculation projects current revenue growth against current burn and asks whether the lines cross before the cash runs out. It's a rough number and its value is in forcing the question rather than in precision.

Most early companies are default dead and should be — the whole point of venture funding is to spend ahead of revenue. What matters is knowing it, and knowing what it would take to change.

Where it goes wrong

  • Not running the calculation, which is the most common failure.
  • Assuming growth continues at the current rate when projecting.
  • Treating default dead as inherently bad rather than as a dependency to be managed.
  • Discovering the answer when the runway is already short enough to remove the options.

Where the term comes from

Paul Graham introduced the framing in a 2015 essay, arguing that founders should know which state they're in at all times, and that most don't.

How companies are judged

Founder-market fit#

Whether these specific people are the right ones for this problem. At pre-seed, where there's little else to underwrite, this is most of the decision.

Why it matters

Founder-market fit is whether this particular team has an unusual advantage in this particular market — domain knowledge, distribution access, or experience that can't be acquired quickly.

At pre-seed it carries most of the weight, because there's little else to evaluate. It's the reason to believe this team will reach the insight before a better-funded competitor.

What it looks like in practice

The evidence is specific rather than general: years inside the problem, a network of the right people, a prior attempt that failed instructively, or access to data or customers others can't reach.

The counterexample is worth holding: plenty of outsiders have built great companies precisely because they didn't know what was supposed to be impossible. Fit is a strong prior, not a rule.

Where it goes wrong

  • Accepting general enthusiasm for a market as founder-market fit.
  • Treating credentials as equivalent to operating experience in the problem.
  • Applying it so strictly that outsider founders are systematically filtered out.
  • Assuming fit in an adjacent market transfers. It often doesn't.

Prior shared experience#

Whether co-founders knew each other before starting. The single strongest team signal in the unicorn data.

Picture this: of 1,377 multi-founder unicorns, 68.6% had co-founders who previously worked or studied together — 57.8% same employer, 33.3% same university. Working together beats studying together. "We met at a hackathon last month" is a real risk factor.

Why it matters

Founding teams who have worked together before have already tested the thing that most often breaks companies: whether they can disagree productively under pressure. That's not observable in a pitch, and it's not learnable quickly.

The research on founding team composition consistently finds prior shared experience predictive, which makes it one of the few team signals with evidence behind it.

What it looks like in practice

What matters is whether they've worked together through something difficult, not whether they've known each other a long time. Friends who have never built anything together are a different proposition from colleagues who shipped under pressure.

The diligence question is direct: tell me about the biggest disagreement you two have had, and how it resolved. Teams who have been through it answer easily.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating long friendship as equivalent to having worked together.
  • Ignoring that co-founders who met recently can still be excellent — it's a prior, not a rule.
  • Not asking how they handle disagreement, which is the thing being tested.
  • Assuming prior shared experience removes the need for vesting.

Odds ratio#

How overrepresented a background is among winners, compared to how common it is among all VC-backed founders. Above 1.0 means it predicts something; below means it doesn't.

Picture this: Facebook/Meta alumni sit at 4.0x, Google at 2.9x, the Israel Defense Forces at 2.6x. Harvard is 0.89 — below parity. Prestige and predictive power are different things, and this number tells them apart.

Why it matters

An odds ratio compares the likelihood of an outcome in one group against another — how much more likely a founder from a given background is to build a successful company. It's how the research on founder backgrounds is usually expressed.

It matters because it forces a distinction between a signal that is real and one that is merely visible. Many things correlate with success weakly and are treated as though they were decisive.

What it looks like in practice

The interpretation trap is base rates. A background with three times the odds of producing a successful founder still produces very few of them in absolute terms, because the base rate is tiny.

It's also correlation. Selective institutions and companies select for people who were already likely to succeed, which means the ratio measures the selection as much as the experience.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reading an odds ratio as a probability.
  • Ignoring base rates, which makes small ratios look decisive.
  • Treating correlation in the data as causation in the individual.
  • Using population statistics to make a judgment about a specific founder in front of you.

Talent factory#

A company whose alumni disproportionately go on to found winners — and the fact that these decay.

Picture this: the PayPal Mafia's odds ratio collapsed from 12.0 before 2016 to 1.7 after. Meanwhile Google rose from 4.4% to 9.1% of unicorn founders, Facebook from 0.9% to 5.3%, and OpenAI went from zero to 1.8% — 21 unicorn founders since 2016. Where talent comes from is a moving target; today's edge is watching the current factories, not the famous old one.

Why it matters

Some companies produce a disproportionate number of founders — the alumni networks of certain firms show up repeatedly in successful cap tables. Those organisations function as talent factories.

For sourcing this is a practical filter. Knowing which organisations in your sector reliably produce founders tells you where to build relationships years before anyone starts a company.

What it looks like in practice

The mechanism is a combination of selection, training, and network. These companies hire well, expose people to hard problems at scale, and create a peer group where starting something is normal.

The signal decays with distance. Someone who spent four years in a core team is a different proposition from someone who spent nine months in an adjacent function, and the logo doesn't distinguish them.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating the logo as the signal rather than what the person actually did there.
  • Over-indexing on a small number of well-known companies and missing sector-specific ones.
  • Assuming the factory effect transfers to a completely different domain.
  • Using it as a filter rather than as a sourcing map.

University signal#

Which schools actually overproduce unicorn founders, by volume and by rate.

Picture this: Stanford leads on raw count (113 unicorns), then MIT (89) and Harvard (76). But by odds ratio the leader is University of Utah at 3.72x, then University of Washington at 2.57x. Michigan and Penn are top-13 by count yet below 1.0 by odds. Only Stanford and MIT lead on both — and the Seattle note is that UW is second in the country on rate.

Why it matters

Founders from a handful of universities appear disproportionately in successful companies, and the research quantifies it. The question is what the signal actually measures.

Most of it is selection and network rather than education. Selective institutions admit people who were already likely to do well, and then connect them to each other and to capital.

What it looks like in practice

Used as a sourcing input it's reasonable — these networks are dense and worth being part of. Used as a filter it's a way to systematically miss founders whose advantage came from somewhere else.

The stronger version of the same information is what the person did, not where they were. A specific project, a shipped product, a research result — all of those carry more information than the institution.

Where it goes wrong

  • Using it as a screening criterion rather than as one weak input.
  • Confusing the network effect with the education.
  • Ignoring base rates — most founders from any university don't succeed.
  • Letting it substitute for evaluating what the founder has actually built.

Read the original

  • Ilya Strebulaev (Stanford GSB) — venture capital research↗

How companies are judged

Unit economics#

Whether a single customer makes or loses money, once you count what it cost to get them and what it costs to serve them.

Picture this: $1,800 to acquire, $60 a month in revenue, $14 a month to serve. You're profitable on that customer in month 40 — assuming they stay that long, which they don't.

Why it matters

Unit economics is where growth either compounds or accelerates the collapse. A company losing money per customer that raises money to acquire more customers is buying its own failure faster, and the revenue chart looks great the whole time.

For a pre-seed investor the numbers are unreliable — too few customers, too short a history — but the founder's grip on them isn't. Someone who knows their real cost to serve, including support and infrastructure, is running a business rather than a product.

What it looks like in practice

The honest calculation uses fully loaded costs: all sales and marketing spend divided by customers acquired, not just ad spend; cost to serve including support, hosting, and inference; and a retention estimate grounded in actual cohorts rather than an assumption.

For AI products the cost side is genuinely different from classic SaaS, because serving costs scale with usage. Gross margins of 40–60% are common where SaaS assumed 80%, and every model built on the old assumption is wrong.

Where it goes wrong

  • Excluding salaries from CAC, which understates it by a lot.
  • Using an LTV built on an assumed retention curve rather than a measured one.
  • Ignoring inference and infrastructure cost in cost-to-serve.
  • Scaling acquisition before the unit is profitable, on the theory that scale will fix it.

Gross margin#

Revenue minus the direct cost of delivering it, as a percentage — what's left to fund everything else.

Picture this: $100 of revenue costs $38 in inference, hosting, and support. Gross margin is 62%. That 62% is what has to cover engineering, sales, and everything else before there's a profit.

Why it matters

Gross margin decides what kind of company you are, and it's the number that drives valuation multiples more than growth rate does at the margin. An 85% gross margin business and a 35% one at the same revenue are not comparable assets.

It's also the constraint on everything downstream. Low margin means less room to acquire customers, less room to hire, and a much higher revenue bar before the company can fund itself.

What it looks like in practice

The judgment call is what counts as cost of revenue. Hosting, third-party APIs, inference, payment processing, and customer support attributable to delivery all belong in it. Sales, marketing, and R&D don't.

AI-native companies are the live case. Where classic SaaS ran at 75–85%, products with heavy inference frequently run at 40–60% — which is a real business, just not a SaaS one, and it should be modelled and valued accordingly.

Where it goes wrong

  • Excluding inference or infrastructure costs to make margins look like SaaS.
  • Putting customer success entirely in operating expense when much of it is delivery.
  • Reporting margin before payment processing and refunds.
  • Assuming margin improves with scale without knowing which cost actually falls.

ARR, MRR, and ACV#

Annual recurring revenue, monthly recurring revenue, and average contract value — three views of the same subscription base.

Picture this: MRR of $84,000 means ARR of about $1M. If that's spread over 40 customers, ACV is $25,000 — a mid-market business. Over 4 customers, ACV is $250,000 and it's an enterprise one with concentration risk.

Why it matters

These are the numbers every investor asks for first, and the ones most often reported loosely. Recurring means contractually repeating — not revenue that happened to recur, and not one-off implementation fees annualised into a bigger-sounding number.

ACV is the one founders skip and investors care about, because it determines the go-to-market. A $2,000 ACV cannot support a salesperson; a $200,000 ACV cannot be sold self-serve. The number implies the whole cost structure.

What it looks like in practice

ARR is normally MRR times twelve rather than trailing revenue, which makes it a run-rate — a forward-looking snapshot, not a historical figure. That's fine as long as everyone knows which is being quoted.

The variants matter in diligence: committed versus annualised, gross versus net of churn, and whether services revenue is included. Founders quoting a big number without specifying which are the ones to slow down.

Where it goes wrong

  • Annualising a single good month into ARR.
  • Including one-off setup, services, or usage overage in recurring revenue.
  • Counting signed pilots that haven't started billing.
  • Reporting ARR growth without ACV, hiding whether growth came from more customers or bigger ones.

Related terms

Customer acquisition cost (CAC)#

Everything spent to win a customer, divided by the number of customers won.

Picture this: $60,000 on marketing and sales in a quarter — including the salaries — produced 30 customers. CAC is $2,000. Counting only ad spend would have said $700, and every decision built on that number would be wrong.

Why it matters

CAC is half of the central question in any growth business: does a customer generate more than they cost. It's also the number most often understated, because the honest version includes salaries and the flattering version doesn't.

The trend matters more than the level. CAC that rises as you scale means you've exhausted the cheap channel and are buying progressively less interested customers — which is the normal path, and the thing to know about before raising a round to accelerate it.

What it looks like in practice

Fully loaded means all sales and marketing costs: salaries, commissions, tooling, content, events, and ad spend, over the period that produced the customers. Blended CAC mixes organic and paid; paid CAC isolates what you actually control.

Segment it. One channel at $400 and another at $6,000 average to something meaningless, and the decision you want to make is about the channels, not the average.

Where it goes wrong

  • Counting only ad spend.
  • Using blended CAC to justify scaling paid acquisition.
  • Attributing customers to the period the spend happened rather than the period they closed.
  • Comparing your CAC to a benchmark from a company with a different ACV.

Related terms

CAC payback period#

How long it takes for a customer's gross profit to repay what it cost to acquire them.

Picture this: CAC of $2,400, gross profit of $200 a month. Payback is 12 months. Every customer is a twelve- month loan the company makes to itself, funded by the last round.

Why it matters

Payback is the cash-flow view of unit economics, and it's the one that actually constrains growth. A business with excellent lifetime value and a 30-month payback needs enormous capital to grow, because every new customer consumes cash for two and a half years before returning any.

It's a better early metric than LTV/CAC because it depends on far fewer assumptions. You need CAC and gross margin, both measurable now, rather than a retention curve you're guessing at.

What it looks like in practice

Under 12 months is strong for B2B SaaS, 12–18 is workable, and beyond 24 the business is capital-hungry regardless of how good the lifetime value looks. Consumer businesses generally need much faster payback because retention is shorter and less certain.

Use gross profit rather than revenue. Paying back on revenue ignores the cost of serving the customer and overstates the speed by whatever your margin isn't.

Where it goes wrong

  • Calculating on revenue instead of gross profit.
  • Ignoring that payback lengthens as you move to more expensive channels.
  • Accepting a long payback because LTV/CAC looks good — the constraint is cash, not ratio.
  • Averaging across segments with very different payback profiles.

Lifetime value (LTV)#

The total gross profit expected from a customer across the whole relationship. A projection, not a measurement.

Picture this: $200 a month gross profit and an average life of 30 months gives an LTV of $6,000. Against a CAC of $2,000 that's a 3:1 ratio — entirely dependent on a 30-month assumption that a two-year-old company cannot have observed.

Why it matters

LTV is the most confidently quoted and least reliable number in early-stage decks, because it's a projection built on a retention curve that hasn't happened yet. Small changes in assumed churn produce enormous changes in LTV.

The 3:1 LTV/CAC benchmark gets repeated as though it were a law. It's a rule of thumb from mature SaaS, and applying it to a company with eleven months of history is arithmetic dressed as evidence.

What it looks like in practice

Use gross profit rather than revenue, and be explicit about the churn assumption — ideally from measured cohorts rather than an average. Where retention hasn't been observed long enough, the honest move is to report the payback period instead and say so.

Segmented LTV is more useful than blended, because retention usually varies far more between segments than within them, and the segment with strong retention is the one worth acquiring more of.

Where it goes wrong

  • Computing LTV on revenue rather than gross profit.
  • Assuming a retention curve far longer than anything observed.
  • Quoting an LTV/CAC ratio without stating the churn assumption underneath it.
  • Treating a projection as a measurement in a board deck.

Gross burn vs. net burn#

Gross burn is total cash going out. Net burn is that minus cash coming in — what actually shortens the runway.

Picture this: $420,000 out and $180,000 in each month. Gross burn is $420K, net burn is $240K. Runway is calculated on the $240K, but a revenue stumble moves you toward the $420K fast.

Why it matters

Net burn is the number that determines survival, but gross burn is the number that determines exposure. A company with high gross burn and high revenue looks healthy until revenue moves, and then the cost base is revealed at full size.

The distinction matters most for businesses with concentrated or volatile revenue. Losing one large customer converts a comfortable net burn into an emergency without any change in spending.

What it looks like in practice

Track both, and understand runway under a scenario where revenue falls. The gap between the two is a measure of how dependent survival is on revenue continuing exactly as forecast.

Non-recurring items distort both. A one-off legal bill or an annual prepayment can make a month look alarming or reassuring, which is why a three-month average is the usual basis for runway.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reporting only net burn, hiding the size of the fixed cost base.
  • Calculating runway from a single unusually good month.
  • Ignoring what happens to runway if the largest customer leaves.
  • Treating collections as revenue — cash timing and recognition are different things.

Related terms

Runway extension levers#

The specific moves available to buy more time — cutting cost, accelerating collections, raising a bridge, or growing revenue.

Picture this: seven months of runway. Cutting discretionary spend buys one month. Moving customers to annual prepay buys two. A bridge from existing investors buys six. Each has a different cost and a different signal.

Why it matters

Every lever gets more expensive the later you pull it. A cost reduction at nine months of runway is a decision; the same reduction at three months is a crisis, and everyone — investors, employees, customers — can tell the difference.

For an investor, which lever a founder reaches for first is informative. Founders who cut early and communicate clearly tend to survive; founders who wait for the raise to solve it tend to run out of options.

What it looks like in practice

The levers in rough order of speed: discretionary spend, hiring freeze, moving customers to annual prepayment, collections discipline, headcount reduction, then financing. Revenue growth is the best lever and the slowest, which is why it rarely solves a runway problem on its own.

The rule that holds up is to cut once and deeply rather than three times shallowly. Repeated small reductions destroy morale far more than a single decisive one.

Where it goes wrong

  • Waiting until under three months of runway, when every option is worse.
  • Cutting in small increments repeatedly, which is worse for the team than cutting once.
  • Assuming a bridge is available. It depends on existing investors' conviction, not need.
  • Cutting the things that generate revenue to preserve the things that don't.

Related terms

RunwayHow many months until the money runs out.Burn rateHow much cash a company spends per month.Bridge roundA small round to get a company from where it is to its next real round or milestone. Cohort retention#

Tracking each group of customers who started in the same period separately, so you can see whether retention is improving.

Picture this: the January cohort is at 34% after six months. The June cohort is at 61% at the same age. The product got better, and only cohort analysis shows it — the blended number hides it completely.

Why it matters

Blended retention mixes customers who joined at different times under different products, which makes it nearly useless in a company that's changing. A growing company's blended number is dominated by recent joiners and looks better than the business is.

Cohorts are also the only honest basis for LTV. A retention curve that flattens — where some share of each cohort stays indefinitely — is a fundamentally different business from one that decays to zero, and you cannot tell which you have from an average.

What it looks like in practice

Plot each cohort's survival against age rather than calendar date, so cohorts are comparable. What you're looking for is whether later cohorts sit above earlier ones at the same age, and whether the curve flattens.

The flattening point is the most important feature. A curve that stabilises at 40% means a durable base; one that keeps declining means the business has to keep replacing everyone, forever.

Where it goes wrong

  • Reporting blended retention in a company that's growing quickly.
  • Comparing cohorts by calendar date instead of by age.
  • Judging a cohort before it's old enough to show the shape of the curve.
  • Measuring logo retention only, when revenue retention tells a different story.

Related terms

Retention / churnWhether people who started using it are still using it. Above 100% means the existing base grows without adding anyone.

North Star metric#

The single number that best captures the value customers get, used to align what everyone works on.

Picture this: not signups, and not revenue. Something like "weekly active teams completing at least one workflow" — a number that only goes up when the product is genuinely being used for its purpose.

Why it matters

Teams optimise what they measure, and most companies measure things that can be improved without improving the product. Picking one number that can't be gamed is a coordination device more than a measurement one.

The failure it prevents is a common one: marketing optimising signups, product optimising engagement, sales optimising bookings, and the company as a whole getting worse while every dashboard is green.

What it looks like in practice

A good north star measures delivered value, moves before revenue does, and is influenceable by the team. Revenue itself is usually a bad choice because it lags too far behind the work and can be moved by pricing rather than product.

It's a focusing device, not the only number worth watching. Retention, burn, and margin still need attention — the north star just decides what gets prioritised when they conflict.

Where it goes wrong

  • Choosing a metric that can be improved without the product getting better.
  • Picking revenue, which lags and hides what caused it.
  • Changing it every quarter, which defeats the purpose of having one.
  • Treating it as the only metric, and letting margin or burn drift.

TAM, SAM, and SOM#

Total addressable market, serviceable addressable market, and serviceable obtainable market — the market, the slice you could actually sell to, and the slice you could realistically win.

Picture this: TAM: everyone with this problem. SAM: those in your geography, segment, and price band. SOM: what you could win in five years given a real sales motion. The third number is the only one that constrains anything.

Why it matters

Market size is the term investors most expect to be inflated, so an inflated number costs credibility rather than buying it. A $90B TAM assembled from an industry report signals that the founder hasn't done the work.

What the number is actually for is checking whether the outcome can be large enough to matter to a fund. Under the power law, a company that can only ever be worth $60M is not a fit for a fund needing one investment to return everything — regardless of quality.

What it looks like in practice

The credible version is built bottom-up: number of potential customers times realistic annual contract value. That produces a smaller number and a much better conversation, because every input can be examined.

SOM is where the argument actually lives. It forces a statement about the go-to-market — how many customers can be reached, at what rate, through what channel — which is the part that reveals whether the founder has a plan.

Where it goes wrong

  • Quoting an analyst report's industry figure as TAM.
  • The 1% fallacy — "if we capture 1% of a $50B market" — which describes no plan at all.
  • Defining TAM so broadly it includes people who will never buy this.
  • Presenting only TAM and skipping SAM and SOM, where the real constraint is.

Related terms

Bottom-up market sizingBuilding the market number from actual units — how many customers exist, and what each would pay — instead of taking a share of an industry total.TAMTotal Addressable Market. Not a quirk — the organizing principle of the whole asset class.

Bottom-up market sizing#

Building the market number from actual units — how many customers exist, and what each would pay — instead of taking a share of an industry total.

Picture this: 28,000 US clinics of the right size, times $14,000 a year, is a $392M market. Every input is checkable and arguable, which is exactly what makes it credible.

Why it matters

Top-down sizing produces a number nobody believes, including the person presenting it. Bottom-up produces a smaller number that survives scrutiny — and surviving scrutiny is the entire purpose of putting a market size in a deck.

It also forces the founder to know their customer. You cannot build a bottom-up estimate without a concrete ICP and a defensible price, which means the exercise itself surfaces whether those exist.

What it looks like in practice

Start from a countable population — companies of a given size in a given industry, or people in a defined situation — narrow it by the criteria in the ICP, and multiply by realistic annual contract value based on what people currently pay for the alternative.

Showing the sources for each input is what converts it from a claim into an argument. An investor who disagrees with one assumption can substitute their own, which is a far better conversation than disagreeing with the total.

Where it goes wrong

  • Using a list price nobody actually pays as the ACV input.
  • Counting the entire industry rather than the segment matching the ICP.
  • Presenting the result without the inputs, which returns it to being an unverifiable number.
  • Assuming 100% of the countable population is reachable through your channel.

How companies are judged

First ten hires#

The first employees after the founders — the hires that set the culture and determine what the company can execute.

Picture this: hire ten generalists who can each do three jobs badly, and you get a company that ships slowly. Hire ten specialists too early and you get a company that can't change direction. Both mistakes are expensive at this size.

Why it matters

At ten people every hire is 10% of the company, and the compounding is cultural as well as operational — early employees set the hiring bar for everyone after them. A weak fifth hire produces a weak fifteenth.

For an investor this is where a lot of post-investment risk lives. A founder who can attract people better than themselves into a risky, underpaid role is demonstrating something that no metric captures.

What it looks like in practice

The pattern that works is generalists early, specialists as the shape of the work becomes clear. The first hires need to be comfortable with undefined roles, because the roles genuinely are undefined and will change twice in the first year.

Compensation is the visible constraint and rarely the binding one. Early employees join for the problem, the people, and the ownership. The equity has to be meaningful enough to matter, which at ten people means whole percentage points for the first few.

Where it goes wrong

  • Hiring specialists before knowing what the job actually is.
  • Lowering the bar to fill a role quickly, which resets the bar permanently.
  • Under-granting equity to the first hires, then trying to correct it two years later.
  • Hiring people who need structure into a company that doesn't have any yet.

Getting out

Exit#

The event that turns shares into money: acquisition, IPO, or secondary sale.

Why it matters

The exit is the only event that converts a position into money. Everything before it — markups, valuations, TVPI — is an estimate of what an exit might produce.

It's also the constraint the fund structure imposes on the company. A ten-year fund needs exits within its life, which is why GPs push for liquidity on timelines that sometimes have nothing to do with what's best for the business.

What it looks like in practice

The routes are acquisition, IPO, secondary sale, or acqui-hire, and the distribution is heavily skewed toward acquisition. IPOs are rare and getting rarer as companies stay private longer.

What each holder receives depends on the waterfall, not the headline price. A well-publicised exit can pay common shareholders nothing if the preference stack exceeds the proceeds.

Where it goes wrong

  • Modelling exit value without running it through the preference stack.
  • Assuming an IPO is a realistic base case. For almost all companies it isn't.
  • Reading an announced acquisition price as what shareholders received.
  • Ignoring that fund life creates pressure to exit that the company doesn't share.

Related terms

Liquidity eventAny moment shareholders can convert equity to cash.M&AAnother company buys this one. The most common exit by far.IPOThe company lists publicly. Rare, slow, and the outcome everyone talks about.Secondary saleSelling your existing shares to another investor without the company raising anything.DistributionCash — or sometimes shares — actually leaving the fund and landing with LPs. Not a valuation, not a markup. Money out the door.Deemed liquidation eventThe definition of what counts as a liquidation for the purpose of paying out preferences — usually including an acquisition, not just a winding up.

Liquidity event#

Any moment shareholders can convert equity to cash.

Why it matters

A liquidity event is any moment shareholders can convert holdings into cash. It's broader than an exit — secondary sales and tender offers create liquidity for some holders without ending the company's independence.

The distinction matters because companies stay private far longer than they used to. Partial liquidity has become a normal part of a long private life rather than something that only happens at the end.

What it looks like in practice

The charter's definition of a deemed liquidation event is what determines whether preferences trigger. Not every liquidity event is one — a secondary sale between shareholders usually isn't.

For employees the practical forms are tender offers and secondary sales, both controlled by the company and both subject to the transfer restrictions in the shareholder agreements.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming every liquidity event triggers liquidation preferences.
  • Confusing partial liquidity with an exit for fund accounting purposes.
  • Ignoring transfer restrictions that make a private sale impossible without consent.
  • Treating a tender offer as equivalent to an exit for the employees who participate.

Related terms

Getting out

M&A#

Another company buys this one. The most common exit by far.

Why it matters

Acquisition is how the large majority of venture-backed exits happen. IPOs get the attention; M&A produces the returns.

The process is where all the terms negotiated years earlier come due at once — the preference stack, the drag-along, the deemed liquidation definition, vesting acceleration. None of them matter until they all matter simultaneously.

What it looks like in practice

The sequence runs from approach through LOI with exclusivity, diligence, definitive agreements, and close. Leverage peaks before the LOI is signed and declines steadily afterwards.

The most common failure is a retrade: diligence surfaces something, the price drops, and the seller has no alternative because exclusivity removed it. Cleaning up diligence problems before starting is the main defence.

Where it goes wrong

  • Signing a long exclusivity without a closing deadline.
  • Starting a process without knowing where the disagreement range sits.
  • Leaving known diligence problems to be discovered by the buyer.
  • Running a process with one buyer, which removes every source of leverage.

Getting out

IPO#

The company lists publicly. Rare, slow, and the outcome everyone talks about.

Why it matters

An IPO converts private shares into publicly traded ones. For a fund it's rarely an immediate liquidity event, because lock-ups prevent selling for months after listing.

It's also the trigger for automatic conversion of preferred into common, which is why the qualified IPO thresholds in the charter matter — set wrong, they can block the offering the company needs.

What it looks like in practice

Companies stay private much longer than they did, which has pushed IPOs later and made them rarer as a share of exits. That change is what created the market for secondary sales and tender offers.

After the lock-up expires the fund either sells into the market or distributes shares in kind to LPs. Both have market-impact and timing consequences.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating an IPO as an immediate liquidity event. The lock-up usually runs 90–180 days.
  • Marking a position at the offer price and treating it as realised.
  • Not checking whether the qualified IPO threshold in the charter is realistically achievable.
  • Distributing in kind to LPs who cannot hold public securities.

Secondary sale#

Selling your existing shares to another investor without the company raising anything.

Picture this: you invested at $10M. Five years later the company is worth $400M but nowhere near an IPO. You sell part of your stake to a growth fund and take real money off the table.

Why it matters

A secondary sale is an existing shareholder selling to a new buyer, rather than the company issuing new shares. It provides liquidity without a company exit, which matters when companies stay private for a decade.

For a fund approaching the end of its life it's often the only way to realise a position in a company that isn't selling and isn't going public.

What it looks like in practice

Transfer restrictions govern what's possible: rights of first refusal, co-sale rights, and board consent all apply, and each adds delay. A sale that looks straightforward can take months.

Secondaries usually price at a discount to the last round, partly because the buyer gets common or a less favourable class, and partly because the seller needs the liquidity more than the buyer needs the position.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming shares can be sold freely. Almost always they can't.
  • Not budgeting for the ROFR and co-sale windows.
  • Reading a secondary price as the company's valuation. The terms and class differ.
  • Ignoring the effect on the 409A when a large secondary establishes a common price.

Related terms

It controls who ends up on the cap table.Tag-along rightsIf big shareholders sell, small ones can join on the same terms. Getting out

Lock-up period#

After an IPO, insiders can't sell for a set window — typically 90–180 days.

Why it matters

The lock-up prevents insiders from selling for a set window after an IPO — typically 90 to 180 days. It exists so the market isn't flooded with insider selling immediately after listing.

For a fund it means an IPO is not liquidity. The position remains at market risk through the lock-up, and the price at expiry may bear little relation to the offer price.

What it looks like in practice

Expiry is a known, dated event, which means the market prices in the expected supply ahead of it. Prices frequently soften into a lock-up expiry for exactly that reason.

Staggered releases and early-release provisions tied to price thresholds have become more common, which spreads the supply and reduces the cliff effect.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating the IPO date as the realisation date.
  • Marking the position at the offer price through the lock-up.
  • Not planning the disposal strategy before expiry, when everyone else is selling.
  • Assuming the lock-up terms are standard. Early-release provisions vary.

Getting out

Acqui-hire#

An acquisition made mostly for the team, where the product is usually shut down.

Picture this: a company that raised $6M and didn't find a market sells for $9M. The engineers get retention packages worth more than the shareholders receive. Investors get their money back, and not much more.

Why it matters

Acqui-hires are how a large share of venture-backed companies actually end, and the economics are very different from a real acquisition. Most of the value goes to the team as compensation rather than to shareholders as proceeds, which is a structural conflict.

For a fund it's a soft landing rather than a return — capital back, occasionally a small multiple, never a fund-returner. Under the power law it barely moves the outcome, which is why funds are generally relaxed about them.

What it looks like in practice

The negotiation is about how consideration splits between purchase price and retention compensation. Acquirers prefer retention because it buys what they're actually after; investors prefer purchase price because that's what pays the preference stack.

This is where founder and investor interests genuinely diverge, and where the protective provisions and drag-along matter — an acqui-hire that pays founders well and shareholders poorly usually needs approval from the people being paid poorly.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating it as a success in an update. Investors can read the numbers.
  • Negotiating retention packages without regard for the preference stack, then needing consent.
  • Assuming the product survives. It usually doesn't, and customers should hear it from you.
  • Forgetting that a team without acceleration may have little incentive to accept.

Getting out

Letter of intent (LOI)#

A mostly non-binding document setting out the shape of an acquisition before the definitive agreements are drafted.

Picture this: the LOI says $60M, subject to diligence, with 45 days of exclusivity. The price is non-binding and the exclusivity is binding — which is the part that actually changes the company's position.

Why it matters

The LOI is where leverage peaks and then starts to decline. Once signed with exclusivity, the company can't shop the deal, and every diligence finding becomes a reason to renegotiate against a seller with no alternative.

Price in an LOI is an opening position, not a commitment. Retrading after diligence is common enough that experienced sellers negotiate the terms that constrain it before signing rather than after.

What it looks like in practice

The binding parts are usually exclusivity, confidentiality, and who pays costs. Everything about price and structure is subject to diligence and definitive documents.

Shorter exclusivity is better for the seller, and specifying what can trigger a price adjustment narrows the room for a retrade. Both are much easier to negotiate before signing than after.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting long exclusivity, which removes the only leverage the seller has.
  • Treating the stated price as agreed.
  • Signing before cleaning up diligence problems that will surface anyway.
  • Letting the process run without a fallback plan if the deal dies.

Related terms

Getting out

Asset sale vs. stock sale#

Whether the buyer purchases the company's assets or its shares. It changes who keeps the liabilities and how everyone is taxed.

Picture this: in a stock sale the buyer takes the whole company, history and liabilities included. In an asset sale they take the parts they want, leave the rest behind, and the selling entity has to be wound up afterwards.

Why it matters

Buyers prefer asset sales because they leave unknown liabilities behind and often get better tax treatment. Sellers prefer stock sales because they're cleaner and usually taxed more favourably. The structure is one of the most consequential terms after price.

For shareholders it can matter more than the headline number. An asset sale can trigger different tax treatment and can complicate QSBS eligibility, which for founders holding qualifying stock is a very large difference on the same nominal price.

What it looks like in practice

Asset sales require transferring contracts individually, and many contracts have change-of- control or anti-assignment clauses that give counterparties a veto. That makes them slower and gives customers leverage at exactly the wrong moment.

The structure is usually settled in the LOI, which is another reason the LOI matters more than its non-binding label suggests.

Where it goes wrong

  • Negotiating price without pricing in the tax consequences of the structure.
  • Assuming contracts transfer automatically in an asset sale. Many don't.
  • Overlooking the QSBS implications for founders and early employees.
  • Leaving structure to the definitive documents rather than settling it in the LOI.

Getting out

Earnout#

Part of the purchase price paid later, contingent on the business hitting agreed targets after the acquisition.

Picture this: $40M at close, plus $20M if revenue doubles within two years. The founders no longer control the budget, the sales team, or the roadmap — but the $20M depends on all three.

Why it matters

Earnouts exist to bridge a disagreement about value, and they resolve it by transferring risk to the seller. The seller keeps the upside case they were arguing for, and takes the chance that it doesn't happen under someone else's management.

The structural problem is that the person responsible for hitting the targets no longer controls the resources. Earnouts are among the most common sources of post-acquisition litigation for exactly this reason.

What it looks like in practice

The terms that make an earnout achievable are about control and measurement: what resources are guaranteed, how the acquired business is accounted for separately, what happens if it's reorganised or merged into another unit, and precisely how the metric is calculated.

Revenue-based earnouts are more achievable than profit-based ones, because profit can be reduced by allocated overhead the seller doesn't control. Simple, countable metrics beat sophisticated ones.

Where it goes wrong

  • Accepting an earnout on profit, which the acquirer can affect through cost allocation.
  • Not securing the resources needed to hit the targets in writing.
  • Failing to address what happens if the business is reorganised or the product is discontinued.
  • Valuing the company at the full earnout, when most of it goes unpaid.

Tender offer (employee liquidity)#

A company-organised process letting employees and early shareholders sell some shares to investors, without an exit.

Picture this: at Series D the company runs a tender: employees with vested shares can sell up to 20% of their holding to the incoming investor. People who've been there six years get to buy a house without waiting for an IPO.

Why it matters

Companies stay private far longer than they used to, which means employees can hold illiquid paper for a decade. Tender offers exist to release some of that pressure without an exit, and they've become a standard retention tool at later-stage companies.

They're structured rather than ad hoc for good reasons: uncontrolled secondary sales create a messy cap table, unknown shareholders, and price signals the company doesn't control.

What it looks like in practice

The company sets the terms — who is eligible, what proportion can be sold, and at what price — and the buyer is usually an incoming or existing investor. Because the transaction establishes a price for common stock, it can affect the 409A valuation and therefore future option strike prices.

Eligibility rules typically require a minimum tenure and cap the percentage sellable, so the process provides relief without removing the incentive it was designed to preserve.

Where it goes wrong

  • Running one before the company can support the resulting 409A increase.
  • Allowing unrestricted selling, which removes the retention value entirely.
  • Ignoring the tax treatment for employees, which differs from an exit and can surprise people.
  • Letting uncoordinated secondary sales happen instead, and losing control of the cap table.

Related terms

Who the customer is

Everything above is about money and structure. This is the part that decides whether any of it was worth doing — who the company is actually for, and how you tell whether the founder knows.

Who the customer is

Ideal Customer Profile (ICP)#

A description of the customer a product serves best — specific enough that you can look at any company and say yes or no.

Picture this: not "mid-market SaaS companies." More like: "US healthcare practices with 8–40 clinicians, no in-house IT, already paying for a scheduling tool they complain about." The first one is a category. The second one is a list you can actually build.

Why it matters

The ICP is the single fastest read on whether a founder has done the work. A vague ICP means every downstream number is guesswork — the market size, the CAC, the sales cycle, all of it. A sharp ICP means the founder has talked to enough people to know who says yes quickly and who wastes six weeks before saying no.

It also predicts burn. Selling to everyone means qualifying nobody, and a seed-stage company cannot afford a sales motion that discovers the customer isn't a fit on call four.

What it looks like in practice

Ask a founder who their customer is and listen for whether the answer contains a filter you could apply to a database. Headcount, industry, the tool they use today, who signs, what breaks. If the answer is a size band and a vertical, they are guessing.

The good version usually arrives with evidence attached: "these twelve closed in under three weeks, these four took a quarter and two churned, and the difference is whether they have a dedicated ops person." That is a founder who found the ICP rather than assumed it.

Where it goes wrong

  • Writing the ICP from the market you want rather than the customers who actually bought.
  • Confusing it with a persona. The ICP is the account; the persona is the human inside it.
  • Making it so broad it excludes nobody, which makes it useless as a filter.
  • Never revising it. The first ICP is a hypothesis, and the first twenty customers are the test.

Who the customer is

Segment vs. persona#

A segment is the kind of company you sell to. A persona is the individual human inside it you have to convince.

Picture this: the segment is "dental practices with 5–15 chairs." The personas are the practice owner who signs, the office manager who uses it daily, and the hygienist who will quietly refuse to log in. Three different pitches, one segment.

Why it matters

Founders collapse these two and then wonder why a deal that should have closed stalled. Segment tells you where to aim the go-to-market. Persona tells you what the message has to say. Get the segment right and the persona wrong and you generate meetings that never convert.

For an investor it's a diligence shortcut: a founder who can name both, and describe how the message changes between them, has run a real sales process. One who only has a segment has run a market-sizing exercise.

What it looks like in practice

In B2B the split shows up as an org chart. The segment defines the account; inside it there is someone with the problem, someone with the budget, and someone who has to change how they work. A pitch aimed at the budget-holder talks about cost and risk. The same product pitched to the daily user talks about the twenty minutes they get back.

In consumer the segment is often demographic and the persona is behavioural, and the behavioural one matters more — two people the same age with the same income can have completely different reasons to buy.

Where it goes wrong

  • Building elaborate personas with stock photos and names before talking to anyone real.
  • Targeting a segment but writing all the copy for one persona inside it.
  • Assuming the user and the buyer are the same person. In B2B they usually aren't.
  • Treating persona work as a marketing exercise rather than a sales one.

Who the customer is

Jobs to Be Done (JTBD)#

The framing that people don't buy products, they hire them to make progress on something. The job is the progress, not the product.

Picture this: the classic study: a fast-food chain wanted to sell more milkshakes. Nearly half were bought before 9am by solo commuters. The job wasn't dessert — it was a one-handed thing that lasts the whole drive and stops you being hungry until lunch. The real competition was bananas and bagels, not other milkshakes.

Why it matters

It reframes the competitive set, which is the part founders get wrong most often. If you only look at companies that build what you build, you will miss that most of your losses are to a spreadsheet, an intern, or doing nothing at all.

It also changes what you build. A feature request is a proposed solution; the job is the reason behind it. Founders who chase requests build a cluttered product. Founders who chase the job build a coherent one.

What it looks like in practice

The useful question isn't "what do you want?" It's "walk me through the last time you dealt with this." What triggered it, what they tried, what they gave up on, what made the current workaround tolerable enough to keep using.

In practice you're listening for the moment of struggle and what they hired to solve it. When someone says they use a Google Sheet and three Slack reminders, that stack is the incumbent — and it's free, familiar, and already integrated into how they work.

Where it goes wrong

  • Turning it into a template exercise instead of listening to how people actually describe struggle.
  • Writing the job at the level of the feature ("send invoices faster") rather than the progress ("get paid without chasing people").
  • Ignoring the emotional and social parts of the job. Nobody wants to look disorganised in front of their boss.
  • Using it to justify a product you already built, rather than to find out what to build.

Where the term comes from

The framing is Clayton Christensen's, developed at Harvard Business School and set out most fully in Competing Against Luck (2016), though he had been teaching it for years before — the milkshake study dates to work with Bob Moesta in the mid-2000s. Christensen's line was that customers don't buy products, they hire them to do a job.

Who the customer is

Painkiller vs. vitamin#

Whether the product solves a problem that already hurts, or offers an improvement that is nice to have.

Picture this: payroll compliance software is a painkiller — get it wrong and you're fined. A tool that makes team retros 20% more engaging is a vitamin. In a good year both sell. In a budget freeze only one survives, and it isn't the vitamin.

Why it matters

It's the fastest predictor of sales cycle length, churn, and how the company does in a downturn. Painkillers get bought with existing budget and urgency attached. Vitamins need a budget created for them, which means a longer cycle, more stakeholders, and first place on the cut list when spending tightens.

Vitamins can build enormous companies — but usually on consumer scale and habit, not on enterprise budget. The mistake is selling a vitamin with a painkiller's go-to-market.

What it looks like in practice

The tell is what the customer was doing before. If they had built a fragile internal workaround, hired someone to do it manually, or were paying for something they complained about, the pain is real and pre-budgeted. If the honest answer is "nothing, we just lived with it," you are a vitamin.

Another tell is who initiates. Inbound requests with a deadline attached signal pain. Enthusiastic meetings that never reach procurement signal a vitamin.

Where it goes wrong

  • Believing enthusiasm proves pain. People are generous with praise and stingy with budget.
  • Selling a vitamin as if it were a painkiller and then blaming the sales team for slow cycles.
  • Missing that the same product is a painkiller for one segment and a vitamin for another — that difference is often the whole ICP.
  • Assuming pain is permanent. Regulation changes, and so does what hurts.

Who the customer is

Design partner#

An early customer who commits to building alongside you — real usage and real feedback, in exchange for influence over the product and usually favourable terms.

Picture this: a pre-seed company signs three hospitals as design partners. They pay a reduced rate, get weekly calls with the founders, and shape the roadmap. In return the company gets something no amount of user research buys: a real workflow to build against, and three logos that become references.

Why it matters

At pre-seed there is nothing to look at except the team and the evidence they've gathered. Signed design partners are the strongest evidence available — they mean someone with a budget and a reputation agreed to spend time on this.

The risk is the opposite failure: building a bespoke product for three customers and calling it a company. The point of a design partner is to find the shared shape of the problem, not to take orders.

What it looks like in practice

A real design-partner agreement has obligations on both sides written down — a cadence, named people, access to real data or real users, and an end date with a decision at it. The weak version is a friendly logo and a monthly call that gets rescheduled.

The signal to watch is whether they use it when you're not in the room. A design partner who only opens the product before the weekly call is giving you feedback, not usage.

Where it goes wrong

  • Signing partners who are unusual, and building for the exception rather than the pattern.
  • Giving away too much — perpetual free access, exclusivity, or roadmap veto — for a logo.
  • Letting the relationship stay free forever. The conversion to paid is the actual test.
  • Treating their feature requests as a roadmap instead of as evidence about the underlying job.
