Who the customer is

Early adopter#

The customer who buys before the product is finished, because their problem is bad enough that an unpolished solution still beats what they have.

Picture this: the first buyers of a compliance tool are usually the teams that just failed an audit. They will tolerate bugs, missing features, and a founder doing implementation personally — because the alternative is failing the next one.

Why it matters

Early adopters are the only customers available to a company that hasn't built the thing yet, so who they are shapes everything: what gets built, what the pricing anchors to, and what the first case studies say.

They are also the biggest source of false signal. Early adopters tolerate things the mainstream will not, and they buy for reasons the mainstream doesn't share. A product tuned entirely to them can stall the moment it tries to cross over.

What it looks like in practice

You find them by looking for people already trying to solve the problem badly — the ones with a homemade spreadsheet, a contractor on retainer, a Zapier chain held together with hope. That effort is a budget and an urgency that already exists.

The distinction that matters later is whether the early adopters bought because the problem is acute, or because they enjoy trying new tools. The first group predicts a market. The second group predicts nothing.

Where it goes wrong

  • Mistaking enthusiasm for novelty with genuine need. Some people just like new software.
  • Building every feature the early adopters ask for and ending up with a product only they can use.
  • Assuming the mainstream buyer will accept the same rough edges. They won't.
  • Never asking why they were willing to go first. The answer is the sharpest version of your pitch.

Who the customer is

Customer discovery interview#

A structured conversation about what someone actually does today — run to learn, not to sell or to get validation.

Picture this: a founder asks thirty people "would you use a tool that does X?" and gets twenty-six yeses. Zero of them buy. The question that would have worked: "what did you do the last time this came up, and how long did it take?"

Why it matters

It is the cheapest way to be wrong before it costs anything. A month of interviews can kill an idea that would have taken a year and a seed round to disprove.

For an investor, how a founder runs these is a direct read on how they'll handle every other kind of evidence. Founders who interview to confirm what they already believe will read their metrics the same way.

What it looks like in practice

The good version is almost entirely about the past. What happened, when, who was involved, what it cost, what they tried first, why they stopped. Past behaviour is data. Future intention is politeness.

You are listening for specifics that a person could not invent on the spot — names of tools, dollar amounts, the week it went wrong. Vague agreement is the sound of someone being nice to you.

Where it goes wrong

  • Pitching. The moment you describe your solution, the interview is over and a sales call has begun.
  • Asking about hypothetical futures instead of actual pasts.
  • Only talking to people who like you. Friendly interviews are the least informative kind.
  • Stopping after five conversations because the first five agreed.

Where the term comes from

The discipline comes out of Steve Blank's customer development work at Stanford and Berkeley in the 2000s — the argument that startups fail from lack of customers, not lack of product, and that founders should "get out of the building." Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) is the practical companion on how to ask without fishing.

Who the customer is

Leading questions#

Questions that carry the answer inside them, so the response confirms what you already hoped rather than telling you anything.

Picture this: "Wouldn't it be useful if this took five minutes instead of an hour?" Of course. Everyone says yes. You have learned nothing except that faster is better than slower.

Why it matters

This is the specific mechanism by which founders fool themselves. It doesn't feel like bad research while it's happening — it feels like enthusiastic validation, because that's exactly what it produces.

It matters to an investor because a deck full of "92% of respondents said they would use this" usually means the survey was written to produce that number. The right follow-up is always: what was the question, and what did they do afterwards?

What it looks like in practice

The fix is to ask about behaviour that already happened, and to stay quiet. "What do you use today?" beats "would you switch?" "How long did that take?" beats "would saving time be valuable?"

Silence does a lot of the work. Founders fill pauses by suggesting the answer; the discipline is to let the other person fill it instead.

Where it goes wrong

  • Describing your solution and then asking whether it's a good idea.
  • Asking about willingness to pay in the abstract — the answer is always a polite yes.
  • Counting hypothetical yeses as demand, then putting the number in a deck.
  • Interviewing to find agreement rather than to find the flaw.

Who the customer is

Problem validation vs. solution validation#

Two different questions: does this problem actually hurt enough that someone will pay to fix it, and does this particular fix work?

Picture this: a team spends four months building a beautiful scheduling tool. It works perfectly. Nobody buys, because the scheduling was annoying but never expensive enough to justify a purchase order. Solution validated, problem never was.

Why it matters

Doing these in the wrong order is the most expensive common mistake in early-stage building. Problem validation is cheap — conversations, a landing page, a manual pilot. Solution validation costs engineering months. Teams routinely skip the cheap one and pay for the expensive one.

It also explains a specific failure mode investors see often: a technically excellent product with real users and no revenue. The solution works. The problem was never worth money.

What it looks like in practice

Problem validation looks like evidence that the pain already costs something — people paying for a bad alternative, hiring around it, or building internal tooling. Solution validation looks like usage: they tried yours, they kept using it, they stopped using the old thing.

The strongest early signal collapses both: someone pays before the product is finished. That's a validated problem and a credible solution in one transaction.

Where it goes wrong

  • Building first and validating the problem afterwards, when the sunk cost makes honesty hard.
  • Reading "this is a real problem" as "people will pay to solve it." Those are different claims.
  • Validating the problem with one segment and the solution with another.
  • Treating a working product as proof the problem mattered.

Related terms

Painkiller vs. vitaminWhether the product solves a problem that already hurts, or offers an improvement that is nice to have.Customer discovery interviewA structured conversation about what someone actually does today — run to learn, not to sell or to get validation.Minimum viable product (MVP)The smallest thing you can build that produces a real answer to the riskiest question you have.Jobs to Be Done (JTBD)The framing that people don't buy products, they hire them to make progress on something. The job is the progress, not the product.Willingness to payThe most a specific customer would actually hand over, discovered through behaviour rather than asked in a survey.

Who the customer is

Switching costs#

Everything it costs a customer to move off what they use now — migration, retraining, integrations, contracts, and the risk of it going wrong.

Picture this: a hospital's scheduling system is bad, everybody complains, and it will not be replaced. Twelve years of data live in it, four other systems read from it, and the person who would own the migration is already at capacity. Your product being better is not the obstacle.

Why it matters

Switching costs cut both ways, and founders usually only think about one. High switching costs protect you once you're in — that's most of what a moat actually is in software. They also stand between you and every customer you don't have yet.

For an early company the incumbent's switching costs are the real competitor. Being 30% better rarely clears them. Being 10x better on one specific thing sometimes does, which is why wedges exist.

What it looks like in practice

Add up what actually has to happen: exporting data that may not export cleanly, rebuilding integrations, retraining staff, running both systems in parallel, and one person staking their reputation on it. That last one is usually the binding constraint.

The strategies that work are the ones that lower the cost rather than argue with it — doing the migration yourself, running alongside the incumbent instead of replacing it, or entering through a workflow nobody has automated yet.

Where it goes wrong

  • Assuming a better product is enough to overcome them. It usually isn't.
  • Ignoring the political cost — someone has to own the decision and wear the failure.
  • Building switching costs so high they become the reason customers resent you.
  • Forgetting that your own customers face the same arithmetic when they consider leaving.

Related terms

Competitive moatThe structural reason a competitor with money and talent still can't take your customers.Substitute vs. direct competitorA direct competitor sells something like yours. The least gameable number a young company has.

Who the customer is

Pilot vs. paid contract#

A pilot is a time-boxed trial with an exit. A paid contract is a commitment. They look similar on a slide and mean completely different things.

Picture this: "we're in pilot with three enterprises" can mean three signed six-figure deals with a proof period, or three free trials with a friendly manager who hasn't told procurement. Ask which, and the meeting changes.

Why it matters

Pilots are the most inflated number in early-stage fundraising, and the inflation is usually not deliberate — founders genuinely feel like a pilot is traction. Sometimes it is. A paid pilot with a named conversion trigger is real. An unpaid one with no end date is a long meeting.

The conversion rate from pilot to contract is the number that matters, and it's the one least often volunteered.

What it looks like in practice

The questions that resolve it: is money changing hands, who signed, what specifically has to be true at the end for it to convert, and what date is that decision. A pilot with a defined success metric and a budget owner attached converts. One without either drifts.

Pilot purgatory is the failure mode — a company with eight pilots running, all consuming founder time, none converting, and a fundraise built on the count.

Where it goes wrong

  • Counting unpaid pilots as traction in a deck.
  • Running pilots with no defined success criteria, which makes the conversion conversation subjective and losable.
  • Letting pilots run past their end date because ending one feels like losing a logo.
  • Optimising for pilot count instead of conversion rate.

Related terms

How the company makes money

A revenue model is how the cash arrives. A business model is the whole machine. Founders conflate them constantly, and the conflation hides whether the thing can actually work at scale.

How the company makes money

Business model vs. revenue model#

The revenue model is how cash arrives. The business model is the whole machine — who you serve, what you deliver, what it costs, and why the economics hold.

Picture this: "subscription" is a revenue model. The business model is: mid-size clinics pay $800 a month, we acquire them for $2,400 through partner referrals, they stay four years, and gross margin is 78% because support is self-serve.

Why it matters

Founders answer the business-model question with a revenue model and think they've answered it. They haven't — and the missing half is exactly where the thing usually breaks. You can charge a subscription and still lose money on every customer.

For an investor the distinction is a diligence tool. Anyone can say "marketplace, 15% take rate." Fewer can explain what it costs to bring both sides, how long they stay, and at what volume the margin turns positive.

What it looks like in practice

The full answer connects four things: who pays, what they get, what delivering it costs, and what acquiring them costs. If any of the four is missing the model isn't described yet — it's just priced.

The same revenue model can be a great business or a terrible one depending on the other three. Subscription with 85% gross margin and organic acquisition is a different company from subscription with 30% margin and paid acquisition, even at identical revenue.

Where it goes wrong

  • Answering "what's the business model?" with a single word.
  • Copying a revenue model from a company with a completely different cost structure.
  • Leaving out cost of delivery, which is where AI-heavy products often get into trouble.
  • Assuming the model that works at ten customers works at ten thousand.

Related terms

Unit economicsWhether a single customer makes or loses money, once you count what it cost to get them and what it costs to serve them.Pricing modelsThe structure of the charge — per seat, per usage, flat tier, per outcome — as distinct from how much it costs.Gross marginRevenue minus the direct cost of delivering it, as a percentage — what's left to fund everything else.Subscription business modelCustomers pay a recurring fee for continued access, usually monthly or annually.

How the company makes money

Subscription business model#

Customers pay a recurring fee for continued access, usually monthly or annually.

Picture this: $500/month per clinic, billed annually with a 15% discount. Predictable revenue, but you have to earn it again every renewal — and the annual discount means you find out about problems twelve months late.

Why it matters

It is the default model for software because it turns a sales problem into a retention problem, and retention compounds. It's also the reason SaaS gets valued on revenue multiples: recurring revenue is predictable in a way transaction revenue isn't.

The catch is that recurring cuts both ways. Churn compounds exactly as hard as growth does, and a business losing 4% of revenue a month has to run very fast to stand still.

What it looks like in practice

The health of a subscription business lives in three numbers: what it costs to acquire a customer, how long they stay, and whether existing accounts grow. Net revenue retention above 100% means the base grows without any new logos — that's the quiet engine behind most great SaaS companies.

Annual contracts improve cash and hide problems. Monthly contracts show you churn in real time and starve you of working capital. Most companies end up with both, aimed at different segments.

Where it goes wrong

  • Discounting annual plans so aggressively that a year passes before you learn people aren't using it.
  • Reporting ARR that includes one-off implementation fees.
  • Treating churn as a customer-success problem when it's a product-fit problem.
  • Adding seats-based pricing to a product whose value doesn't scale with seats.

Related terms

ARR, MRR, and ACVAnnual recurring revenue, monthly recurring revenue, and average contract value — three views of the same subscription base.Retention / churnWhether people who started using it are still using it. The least gameable number a young company has.Net revenue retention (NRR)What last year's customers are worth this year, including expansion, minus churn. Above 100% means the existing base grows without adding anyone.Pricing modelsThe structure of the charge — per seat, per usage, flat tier, per outcome — as distinct from how much it costs.Cohort retentionTracking each group of customers who started in the same period separately, so you can see whether retention is improving.

How the company makes money

Two-sided marketplace#

A business that creates value by connecting two distinct groups who need each other, and takes a cut of what happens between them.

Picture this: riders and drivers, guests and hosts, patients and clinicians. The product isn't the app — it's the fact that when one side shows up, the other side is already there.

Why it matters

Marketplaces have the best endgame and the worst beginning. Once liquidity exists, the network defends itself and margins are structurally good. Before it exists, you're running two customer- acquisition problems simultaneously and neither side has a reason to be there.

That chicken-and-egg period is where nearly all marketplaces die, and it's the part a pre-seed investor is actually underwriting.

What it looks like in practice

The solutions are all variations on faking one side until the other arrives — subsidising supply, hand-recruiting it, being the supply yourself, or launching in a geography so narrow that a small absolute number creates real density. Liquidity is local, not global; a marketplace with a thousand sellers spread across a country has none.

The number that matters is match rate: of the people who show up wanting something, what share get it. Everything else is vanity until that works in at least one place.

Where it goes wrong

  • Measuring total users on both sides instead of liquidity in a single market.
  • Expanding geographically before density works anywhere.
  • Ignoring disintermediation — once two sides meet, they have every reason to transact off- platform.
  • Setting the take rate before knowing which side is harder to acquire.

Related terms

How the company makes money

Transaction fee (take rate)#

The platform takes a percentage of each transaction it enables, rather than charging for access.

Picture this: a booking platform charges 12% of every job. A $400 job earns $48. Revenue only exists when the customer succeeds — which is either beautifully aligned or brutally exposed, depending on the week.

Why it matters

The take rate is the single most consequential number in a marketplace, and it's constrained from both directions. Too low and the business can't fund itself. Too high and both sides start looking for ways to transact around you.

It also determines what business you're in. A 3% take rate is a payments business that needs enormous volume. A 25% take rate is a services business that has to justify itself with real work — trust, insurance, dispute resolution, demand generation.

What it looks like in practice

Sustainable take rates track how much of the value you actually create. Platforms that only introduce two parties struggle to hold double digits. Platforms that handle payment, guarantee quality, resolve disputes, and generate the demand can hold 20–30%.

Watch for leakage: high-frequency, high-trust relationships migrate off-platform fastest. If a cleaner and a household will work together weekly for years, the second booking is where the take rate quietly disappears.

Where it goes wrong

  • Benchmarking against a platform that provides far more or far less than you do.
  • Raising the take rate to fix unit economics and triggering the leakage that kills them.
  • Reporting gross transaction volume as revenue.
  • Charging the side that's harder to acquire.

Related terms

How the company makes money

Freemium#

A free tier that's genuinely useful, with paid tiers for the users who need more.

Picture this: the free plan handles three projects. It's real, people use it for years, and it costs you money. The bet is that enough of them hit four projects — and that the free users bring the paying ones in.

Why it matters

Freemium replaces a sales force with a product, which is why it produces such good margins when it works. It also means the free tier is a permanent cost centre, and it only pays for itself if free users either convert or bring in people who do.

For AI-native products the arithmetic is harsher than it was for classic SaaS: free users consume inference, so every free account has real marginal cost. Freemium models designed in a zero-marginal-cost world don't transfer cleanly.

What it looks like in practice

It works when the free tier delivers real value but hits a natural, honest limit tied to success — more usage, more collaborators, more data. It fails when the limit feels artificial, because then the free tier teaches people to resent you.

Conversion rates are lower than founders expect. Low single digits is normal. The model only works at volume, which means it needs a product people find without being sold to.

Where it goes wrong

  • Making the free tier so generous nobody needs to upgrade.
  • Making it so thin nobody sticks around long enough to want to.
  • Ignoring the serving cost of free users, especially where inference is involved.
  • Bolting freemium onto a product that requires onboarding help to be useful at all.

How the company makes money

Platform vs. pipeline#

A pipeline business creates value and sells it. A platform lets others create value and takes a cut of the exchange.

Picture this: a studio that makes films is a pipeline. A service where anyone can publish and viewers choose is a platform. Same industry, completely different cost structures, growth curves, and defensibility.

Why it matters

The distinction predicts how the business scales and where it's vulnerable. Pipelines scale by adding cost — more output means more input. Platforms scale by adding participants, which is why they can grow revenue far faster than headcount.

It also predicts quality control. Pipelines own quality and can guarantee it. Platforms inherit whatever their participants produce, and moderating that becomes a permanent, expensive obligation.

What it looks like in practice

Most real companies are hybrids and get there deliberately: start as a pipeline to guarantee quality and prove demand, then open up once there's enough demand to attract third-party supply. Going the other way is much harder.

The tell in a pitch is what happens when demand doubles. If the answer involves hiring proportionally, it's a pipeline — which is fine, but it should be valued and funded like one.

Where it goes wrong

  • Calling a pipeline a platform because it has an API.
  • Opening a platform before demand exists, and getting supply with nobody to serve.
  • Underestimating what moderation and quality control cost at scale.
  • Assuming platform economics apply before network effects actually kick in.

How the company makes money

B2B2C#

Selling to a business that puts your product in front of its own consumers, so the business pays and the consumer uses.

Picture this: a benefits tool sells to employers; employees use it. One signature reaches four thousand users — and if that employer leaves, four thousand users leave with them.

Why it matters

It solves distribution and creates concentration in the same move. Instead of acquiring consumers one at a time, you acquire them in blocks — which is enormously efficient and means a handful of contracts control most of your revenue.

The structural problem is that the payer and the user are different people with different interests. The employer wants cost control and reporting. The employee wants the thing to be good. Build only for the buyer and engagement dies; build only for the user and you don't renew.

What it looks like in practice

The businesses that work here serve both masters explicitly — usage dashboards and ROI reporting for the buyer, a product the end user would choose voluntarily. Engagement rate is the number that predicts renewal, because a contract with 6% adoption doesn't survive a budget review.

Watch the concentration. Three partners at 70% of revenue is a real risk, and it shows up in diligence as customer concentration whether or not the founder frames it that way.

Where it goes wrong

  • Optimising entirely for the buyer and ending up with a product nobody opens.
  • Reporting the consumer count as customers when the contracts are what churn.
  • Underpricing because the partner delivers volume, then discovering support costs scale with users.
  • Having no direct relationship with end users, so you learn about dissatisfaction at renewal.

How the company makes money

Direct-to-consumer (D2C)#

Selling straight to the end customer, skipping retailers and distributors.

Picture this: a mattress brand sells online, owns the customer relationship, keeps the retail margin — and pays for every single customer through ads, which is the part that got expensive.

Why it matters

D2C trades distribution cost for acquisition cost, and whether that's a good trade depends entirely on the margin structure. You keep the retailer's cut, but you inherit their job — finding customers — and unlike shelf space, paid acquisition gets more expensive as you scale.

The 2010s D2C boom and bust was largely this arithmetic catching up. Cheap social ads made the model look structurally sound; when acquisition costs rose, businesses with 40% gross margins discovered they had no room.

What it looks like in practice

The businesses that hold up have high gross margin, real repeat purchase, or both. Margin buys room to acquire; repeat purchase means you only pay acquisition once. A product with 70% margin bought four times a year is a different business from one with 35% margin bought once.

The direct relationship is the real prize when it's used — first-party data, faster product iteration, and the ability to launch adjacent products to an audience you already own.

Where it goes wrong

  • Building on a single acquisition channel whose price you don't control.
  • Confusing first-order profitability with a business — most D2C only works on repeat.
  • Ignoring returns, shipping, and payment processing when calculating margin.
  • Scaling ad spend before knowing the payback period.

How the company makes money

Licensing#

Charging others to use your technology, brand, or IP inside their own product, rather than selling a product yourself.

Picture this: a speech-recognition company licenses its engine to four device makers. It never touches an end user, has almost no support burden, and lives entirely on the commercial health of four partners.

Why it matters

Licensing is the highest-margin model available — the marginal cost of another licence is near zero — and the least defensible position to occupy. Your licensees have every incentive to build it themselves once volume justifies it, and they can see exactly what it's worth to them.

For AI companies this is the live question. Licensing a model or a capability into someone else's distribution is fast revenue and a weak long-term position, because the layer you're licensing is exactly the layer everyone is trying to commoditise.

What it looks like in practice

It works best where the IP is genuinely hard to reproduce, protected, or improving faster than a licensee could catch up. It works badly where the licensee's engineering team could rebuild it in two quarters.

Deal structure matters as much as price: exclusivity limits your market, minimum commitments protect you from a partner who signs and then deprioritises, and field-of-use restrictions keep one licensee from foreclosing an entire industry.

Where it goes wrong

  • Granting broad exclusivity early for a headline number.
  • Licensing to a partner who is simultaneously building the same capability internally.
  • Having no minimum commitments, so a signed deal produces no revenue.
  • Assuming high margins mean low risk. Concentration is the risk.

Related terms

How the company makes money

Advertising-supported#

The product is free to users, and revenue comes from selling their attention to advertisers.

Picture this: a news app with two million monthly readers earning $8 per thousand impressions. The reader is not the customer — the advertiser is, and the reader is the inventory.

Why it matters

Advertising removes all friction from adoption and puts the business in permanent tension with its own users. Every decision that increases revenue — more ads, more tracking, more engagement optimisation — makes the product slightly worse for the person using it.

It also demands scale that most startups never reach. At realistic ad rates, meaningful revenue requires millions of engaged users. A company with fifty thousand users cannot fund itself on ads, no matter how good the engagement.

What it looks like in practice

The economics come down to how much attention you have and how well you can target it. Niche audiences with clear purchase intent command far higher rates than large general ones — a newsletter for procurement managers can out-earn a general-interest app with fifty times the readers.

Privacy changes have made third-party targeting materially worse, which pushed value toward first-party data and contextual placement. That favours products where the content itself signals intent.

Where it goes wrong

  • Choosing ads for a product that will never reach advertising scale.
  • Optimising engagement metrics that make the product worse and users leave slowly.
  • Building on third-party tracking that platform policy can remove overnight.
  • Treating users as the customer in product decisions and advertisers as the customer in the model.

How the company makes money

On-demand (gig)#

Connecting customers who want something now with independent workers who deliver it, coordinating supply in real time.

Picture this: a delivery app at 7pm on a Friday. Demand triples, and the whole business is whether enough couriers chose to be online in that specific neighbourhood in that specific hour.

Why it matters

It's a marketplace with the hardest possible constraint: liquidity has to exist right now, in one place. A restaurant marketplace can tolerate a slow match. A delivery one can't — the customer leaves in four minutes.

That constraint drives the economics. Guaranteeing availability means paying for idle supply, and idle supply is pure cost. Most on-demand businesses spend years trying to get utilisation high enough to stop subsidising it.

What it looks like in practice

The levers are density, prediction, and pricing. Density means enough demand in a small enough area that workers stay busy. Prediction means knowing Friday needs triple supply before Friday. Surge pricing is the blunt instrument that clears the market when the first two fail.

Worker classification is a live legal and cost question in most jurisdictions, and a reclassification changes the unit economics of the entire business, not just its compliance posture.

Where it goes wrong

  • Expanding to a new city before utilisation works in the first one.
  • Subsidising both sides indefinitely and calling the resulting growth product-market fit.
  • Treating worker classification as a legal footnote rather than a model risk.
  • Measuring average utilisation, which hides that mornings are dead and evenings are short.

How the company makes money

Pay-for-performance (results-as-a-service)#

Charging for the outcome rather than the tool — a share of savings, a fee per result, a cut of recovered revenue.

Picture this: a claims-recovery product takes 25% of what it recovers. The hospital pays nothing up front and can't really say no, because the alternative is recovering nothing.

Why it matters

It's the easiest sale in enterprise software because it removes the buyer's risk entirely, which matters enormously when you're a two-year-old company asking a large organisation to trust you. It also inverts the risk onto you.

This model is having a moment because of AI: when software can actually do the work rather than help someone do it, charging for the work becomes possible, and it captures far more value than a per-seat licence ever could.

What it looks like in practice

It requires an outcome both sides can measure and attribute without arguing. Recovered dollars, closed tickets, filled shifts — countable things with a clear baseline. Where attribution is contestable, the model produces disputes instead of revenue.

Cash flow is the hidden problem: you carry the delivery cost and get paid after the result lands, sometimes much later. That's a working-capital business wearing a software business's clothes.

Where it goes wrong

  • Picking an outcome you can't measure cleanly, so every invoice becomes a negotiation.
  • Failing to agree the baseline before starting — without it, you can't prove you caused anything.
  • Ignoring the cash gap between doing the work and being paid for it.
  • Capping the upside so tightly that a great result earns the same as a mediocre one.

How the company makes money

Pricing models#

The structure of the charge — per seat, per usage, flat tier, per outcome — as distinct from how much it costs.

Picture this: the same $50,000 a year can be 100 seats at $500, 5 million API calls at a cent, or a flat platform fee. Identical revenue, completely different incentives about whether the customer lets more people use it.

Why it matters

The structure decides how revenue grows once the customer is in. Per-seat pricing grows when the customer hires. Usage pricing grows when they use it more. Flat pricing doesn't grow at all without a renegotiation.

That's why the structure drives net revenue retention, and NRR is what separates a good SaaS business from an ordinary one. Choosing the axis is a strategic decision, not a finance one.

What it looks like in practice

The right axis is the one that tracks the value the customer receives, so their bill grows when they're getting more and never grows when they're not. Per-seat works when value scales with people. Usage works when it scales with volume — but it also makes revenue less predictable and gives customers a reason to ration usage.

For AI products usage pricing has a second job: it passes through inference cost. Flat pricing on a variable-cost product is how gross margin quietly disappears.

Where it goes wrong

  • Pricing per seat on a product where one power user does all the work.
  • Flat pricing on top of a variable cost base.
  • Changing the pricing axis on existing customers without grandfathering, which reads as a bait and switch.
  • Copying a competitor's structure when your cost base is different.

How the company makes money

Value-based pricing#

Setting price from what the outcome is worth to the customer, rather than from what it costs you to deliver or what competitors charge.

Picture this: the software costs $4 a month to run. It saves a mid-size firm 60 hours of paralegal time a month. Cost-plus says charge $20. Value-based says the conversation starts far higher, and the customer will still be delighted.

Why it matters

It's the difference between capturing a slice of the value you create and capturing almost none of it. Cost-plus pricing is the single most common way early companies leave money on the table, and the mistake compounds — every later price rise is a fight, and the first price anchors the segment you attract.

It matters especially for AI products, where cost of delivery is falling and has almost no relationship to the value of the output.

What it looks like in practice

The work is quantifying the outcome in the customer's own numbers: hours saved times loaded cost, error rate reduction times cost of an error, revenue recovered. Then you price at a fraction of that — enough that the ROI is obvious and the customer keeps most of the gain.

Different segments value the same outcome differently, which is the honest argument for tiered pricing. The enterprise isn't subsidising the startup; it's buying a bigger outcome.

Where it goes wrong

  • Pricing off your own cost base, which the customer neither knows nor cares about.
  • Quantifying value with numbers you made up rather than ones the customer gave you.
  • Setting one price for segments that get wildly different value.
  • Confusing it with charging as much as possible — the customer has to keep the larger share.

Related terms

Willingness to payThe most a specific customer would actually hand over, discovered through behaviour rather than asked in a survey.Pricing modelsThe structure of the charge — per seat, per usage, flat tier, per outcome — as distinct from how much it costs.Pay-for-performance (results-as-a-service)Charging for the outcome rather than the tool — a share of savings, a fee per result, a cut of recovered revenue.Gross marginRevenue minus the direct cost of delivering it, as a percentage — what's left to fund everything else.PositioningThe place your product occupies in the buyer's head — what kind of thing it is, who it's for, and what it's better than.

How the company makes money

Willingness to pay#

The most a specific customer would actually hand over, discovered through behaviour rather than asked in a survey.

Picture this: "would you pay $200 a month for this?" gets a yes from eight out of ten. An invoice for $200 gets paid by one. The survey measured politeness.

Why it matters

Every revenue projection rests on this number, and it's the number founders are most confidently wrong about. Stated willingness to pay runs far above actual, because agreeing in a conversation costs nothing.

It's also the fastest way to test whether a problem is real. Someone who pays before the product is finished has told you more than a hundred interviews.

What it looks like in practice

Real signal comes from commitments with a cost attached: a deposit, a signed LOI, a pilot with a purchase order, a card on file. Even a small payment sorts genuine interest from courtesy.

The other reliable source is what they pay today — for the incumbent, for the contractor, for the internal headcount doing it manually. That budget already exists and doesn't need to be created, which makes it the easiest money in the market.

Where it goes wrong

  • Asking directly. The answer is a social response, not an economic one.
  • Testing price with existing enthusiasts, who are the least representative buyers you have.
  • Anchoring on competitor pricing when your product does a different job.
  • Setting price low to reduce friction, then discovering low price attracted customers who churn.

Related terms

How it reaches customers

Go-to-market is where good products go to die quietly. These are the terms for how a company finds its first customers and whether that motion can be repeated by someone who is not the founder.

How it reaches customers

Wedge#

The narrow first thing you do so well that a customer will tolerate switching, from which you expand into everything else.

Picture this: a company that eventually wants to run all of a clinic's back office starts with one thing: chasing unpaid insurance claims. Small, painful, measurable, and nobody else wants to own it. That's the way in.

Why it matters

Broad products lose to incumbents because being generally better isn't worth the migration. A wedge wins because on one specific thing the gap is large enough to overcome switching costs, and that thing is usually too small for the incumbent to care about.

It's also a discipline for a small team. A wedge tells you what not to build, which is the harder half of a roadmap at pre-seed.

What it looks like in practice

A good wedge is acute, frequent, and adjacent to where you eventually want to be. Acute so people will move. Frequent so you become part of the routine. Adjacent so expansion is natural rather than a second sale.

The expansion path should already be visible in the wedge itself — the same data, the same users, the same buyer. If moving from the wedge to the vision requires a new buyer and a new dataset, it isn't a wedge, it's two companies.

Where it goes wrong

  • Picking a wedge that is genuinely small — a niche with no path out of it.
  • Describing the whole vision in the pitch and the wedge nowhere.
  • Expanding before the wedge is actually won, and being mediocre at two things.
  • Choosing a wedge that doesn't connect to the eventual product, so expansion starts from zero.

Related terms

Beachhead marketThe first narrow market you take completely, chosen because winning it gives you the credibility and cash to take the next one.Land and expandStart with a small deal in one team, prove it works, then grow into the rest of the organisation.Switching costsEverything it costs a customer to move off what they use now — migration, retraining, integrations, contracts, and the risk of it going wrong.Competitive moatThe structural reason a competitor with money and talent still can't take your customers.DifferentiationThe specific thing you do that competitors don't, stated concretely enough that a customer could repeat it.

How it reaches customers

Beachhead market#

The first narrow market you take completely, chosen because winning it gives you the credibility and cash to take the next one.

Picture this: not "legal tech." More like "immigration law firms with 5–20 attorneys in California." Small enough to dominate, connected enough that the reference travels, adjacent to the next segment you want.

Why it matters

Winning 80% of a tiny market beats 2% of a big one, and not just for morale. Concentration makes word of mouth work, makes references land, makes the product coherent, and makes every sales conversation shorter than the last.

Founders resist it because it sounds like limiting ambition, and because a small first market reads badly in a deck. The good version of the deck shows the beachhead and the sequence out of it.

What it looks like in practice

A beachhead needs three things: the customers talk to each other, they share enough of the same problem that one product serves all of them, and it's adjacent to a bigger market you can move into with the same product.

The test of whether you've won it is whether new customers arrive already knowing who you are. That's when the beachhead has done its job and the next segment becomes cheaper to enter than the first one was.

Where it goes wrong

  • Choosing a beachhead with no adjacency, so success there teaches you nothing about the next market.
  • Leaving too early, before the reference effects that make it worth doing have kicked in.
  • Picking a segment because it's easy rather than because it's connected.
  • Defining it so broadly that it isn't a beachhead, it's a market.

Where the term comes from

The framing is Geoffrey Moore's in Crossing the Chasm (1991) — the D-Day analogy of taking one beach completely before moving inland — later systematised by Bill Aulet at MIT as the first step of Disciplined Entrepreneurship.

How it reaches customers

Founder-led sales#

The founders doing the selling themselves, before there's a repeatable motion to hand to anyone else.

Picture this: the CEO runs every demo for the first forty customers. It doesn't scale, and that isn't the point — the point is that she hears every objection first-hand and changes the product on Monday.

Why it matters

Early sales is research wearing a sales hat. Nobody else can hear an objection and rewrite the roadmap in the same week, and nobody else has the authority to make the promises that close a first customer.

It's also the thing that has to end. A company that can't sell without the founder in the room hasn't found a repeatable motion — it has found a charismatic one, and that's not fundable at Series A.

What it looks like in practice

The output of founder-led sales isn't just revenue, it's a documented pattern: who buys, what objections come up, what makes deals stall, what the sequence is. That documentation is what makes the first sales hire succeed rather than flounder.

The transition point is usually when the founder can predict the outcome of a call before making it. That predictability is the motion; before it exists, hiring a salesperson just adds someone with nothing to follow.

Where it goes wrong

  • Hiring a VP of Sales before a repeatable motion exists, and blaming them when it doesn't work.
  • Doing founder-led sales without writing anything down, so the knowledge stays in one head.
  • Closing deals with bespoke promises that make the product incoherent.
  • Holding on too long, so sales capacity is capped by the founder's calendar.

How it reaches customers

Product-led vs. sales-led growth#

Whether the product acquires and converts users on its own, or people do it through a sales process.

Picture this: one company's users sign up, get value in ten minutes, and hit a paywall on day nine. The other runs a six-week evaluation with three stakeholders and a security review. Both can work. Running the wrong one for your price point doesn't.

Why it matters

The choice has to match the contract size, and the arithmetic is unforgiving. A sales-led motion costs real money per deal — salary, commission, time — which needs a contract large enough to carry it. Product-led motions cost almost nothing per user but need volume and a product simple enough to self-serve.

The mismatch is a common way to burn a seed round: a $3,000-a-year product sold with a $15,000 sales process, or a $200,000 enterprise deal expected to close itself.

What it looks like in practice

Product-led requires a user who can adopt without permission, value visible before a purchase decision, and no mandatory integration work. Sales-led is what you get when the buyer isn't the user, the purchase needs procurement, or the deployment needs someone's help.

Most companies end up with both, aimed at different segments — self-serve for the small end, sales for the enterprise. That's fine as long as they're deliberately separated rather than one motion doing both badly.

Where it goes wrong

  • Choosing PLG because it sounds cheaper, on a product that needs onboarding to be useful.
  • Running enterprise sales on a contract value that can't fund a salesperson.
  • Adding self-serve to an enterprise product and starving it of the support that made it work.
  • Measuring PLG on signups instead of activation.

How it reaches customers

Land and expand#

Start with a small deal in one team, prove it works, then grow into the rest of the organisation.

Picture this: $12,000 with one department in March. By the following March it's $140,000 across six departments, and nobody ran a new sales process — the first team did the selling internally.

Why it matters

It converts an impossible first sale into a possible one. A large organisation will not buy a platform from a two-year-old company, but one director with a budget and a problem might. The expansion then happens against a track record instead of a promise.

It's also the engine behind net revenue retention above 100%, which is the number that makes a SaaS business compound without new logos.

What it looks like in practice

It only works if the pricing structure lets accounts grow — per seat, per usage, per site — and if the product produces visible internal evidence. The expansion is usually driven by the original champion showing results to a peer, so instrumentation that makes results visible is a growth feature, not a reporting one.

The number to watch is expansion revenue as a share of total new revenue. A healthy land-and- expand business generates a large fraction of growth from accounts it already has.

Where it goes wrong

  • Landing so small the deal isn't worth the implementation effort on either side.
  • Pricing flat, so a successful deployment produces no additional revenue.
  • Landing in a team that has no adjacency to the rest of the organisation.
  • Assuming expansion happens on its own. It needs a trigger and someone to notice.

Related terms

How it reaches customers

Channel strategy#

Which routes you use to reach customers — direct, partners, resellers, marketplaces — and what each one costs you.

Picture this: a company sells direct at 100% of revenue and through a cloud marketplace at 80%. The marketplace deals close twice as fast because the budget is already approved. Whether that 20% is worth it is the entire question.

Why it matters

Channels are the difference between a good product nobody finds and a good product with distribution. Most early companies underinvest here because building is more comfortable than partnering, and then discover that the incumbent's advantage was never the product.

Each channel also carries a hidden cost beyond the margin — partner enablement, co-selling, support, and a customer relationship you no longer fully own.

What it looks like in practice

Early on, one channel done properly beats four done partially. The right first channel is wherever your specific buyer already goes to solve this class of problem — which might be a marketplace, an industry association, a systems integrator, or nothing at all but direct outreach.

Partner channels take longer to produce revenue than founders plan for. Six to twelve months from signed agreement to first meaningful deal is normal, and a partner who signs but never sells is the standard outcome without dedicated attention.

Where it goes wrong

  • Signing many partners and enabling none of them.
  • Treating a partner agreement as distribution. It's permission to try.
  • Ignoring channel conflict — direct sales undercutting the partner who sourced the lead.
  • Building a channel motion before the direct motion works, so nobody knows what to teach the partner.

How it reaches customers

User, buyer, and champion#

Three distinct roles in a B2B sale: the person who uses it, the person who pays for it, and the person inside who fights for it.

Picture this: the nurse uses it, the CFO signs it, and the clinic operations lead is the one forwarding your email at 11pm because the current system just broke again. Lose the third and the deal dies quietly.

Why it matters

Deals fail when a founder wins one role and assumes that's the sale. Enthusiastic users with no budget produce months of pleasant meetings. A buyer with no internal champion signs and never deploys.

It's also a diligence question worth asking directly: in your last five closed deals, who was the champion, and what did they get out of it? Founders who can answer have actually run the process.

What it looks like in practice

The champion is the one to invest in, because they do the internal selling you can't. They need ammunition — a business case in their language, numbers they can forward, and a reason this makes them look good.

The risk is single-threading. If your champion leaves, the deal restarts from zero, and champion turnover is one of the more common causes of a stalled enterprise pipeline. Multi-threading into a second relationship is insurance.

Where it goes wrong

  • Selling to the user and never finding out who signs.
  • Single-threading a large deal through one relationship.
  • Giving the champion features when what they need is a business case.
  • Assuming the loudest person in the room is the decision maker.

How it reaches customers

Sales pipeline stages#

The named steps a deal moves through from first contact to closed, each with a definition of what has to be true to advance.

Picture this: not "interested / very interested / really interested." More like: discovery call held, problem confirmed by the buyer, pricing shared, security review passed, contract out. Each one either happened or it didn't.

Why it matters

Stages defined by buyer behaviour give you a forecast. Stages defined by seller optimism give you a story. The difference shows up when a founder projects revenue and misses by 70% — usually because "verbal yes" was counted as a stage.

For an investor it's a quick read on operational discipline. A founder who can tell you conversion rate between two specific stages is running a process; one who reports a single pipeline total is running a hope.

What it looks like in practice

Each stage should have an objective exit criterion tied to something the buyer did — they shared their current spend, they introduced you to procurement, they sent redlines. Things you did don't count.

Once the stages are real, the conversion rates between them tell you where the problem is. A pipeline that fills at the top and dies at security review is a different problem from one that never gets second meetings.

Where it goes wrong

  • Defining stages by how the salesperson feels rather than what the buyer did.
  • Letting deals sit in a stage indefinitely instead of aging out.
  • Skipping stages for a promising deal, then being surprised at the end.
  • Reporting total pipeline value without stage-weighted probability.

How it reaches customers

SQL vs. MQL#

A marketing qualified lead has shown interest. A sales qualified lead has been verified as someone who could actually buy.

Picture this: four hundred people downloaded the whitepaper (MQLs). Eleven of them have the problem, a budget, and authority (SQLs). Reporting the four hundred as pipeline is how forecasts go wrong.

Why it matters

The gap between these two numbers is where marketing and sales usually stop trusting each other, and where founders overestimate their own traction. Interest is cheap and abundant. Qualification is expensive and scarce.

The conversion rate between them is a direct measure of whether the top of the funnel is attracting the right people at all. A very low MQL-to-SQL rate means the content is reaching an audience that will never buy.

What it looks like in practice

Qualification usually comes down to a few checks: do they match the ICP, is there a real problem, is there budget, and is this person able to move it forward. Written down and applied consistently, that filter is what makes a pipeline number mean something.

At pre-seed this machinery is mostly overkill — but the underlying discipline isn't. Even a founder tracking twenty conversations should know which ones are real.

Where it goes wrong

  • Counting MQLs as pipeline in an investor update.
  • Qualifying on job title alone rather than on problem and budget.
  • Setting the bar so high that sales rejects everything and marketing stops trying.
  • Never measuring the conversion rate between the two, which is the only number that says whether the top of the funnel works.

How it reaches customers

Customer reference#

An existing customer willing to tell a prospect, in their own words, that this works.

Picture this: a hospital CIO takes a fifteen-minute call with another hospital CIO. That call closes more deals than any amount of marketing, and it's the asset that took eighteen months to earn.

Why it matters

In markets where being wrong is expensive — healthcare, finance, anything regulated — buyers don't trust vendors, they trust peers. A reference from someone in the same seat at a similar organisation removes the risk that no demo can.

It's also why beachheads work. Concentration in one segment means every new sale has a credible reference available, and the sales cycle shortens with each one.

What it looks like in practice

Good references are built deliberately: pick customers who got a measurable result, ask while the result is fresh, make it easy, and don't overuse them. A reference who has taken nine calls this quarter starts declining.

The strongest version isn't a call at all — it's a customer who brings you up unprompted in their own network. That happens when the result was genuinely notable, not when you asked nicely.

Where it goes wrong

  • Asking a customer to be a reference before they've seen a result.
  • Burning out one enthusiastic reference on every deal.
  • Only having references in a segment you're leaving.
  • Treating a logo on a website as a reference. It isn't — a person on a call is.

What makes it defensible

Every deck claims a moat. Most describe a head start. These terms separate the two, and give you the vocabulary to ask the follow-up question.

What makes it defensible

Competitive moat#

The structural reason a competitor with money and talent still can't take your customers.

Picture this: not "our tech is better." More like: every customer's four years of data lives here, three other systems read from it, and the person who'd own a migration already said no twice.

Why it matters

It's the difference between a company and a head start. At pre-seed nobody has a moat yet — what you're underwriting is whether the thing they're building accumulates one as it grows, or stays equally copyable at every scale.

The question that separates them: what gets harder for a competitor as you get bigger? If the answer is nothing, growth doesn't buy defensibility, and the company is in a permanent fight it has to keep winning on execution alone.

What it looks like in practice

The moats that actually hold are structural: switching costs that rise with usage, network effects where each user makes it better for the next, proprietary data that compounds, regulatory positions that took years to earn, or genuine scale economics.

For AI companies this is the live debate. Model quality is a weak moat because it's temporary and purchasable. Proprietary data flywheels, deep workflow integration, and distribution into places others can't reach are the durable ones.

Where it goes wrong

  • Claiming a technology moat that a well-funded team could reproduce in two quarters.
  • Calling a first-mover advantage a moat. Being early is a position, not a defence.
  • Listing patents as a moat without the resources or intent to enforce them.
  • Confusing a great team with a moat. Teams are an advantage; they aren't structural.

Where the term comes from

The term is Warren Buffett's, used through Berkshire's shareholder letters from the 1980s onward — the image of an economic castle protected by a moat that widens over time. It moved into venture vocabulary largely intact.

What makes it defensible

Differentiation#

The specific thing you do that competitors don't, stated concretely enough that a customer could repeat it.

Picture this: "we're faster and more intuitive" is not differentiation — every competitor says it. "We're the only one that reads handwritten intake forms" is, because it's checkable and it's either true or it isn't.

Why it matters

Undifferentiated products compete on price, and price competition at pre-seed is a way to lose slowly. Differentiation is what lets a small company win a deal against a bigger one with a better brand and more references.

The test is whether the claim survives a competitor's marketing page. If your competitor says the same thing, it isn't differentiation — it's category table stakes described enthusiastically.

What it looks like in practice

Real differentiation is usually narrow and slightly uncomfortable, because it implies the things you're deliberately worse at. A product that's genuinely the best at one workflow is usually mediocre at three others, and saying so out loud is what makes the claim credible.

It also has to matter to the buyer, not just be true. Plenty of products are differentiated on dimensions nobody is choosing on.

Where it goes wrong

  • Differentiating on adjectives every competitor also uses.
  • Being different in a way the buyer doesn't care about.
  • Listing ten differentiators, which reads as none.
  • Claiming differentiation that disappears the moment a competitor ships one feature.

Related terms

PositioningThe place your product occupies in the buyer's head — what kind of thing it is, who it's for, and what it's better than.Competitive moatThe structural reason a competitor with money and talent still can't take your customers.Unfair advantageSomething this specific team or company has that a competitor can't simply decide to acquire — access, data, a relationship, hard-won expertise.WedgeThe narrow first thing you do so well that a customer will tolerate switching, from which you expand into everything else.Substitute vs. direct competitorA direct competitor sells something like yours. A substitute is whatever the customer uses instead — including a spreadsheet, an intern, or nothing.
Read the full entry→
What makes it defensible

Unfair advantage#

Something this specific team or company has that a competitor can't simply decide to acquire — access, data, a relationship, hard-won expertise.

Picture this: two founders spent nine years inside hospital revenue cycle teams. They know which twelve people to call, what the workflow actually looks like at 2am, and why the last three vendors failed. A well-funded competitor can hire engineers. It can't hire that.

Why it matters

At pre-seed there's no product traction to evaluate, so the unfair advantage is a large share of what the investment decision actually rests on. It's the answer to "why this team," and it's the reason to believe they'll get to the moat before someone else does.

Most claimed advantages fail the test of being unfair. Working hard, caring more, and moving fast are available to everyone.

What it looks like in practice

The durable kinds are earned rather than chosen: domain expertise from years inside the problem, distribution access others don't have, a dataset that can't be reassembled, or a founding team that has already worked together through something hard.

The useful diligence question is simply: what would it take for a competent, well-funded competitor to get this? If the answer is money and six months, it isn't unfair.

Where it goes wrong

  • Listing effort, passion, or speed. Everyone has access to those.
  • Claiming proprietary data that's actually publicly available or purchasable.
  • Naming an advisor relationship as if it were a distribution channel.
  • Having a genuine advantage and building something that doesn't use it.

Related terms

What makes it defensible

Category creation#

Defining a new kind of product rather than competing inside an existing one, so buyers evaluate you on terms you set.

Picture this: instead of being the twelfth CRM, you name the thing you do something nobody sells yet. Now there's no feature comparison — but there's also no budget line, and someone has to create one.

Why it matters

Winning a category you defined is the strongest position in business — you set the evaluation criteria and every competitor is measured against your shape. It's also expensive, slow, and mostly attempted by companies that should have just competed.

The hidden cost is education. Existing categories come with existing budget, existing search behaviour, and buyers who already know why they need one. A new category has none of that, and creating it is a marketing spend most pre-seed companies can't fund.

What it looks like in practice

It works when the existing category genuinely can't describe what you do, and when the buyer's problem is real but unnamed. It fails when it's a repositioning exercise on a product that is, in fact, a slightly better version of an existing thing.

A pragmatic middle path most good companies take: sell into an existing category so the budget exists, and describe the new category as the reason you're better at it. Anchor to what they know, differentiate on what they don't.

Where it goes wrong

  • Creating a category to avoid an unflattering comparison rather than because the comparison is wrong.
  • Underestimating the education cost, which is usually years and a marketing budget.
  • Naming a category nobody searches for, so inbound never arrives.
  • Refusing to be compared to anything, which leaves the buyer with no way to evaluate you.

What makes it defensible

Substitute vs. direct competitor#

A direct competitor sells something like yours. A substitute is whatever the customer uses instead — including a spreadsheet, an intern, or nothing.

Picture this: the competitive slide lists four funded startups. The deals are actually lost to Excel and "we'll revisit next year." Those two win more often than all four combined.

Why it matters

Founders build competitive analysis around companies that look like them and miss where the losses actually come from. For most early products the dominant competitor is inertia, and inertia is free, already deployed, and has no sales cycle.

It changes the pitch, too. Competing against a startup means arguing features. Competing against a spreadsheet means arguing that the problem is worth solving at all — a completely different conversation.

What it looks like in practice

The way to find the real competitive set is to ask what customers did before, and what the ones who said no went on to do. That list is usually dominated by manual workarounds and internal tools nobody counts.

The jobs-to-be-done framing helps here: define the competition by what the customer hires to make progress, not by which companies share your category label.

Where it goes wrong

  • Building the competitive slide entirely from funded startups.
  • Dismissing "do nothing" as a competitor when it's the most common outcome.
  • Ignoring internal builds, which are the default substitute in large organisations.
  • Positioning against a startup the buyer has never heard of.

What makes it defensible

Win-loss analysis#

Systematically asking why deals were won or lost, from the buyer rather than from the salesperson.

Picture this: the team believes they lose on price. Six buyer interviews later, the real answer is that the security questionnaire took eleven days and a competitor answered in two.

Why it matters

Internal explanations for losses are systematically wrong in one direction: price. It's the least uncomfortable reason for the person who lost the deal, so it's the reason that gets recorded. The actual causes are usually fixable and much less flattering.

Wins matter as much as losses and get analysed far less. Knowing precisely why you won tells you what to repeat, and it's often not what the team thinks.

What it looks like in practice

The signal comes from the buyer, and preferably not from the person who ran the deal — people are polite to whoever sold to them. Short structured conversations a few weeks after the decision, asking what the alternatives were, what mattered, and what almost changed their mind.

Patterns emerge fast. Ten interviews usually surface two or three recurring causes, and those tend to be operational — response time, a missing integration, a reference they couldn't get — rather than strategic.

Where it goes wrong

  • Recording the reason from the salesperson's notes.
  • Only analysing losses, so you never learn what's working.
  • Accepting "price" without asking what they compared it to and what would have justified it.
  • Doing it once rather than continuously, so you learn about a market that has since moved.

Related terms

What makes it defensible

Positioning#

The place your product occupies in the buyer's head — what kind of thing it is, who it's for, and what it's better than.

Picture this: the same analytics tool positioned as "business intelligence for enterprises" competes with entrenched incumbents and loses. Positioned as "the reporting layer for Shopify stores doing $1M+" it's the obvious choice, at the same price.

Why it matters

Positioning determines the comparison set, and the comparison set determines whether you win. It's the highest-leverage thing a company can change without touching the product, and it's usually the reason a good product isn't selling.

It also cascades. Positioning drives pricing, the ICP, the roadmap, and who you hire. Getting it wrong misdirects all of them at once.

What it looks like in practice

The components are the competitive alternative you're replacing, the capability you have that it doesn't, the value that produces, and the customer who cares most about that value. Those four settle almost every other marketing question.

Good positioning usually feels narrower than founders want. Narrowing is what makes it work — a product positioned for everyone is compared against everything.

Where it goes wrong

  • Positioning against the largest market instead of the one you can win.
  • Confusing it with messaging. Positioning is the strategy; messaging is the words.
  • Positioning on features rather than on the alternative you replace.
  • Changing it every quarter, so the market never learns what you are.

Where the term comes from

Al Ries and Jack Trout's Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind (1981) established the core idea — that positioning happens in the customer's mind, not in the product. April Dunford's Obviously Awesome (2019) is the modern practitioner's version, and the one most B2B founders actually use.

What makes it defensible

Messaging vs. positioning#

Positioning is the strategic decision about what you are and who you're for. Messaging is the words you use to say it.

Picture this: the positioning is "the reporting layer for mid-size Shopify stores." The messaging is the headline, the cold email, and the first line of the demo. Change the words weekly if you like — changing the position weekly means nobody knows what you sell.

Why it matters

Teams try to fix a positioning problem with better copy, and it never works. If a product is positioned against the wrong alternative, no headline rescues it — the buyer is still comparing you to something you lose against.

The diagnostic value is in the order: get positioning right first, then messaging is mostly execution. Do it backwards and you rewrite the website every quarter without improving conversion.

What it looks like in practice

One positioning statement should generate many pieces of messaging — a homepage headline, an outbound email, a conference talk, the first slide of a deck — all pointing at the same claim in different registers.

If the messages contradict each other, that's usually a positioning problem showing through rather than a copywriting one.

Where it goes wrong

  • Rewriting the website when the actual problem is who you're selling to.
  • Having positioning that only lives in one person's head, so messaging drifts.
  • Testing headlines without a stable position underneath them.
  • Treating positioning as a marketing deliverable rather than a company decision.

What makes it defensible

Tagline vs. value proposition#

A tagline is short and memorable. A value proposition explains what you do and why it's worth it. Confusing them costs you the buyer's first ten seconds.

Picture this: "Work, simplified." tells a visitor nothing. "Cut month-end close from nine days to two" tells them whether to keep reading. One is a mood; the other is a claim.

Why it matters

Early-stage companies have no brand equity, and taglines only work when the reader already knows who you are. A famous company can afford three abstract words. A company nobody has heard of has one sentence to explain itself before the tab closes.

It's a small thing that reveals a bigger one — a founder who leads with a mood usually hasn't decided what the specific claim is.

What it looks like in practice

The value proposition should name the outcome, ideally with a number, and be specific enough that a competitor couldn't put it on their own homepage. If it works equally well for three other companies, it isn't saying anything.

The tagline can come later, once enough people know the company that a short phrase has something to attach to.

Where it goes wrong

  • Leading with an abstract tagline before anyone knows what you sell.
  • Writing a value proposition that describes the product rather than the outcome.
  • Using industry language the buyer doesn't actually use.
  • Trying to cover every use case in one sentence, which produces a sentence about nothing.

Building the thing

The product side of judgment — what got built, how the team decides what to build next, and which numbers tell you whether it is working.

Building the thing

Minimum viable product (MVP)#

The smallest thing you can build that produces a real answer to the riskiest question you have.

Picture this: the MVP for a marketplace was a spreadsheet and two founders manually matching people over WhatsApp. It answered the only question that mattered — will both sides show up — without a line of product code.

Why it matters

The point is learning speed, not thrift. An MVP that takes nine months isn't minimum, and an MVP that can't produce a clear yes or no isn't viable. Both failures are common, and the second is more expensive because it feels like progress.

Framing it as "smallest testable version of the riskiest assumption" fixes most of the confusion. Different companies have different riskiest assumptions, so their MVPs look nothing alike.

What it looks like in practice

Start by naming the assumption that would kill the company if wrong, then build only what tests it. If the risk is whether people want it, a landing page and a waitlist might do. If the risk is whether it's technically possible, you have to build the hard part first.

Concierge and Wizard-of-Oz versions — humans doing manually what software will eventually do — are usually the fastest route to a real answer, and they produce better information than a prototype because someone is actually being served.

Where it goes wrong

  • Building a small version of the full product instead of a test of the main risk.
  • Making it so minimal that a bad result tells you nothing about the real idea.
  • Shipping an MVP with no defined question, so the result gets interpreted to taste.
  • Treating the MVP as v1 of the codebase rather than something you expect to throw away.

Where the term comes from

The term predates Lean Startup — Frank Robinson coined it around 2001 — but Eric Ries popularised it in The Lean Startup (2011) as the version of a product that enables a full turn of the build-measure-learn loop with the least effort.

Building the thing

Prototype vs. MVP#

A prototype demonstrates an idea to people. An MVP is used by real customers to do real work.

Picture this: the Figma flow that gets nods in a meeting is a prototype. The rough version that a clinic used to process actual claims last Tuesday is an MVP. Only one of them generated evidence.

Why it matters

The difference is whether anything is at stake for the user. Prototypes collect opinions; MVPs collect behaviour. Opinions are systematically generous and behaviour isn't, which is why an enthusiastic prototype review and a dead MVP are a common sequence.

For an investor it's a diligence distinction worth making explicit. "We have a working product" can mean either, and the two are very different stages of evidence.

What it looks like in practice

Prototypes are the right tool for narrow questions — is this flow comprehensible, does this concept land, can we get alignment internally. They're fast, cheap, and honest about what they are.

The mistake is stopping there. A prototype that tests well tells you the idea is communicable, not that it's wanted. Only usage under real conditions, with real consequences, tells you that.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating positive prototype feedback as validation.
  • Describing a prototype as a product in a deck or a data room.
  • Building a polished prototype when a rough working version would have answered more.
  • Skipping the prototype entirely and building the wrong thing beautifully.

Building the thing

Activation#

The moment a new user first gets real value — and the share of signups who reach it.

Picture this: for a document tool, activation might be "invited a teammate and edited a real file within seven days." Users who cross that line retain at 60%. Those who don't, retain at 4%.

Why it matters

Activation is the highest-leverage number in most product-led businesses, because it sits between acquisition and everything downstream. Doubling signups with a broken activation step doubles the number of people who leave.

It's also the number founders skip. Signups are easy to count and feel like progress; activation requires deciding what value actually means, which is a harder and more revealing question.

What it looks like in practice

Defining it means finding the behaviour that separates users who stay from users who leave — usually an action plus a timeframe. The classic examples are famous for a reason: the specific number matters less than having one at all.

Once defined, the work is removing everything between signup and that moment. Most activation gains come from deleting steps rather than adding onboarding.

Where it goes wrong

  • Defining activation as account creation, which measures nothing.
  • Picking a metric that correlates with retention without asking whether it causes it.
  • Optimising signups while activation is broken.
  • Adding an onboarding tour instead of removing the friction the tour explains.

Related terms

The least gameable number a young company has.

Building the thing

Feature prioritization#

Deciding what to build next, and — more importantly — what not to build.

Picture this: the roadmap has forty items. Engineering capacity is four per quarter. The decision isn't which four are good ideas; thirty of them are good ideas. It's which four move the one number that matters.

Why it matters

At pre-seed the constraint isn't ideas, it's time, and every wrong build is a month the company doesn't get back. Prioritisation is where a small team either compounds or diffuses.

It's also where founder discipline shows. Building what the loudest customer asked for is the path of least resistance, and it reliably produces a product that serves one account well and the market badly.

What it looks like in practice

Most frameworks — RICE, ICE, value versus effort — do the same job: force an explicit comparison instead of an implicit one. The framework matters less than having any stated basis, because the alternative is deciding by whoever asked most recently.

The underlying question is which assumption you're testing. Early on, prioritising by learning value beats prioritising by revenue, because the revenue estimates are guesses anyway.

Where it goes wrong

  • Building whatever the largest customer asked for, and becoming a consultancy.
  • Prioritising by effort alone, so easy things get built and hard important things never do.
  • Maintaining a backlog nobody ever deletes from, which makes it a graveyard rather than a plan.
  • Confusing a prioritisation framework with a decision. The numbers are inputs.
