Building the thing

Product roadmap vs. backlog#

A roadmap is the sequence of outcomes you're pursuing. A backlog is the list of specific work items waiting to be done.

Picture this: the roadmap says "cut time-to-first-value below ten minutes this quarter." The backlog holds the forty tickets that might contribute. Showing a customer the backlog is how you accidentally make forty promises.

Why it matters

Conflating them is how roadmaps become commitment lists, and commitment lists are how product teams lose the ability to change their minds. A roadmap of outcomes can survive new information; a roadmap of features can only be broken.

It also affects what you can show people. Outcomes can be shared with customers and investors safely. A dated feature list shared externally becomes a contract nobody agreed to.

What it looks like in practice

A useful roadmap has themes and rough time horizons — now, next, later — with confidence decreasing as it goes out. The backlog underneath it is where implementation detail lives, and it should be pruned aggressively rather than accumulated.

The honest version admits that the far end is a guess. A roadmap with the same precision at eighteen months as at six weeks is fiction in both places.

Where it goes wrong

  • Publishing a dated feature roadmap externally.
  • Letting the backlog grow forever, so nobody can find anything in it.
  • Writing the roadmap as features, which makes every change look like a failure.
  • Treating the roadmap as fixed for the year when the company is still finding fit.

Building the thing

Technical debt#

The future cost of a shortcut taken now — code that works today and makes tomorrow slower.

Picture this: hardcoding one customer's business rules ships the deal in a week. Two years and eleven customers later, every new rule takes four days and touches nine files.

Why it matters

Some technical debt is correct. A pre-seed company that builds for a scale it may never reach has optimised for the wrong risk — most startups die from not finding customers, not from bad architecture.

The failure is not taking on debt, it's taking it on unconsciously and never paying any of it down. Debt taken deliberately with a repayment plan is leverage. Debt accumulated by accident is how a team's velocity halves without anyone deciding it should.

What it looks like in practice

The signal that it's gone too far is velocity: features that used to take days taking weeks, bugs reappearing, engineers routing around parts of the system. That's the point where paying down is cheaper than continuing.

In diligence it shows up as a question about what would break at 10x. A CTO who can name the three things they'd have to rebuild has a real picture. One who says the architecture scales fine usually hasn't looked.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating all technical debt as bad, and over-engineering a product that hasn't found fit.
  • Taking on debt without recording it, so nobody knows where the landmines are.
  • Rewriting from scratch instead of paying down incrementally.
  • Letting debt accumulate until velocity collapses, then trying to explain the slowdown to a board.

Where the term comes from

Ward Cunningham coined the metaphor in 1992, and later stressed the part people drop: the debt is worth taking as long as you pay it back. The borrowing was never the problem.

Building the thing

Net Promoter Score (NPS)#

One question — how likely are you to recommend this — scored 0–10, with promoters minus detractors giving a number from -100 to +100.

Picture this: 40% score 9–10, 20% score 0–6. NPS is +20. It's a fine trend line and a terrible decision-making tool on its own.

Why it matters

NPS is widely used because it's cheap and comparable, and widely over-trusted for the same reasons. It measures stated sentiment, not behaviour, and stated sentiment and renewal behaviour diverge more than people expect.

For an early company it's usually the wrong thing to optimise. Retention and usage tell you what NPS is trying to approximate, more accurately and without asking anyone.

What it looks like in practice

The value is almost entirely in the free-text follow-up, not the number. "Why did you pick that score?" produces the actionable material; the score itself just sorts whose answer to read first.

Sample bias is the standard trap: the people who respond are the ones with strong feelings, and a 6% response rate makes the resulting number close to meaningless across periods.

Where it goes wrong

  • Treating NPS as a growth metric. It's a sentiment survey.
  • Comparing your score to a cross-industry benchmark. The distributions aren't comparable.
  • Surveying at moments of peak satisfaction and reporting the result as typical.
  • Reading the number and skipping the comments, which is the only part that tells you what to do.

Building the thing

OKRs#

A goal-setting structure: an ambitious Objective, with a few measurable Key Results that say what would have to be true to hit it.

Picture this: Objective: make onboarding effortless. Key results: activation from 22% to 45%, time-to-first- value under ten minutes, support tickets per new account down by half. Not a task list — a set of outcomes.

Why it matters

OKRs matter at the point where a company gets big enough that not everyone is in the same conversation. Before that they're usually overhead — a five-person team that needs OKRs to know what matters has a different problem.

The value is in what they exclude. Three objectives means everything else is explicitly not this quarter, and that clarity is the whole benefit.

What it looks like in practice

Key results have to be outcomes rather than activities. "Ship the new onboarding" is a task and you can complete it while the metric gets worse. "Activation to 45%" is a result and you can't fake it.

Google's convention of treating 70% attainment as success exists to keep objectives ambitious. Teams that hit 100% consistently have learned to sandbag, which quietly defeats the point.

Where it goes wrong

  • Writing key results that are tasks in disguise.
  • Setting fifteen of them, which is a to-do list with a framework's name.
  • Tying OKRs directly to compensation, which guarantees conservative targets.
  • Introducing them at five people, where the overhead exceeds the clarity.

Where the term comes from

Andy Grove developed the practice at Intel in the 1970s, out of Peter Drucker's management by objectives. John Doerr brought it to Google in 1999 and later wrote Measure What Matters about it.
